About this module. Figures from GA p.4-19 and Glossography p.3.

This add-on can be switched on or off in Manage Modules. It needs 1e FRPG (Table Edition) 0.32.0 or later. Characters keep their data either way; with the module off, the deity cleric classes show as unknown keys until it is switched back on.

What the Module Adds

  • Deity clerics: one cleric class for each Greyhawk Adventures deity (Boccob, Celestian, St. Cuthbert, Ehlonna, Fharlanghn, Incabulos, Istus, Iuz, Nerull, Pholtus, Ralishaz, Ulaa), built on the PHB cleric: same hit dice, attacks, saves, spells and turning, with the deity's extra experience cost applied to the level table (Boccob's +5% from 11th level only). A note on the sheet warns when the character's alignment does not fit the deity's clerics.
  • Deity clerics only (a world setting, off by default) removes the plain PHB cleric from the class list.
  • Greyhawk tab on a deity cleric's character sheet: the deity, the clerics' alignment, raiment, weapons, spheres and additional spells, the granted powers by level (later ones in grey), and the worked-out figures: Fharlanghn's chance to avoid getting lost, Incabulos' disease immunity and hypnotism level, Ulaa's chosen foe and damage bonus, Pholtus' rank, Boccob's scrying devices, St. Cuthbert's order, Ehlonna's plant ward, and a roll for the level of Ralishaz's sleep gaze.
  • Greyhawk Weather macro: rolls a day's weather from the Glossography tables (see The World: Rolling the Weather).
  • Compendia: these journals, rewritten in plain words from the three books and arranged by topic; 118 spells (the deities' 12 cleric spells and the wizards' 106); 97 magic items; 13 monsters and 11 avatars; the 14 personalities of the Hall of Heroes as NPCs; 123 roll tables (encounters by region and terrain, birthplaces, and 16 weather tables); the weather macro; and two map scenes of the Flanaess.

What Is Not Automated, and Why

  • Spheres: GA gives them for an optional rule of the second edition game (GA p.5). They are shown, not used to limit the spell list. The additional spells are in the spell compendium; drag the ones a cleric may use onto the sheet.
  • Granted powers are listed with their uses; daily uses are tracked by hand.
  • Personalities: their armor class, THAC0 and damage are given in their biographies as printed. The sheet works out its own from class, abilities and equipment, so set armor and magic items to match.
  • Map scenes are the 1983 poster sheets as images, without a grid. Each hex is 10 leagues (30 miles) across (Glossography p.3).

About the Text

The journals are a plain-words rewrite of the Guide, the Glossography and Greyhawk Adventures, arranged by topic. Each page begins with the book pages it draws on. Statistics, dice and other figures are given as printed; where the book has an apparent misprint it is marked ("printed X"), and where the books disagree the page says so. The source text was read from scans and checked against the page images; every number used by the sheet and the compendia was checked against the page images.

Sources: Glossography p.2 (Foreword); GA p.2 (Introduction). Rewritten in plain words.

This module draws on three books: the Guide to the World of Greyhawk and its companion Glossography (the 1983 boxed setting), and Greyhawk Adventures (GA, 1988). Their material is arranged here by topic rather than by book; each page names the pages it comes from.

The Guide and the Glossography

The Glossography's foreword presents the two books as relics from the world itself, and tells their story this way.

The Savant-Sage lived in the city of Greyhawk during Oerth's Epoch of Magic. There is evidence that this was not the first age of Oerth's history, but nothing shows how many ages came before it or have passed between it and now. Late in that age the Sage compiled his Catalogue of the Land Flanaess, being the Eastern Portion of the Continent Oerik, of Oerth, a work in seven volumes. Only the third survives, A Guide to the World of Greyhawk. What the other six covered is unknown, but the whole is thought to have dealt with nearly every side of life in the Flanaess.

The Sage's work was little read in his lifetime and vanished entirely after his death. Several centuries later a copy turned up in an ilithid's lair in the Riftcanyon. It made its way to the Royal University at Rel Mord, where the scholar and historian Pluffet Smedger the Elder studied it. Though by then centuries out of date, it struck him as fresh and thorough. Smedger spent decades writing glossographies for each volume, adding facts the Sage had missed or that were too recent for him to include. Once finished, the encyclopedia became a standard reference in universities and libraries across the civilized Flanaess.

To help him study the Sage's books, Smedger devised mathematical models, or games, that he used with his students to recreate and examine the history and politics the Sage described. In Smedger's day magic was not lost, but it was apparently fading. Only the third volume (almost certainly an incomplete copy) and Smedger's Glossography for it survive, and how they came to light here and now is, and will probably stay, a mystery. Smedger's game was quite different from the AD&D game, but his treatment of magic and combat has been roughly translated into AD&D terms.

The foreword ends by handing the world to the DM: shape new states from old ones, turn old rivalries into open war, and fit the world to the needs of the players. The editor credited is Steve Winter, with Allen Hammack as product planning manager.

Greyhawk Adventures

James M. Ward's introduction (dated July 4, 1988) opens with a warning that the book is meant for experienced players, not newcomers. When the AD&D game first came out, the Greyhawk campaign had already been running for several years, and every section of GA answers a direct request from its players for more about some part of Oerth. Readers new to Greyhawk are told to start with TSR's earlier Greyhawk material. Ward expects not to please everyone and admits he will be asked for the rest of his life why there is no section on government or a longer one on spells; he tried to give a cross section of what people asked for.

The book's sections, as Ward lists them:

  • Deities: the main gods and goddesses who affect PCs and NPCs, with the idea of avatars presented for the first time and more on playing clerics. (Here: Deities.)
  • Monsters: creatures unique to Oerth, from steaming jungle to dry desert, which can also fit any other campaign. (Here: the monster compendium.)
  • Heroes: powerful and important non-player characters, good and bad, with strengths and weaknesses as springboards for adventures. (Here: Heroes and Personages, and the NPC compendium.)
  • Spells: the spells of the campaign's greatest spellcasters, so characters can cast the spells of Drawmij, Rary and others. (Here: the spell compendium.)
  • Magic Items: items unique to Oerth, including coins, caps, eyepatches, lockets and turbans as well as the usual rings and wands. (Here: the magic item compendium.)
  • Geography: some of Oerth's famous sights, sites of past and future adventures. (Here: Geography.)
  • Adventures: short adventures, which Ward calls a new idea for TSR hardbacks, to be kept or dropped depending on what readers thought. (Here: Adventures.)
  • Zero-Level Characters: an appendix for playing characters who are not yet 1st level. (Here: Zero-Level Characters.)

Ward thanks the many designers and editors who worked on the book, calling it more of a group effort than any recent TSR project, and says it was shaped more than any other AD&D book by players' letters, questions and comments. Credits: design and organization, James M. Ward; design, Daniel Salas, Skip Williams, Nigel D. Findley, Thomas Kane, Stephen Innis, Len Carpenter and Eric Oppen; editing and coordination, Warren Spector; special developmental work, Jon Pickens; cover art, Jeff Easley.

Sources: Guide p.4-5; Glossography p.18-19. Rewritten in plain words.

The World

Oerth has four large continents, four oceans, and a great many smaller seas and islands. The largest continent, Oerik, is treated as the heart of the world, and its eastern part, the Flanaess, is where the civilized human lands lie. The scholars of the Flanaess know little about western Oerik and even less about the peoples of the other continents, and they tend to dismiss those places as unimportant.

Measured around the poles, Oerth is 8,400 leagues (25,200 miles) in circumference. Moving 23 leagues (70 miles, or 2 1/3 map hexes) due north or south shifts a traveler one degree of latitude. The weather rules use this to adjust temperature by latitude; see the Weather entry.

The Sun and the Stars

Flanaess scholars give the sky far more attention than distant lands, because astrology is held in high regard. The sun circles Oerth once every 364 days and passes through the twelve Lairs of the Zodiac in a fixed order. Five wandering stars move among the Lairs, and their positions are said to shape the meaning of any omen. Two works are recommended to anyone wanting the full art: Secrets of Ye Skye Revealed by Selvor the Elder, and Astrology, Divinity, and Mankind by Yestro Bilnigd.

The Two Moons

Luna, the Great Moon (also called the Mistress), runs through a 28-day cycle of phases. The months are built on that cycle, and Luna completes thirteen cycles in a year.

Celene, the Handmaiden, is a small aquamarine moon. It is full only four times a year, on the middle night of each of the four festivals, and the festivals are timed by it.

The two cycles line up so that both moons are full together on Midsummer's Night, during Richfest. On Midwinter's Night only Celene shows; many superstitious peasants call that time the Dark Time or the Dim Nights. A night when both moons are full is believed to bring events of great importance, depending on where the wandering stars stand. The exact phase dates for both moons are in the Weather entry.

Moons and Lycanthropes

Most lycanthropes change with Luna alone. One in ten follows Celene instead, and another one in ten is triggered by either moon. When both moons are full, every lycanthrope is out hunting. That happens on Midsummer's Night, which is bad luck for druids out gathering mistletoe for the coming year.

Sunrise, Sunset and Time

The Baseline Data Chart (Weather entry) gives sunrise and sunset in the middle of each month at 40 degrees north. For each degree of latitude north of 40, add two minutes to the listed times; for each degree south of 40, subtract two minutes. These are the moments the sun crosses the horizon, not the limits of usable light; a deep valley has less useful daylight, and a mountaintop has more.

Along any one line of latitude the sun rises at the same local time everywhere. Time zones only matter on very long east-west journeys; each degree of longitude moves sunrise and sunset by four minutes.

Beyond 60 degrees of latitude the midnight sun appears. Around midsummer the sun never sets far enough for full darkness, and around midwinter there can be days with no sunrise at all. At exactly 60 degrees this happens only on Midsummer Day (no sunset) and Midwinter Day (no sunrise). Each degree past 60 toward a pole adds two more such days, one before and one after the midpoint.

Sources: Guide p.5; Glossography p.19. Rewritten in plain words.

The Year

The year is 364 days long: twelve months of 28 days (the Dozenmonth of the moon) and four festivals of seven days. Each festival falls before a group of three months. Elves and the nomads of the plains use their own names for the months, shown beside the common names.

Sources: Guide p.5; Glossography p.19, 21. Rewritten in plain words.

Climate

The Flanaess has a kind climate. Outside the far north, winter temperatures rarely fall below freezing except during the two winter months, and at night in early spring and late autumn. In the coldest part of winter a few days reach 0 degrees Fahrenheit before things slowly warm again.

The northeast and the central north are much colder, because the seas there make winter last about twice as long. The Dramidj Ocean is the big exception: its warm currents soften the climate of the lands along its shores, making them feel like lands several degrees of latitude further south.

Spring and autumn are usually long. In the central lands of Oerik, summer lasts five months or more. Most of the Flanaess gets enough rain for good harvests.

Prevailing Winds

In autumn and winter the wind usually blows from the north and northeast. The rest of the year it comes from the east and southeast. Mountain ranges and other features can bend these winds locally.

Defining the Seasons

Where a region's seasons need to be worked out, use its average base temperature:

  • Winter: the average is 32 degrees F or lower.
  • Spring: the average climbs from 32 to 50 degrees.
  • Summer: the average climbs above 50 degrees, then drops back to 60.
  • Autumn: the average drops from 60 to 32 degrees.

Where summer is long, its first half (temperatures still rising) is Low Summer and its second half (temperatures falling) is High Summer. Where winter is long, its first half is Early Winter and its second half is Late Winter, also called Bitter Winter. Elves and barbarians have their own names for these periods.

Magic and the Weather

Magic plays a part in Oerth's weather and may even be one of its causes. Some weather spells and items appear in the PHB and DMG, and powerful magic-users may research new ones. Such magic should be used with care: changing the weather in one place can have effects elsewhere in the world, and possibly on other planes too.

Sylvan forests, under the influence of Faerie, should stay mild with little precipitation all year.

Source: Guide p.6-7. Rewritten in plain words.

Unusual Trees

Bronzewood. Thin when young, it fills out only after decades of growth. A typical tree is 40 feet tall, with branches rising at about 45 degrees from the trunk, hard reddish-brown bark, and narrow toothed leaves eight to ten inches long. The wood is heavy and hard enough that only skilled workers can shape it. Seasoned and dried with care, its outer layer becomes nearly as hard as metal without getting any heavier.

Deklo. A huge hardwood, often 15 feet thick and over 100 feet tall. Its stout branches grow almost straight up beside the trunk. The leaves are close to round and grow in dense clusters, reaching more than a foot across on an old tree. Deklos grow in groves that crowd out other plants.

Galda. A fruit tree about 30 feet tall, with yellowish bark and yellow-green leaves. In early spring it sets pale, cone-shaped fruit that ripens by early summer, streaked with gold. The fruit tastes a little sharp and salty, but it is refreshing and nourishing; its many seeds are rich in protein.

Kara. A rough-barked fruit tree 40 feet or taller. Its branches and leaves ooze a resin that makes skin itch. It bears all summer long. The fruit is light brown, about the size of a fist and oddly square; yellow spots mark new fruit, and red shows that it is fully ripe. Unripe karafruit tastes foul and causes bad cramps. Ripe, it is chewy and mildly sweet, and many people rely on it as a staple food.

Hornwood. A handsome hardwood about the size and shape of a small elm, with very straight black trunk and branches and long pointed leaves shaped like a broad spearhead. Treated and seasoned, the wood becomes unusually strong and springy. Hornwood weapons, bows above all, are highly prized.

Ipp. One of the largest trees known, usually 60 feet or more with a thick trunk, greenish bark and big emerald leaves shaped like hands. The ipt, a related kind, grows even larger and is a favorite of sylvan elves. Ipps live for centuries and are rarely troubled by insects or disease.

Phost. Much like an oak, but with shaggy bark and leaves twice as wide as they are long. About a year after it dies, phost wood begins to glow softly, enough to light a 5-foot radius around a branch or a rotting trunk. Rough handling or damp speeds the rot, and the wood crumbles away within a few months.

Roanwood. Similar to a sequoia, but a hardwood, with far larger branches that start lower (around 30 feet up). Its bark is speckled gray and red-brown, which gives it its name. Trees over 150 feet tall have been found. The leaves are fan-shaped and about a foot long. The grain makes it ideal for fine furniture, interior work and carving. Where hardness and strength matter, people usually use hickory, bronzewood, oak or similar woods instead.

Sablewood. A short, thick-trunked evergreen of the north. Its branches make excellent arrow shafts. Trees cut in the cold months have the finest grain, and oiling the wood turns it a glossy black.

Usk. A tall, very thick hardwood, shaped like a maple, usually 8 to 9 feet across and 50 to 60 feet high. Its huge oblong leaves are tough and bendable and have many uses. The fruit, which nearly every creature loves, appears in early summer and lasts until frost. It is pale blue with three or four lobes; ripe, it turns bright blue, smells sweet, and is about as big as a large grapefruit.

Yarpick (daggerthorn). A short, sturdy tree with low spreading branches and broad fringed leaves. Its trunk carries very sharp thorns about six inches long, and the thorns on the larger branches can top two feet, as thick as a finger at the base. The thorns are straight and tough and have been used as weapons or parts of weapons. The small fruit is useless, but the seed inside is good eating when cracked like a nut. Cultivated yarpick "nuts" grow as large as plums and are very nourishing; they are eaten roasted or ground into meal.

Source: Glossography p.18-19. Prose rewritten in plain words; table figures as printed.

In Foundry: the Greyhawk Weather macro (Greyhawk Macros compendium) runs every step below for one to fourteen days and whispers the report to the GM. It asks for the month, latitude, terrain, elevation and sea current, and remembers your last choices. The single tables are also in the Greyhawk Tables compendium, Weather folder. Where the book leaves it open, the macro checks a precipitation type's minimum temperature against the day's high and its maximum against the day's low.

The system works best when the DM rolls the weather a week or two ahead of play. That makes it easy to match the weather to the calendar and to what the party is doing. The exception is a long journey through many kinds of terrain, where the DM cannot tell in advance exactly where the party will be.

Step 1: Temperature

Look up the month's base temperature on the Baseline Data Chart and roll the listed dice for the day's high and low adjustments. Then adjust both figures for terrain and for latitude: add 2 degrees F for every 2 1/3 hexes south of the 40th parallel, and subtract 2 degrees for every 2 1/3 hexes north of it.

The day's high comes about an hour after midday, and the low about an hour before sunrise.

Record Highs and Lows (optional)

To allow unusual heat and cold, roll percentile dice before you look up the base temperature:

d100Result
01Extreme record low
02Severe record low
03-04Record low
05-96Normal temperatures
97-98Record high
99Severe record high
00Extreme record high

For a record high or low, shift the month's base temperature by the largest high or low adjustment the month allows. For a severe record, shift it by twice that amount; for an extreme record, by three times. On each day of the spell, apply the day's high and low rolls and all other adjustments to this new base.

A record spell usually lasts for several days. Roll d20:

d20Duration
011 day
02-032 days
04-103 days
11-144 days
15-175 days
18-196 days
207 days

Step 2: Sky

Roll percentile dice on the Baseline Data Chart to see whether the day is clear, partly cloudy or cloudy.

Step 3: Precipitation

Roll percentile dice against the month's chance of precipitation on the Baseline Data Chart, adjusted for terrain by the Terrain Effects Table.

No precipitation: roll d20 and subtract 1 for the wind speed in miles per hour, then adjust it for terrain. Apply wind chill if needed.

Precipitation: roll percentile dice on the Precipitation Occurrence Table for the kind. On a 00, roll percentile dice on the Terrain Effects Table for a Special Weather Phenomenon, which depends on the terrain. If you like, you can then repeat this step to see whether ordinary precipitation comes along with the special weather.

Some kinds of precipitation need a minimum or maximum temperature, as the Precipitation Occurrence Table shows. If the day does not meet the condition, either roll again or cancel the precipitation.

Step 4: Effects and Duration

Look up the precipitation on the Standard Weather Table or the Special Weather Phenomena Table (Weather Effects page) for its effect on wind, movement, vision and so on, and for how long it lasts. When that time runs out, roll percentile dice. If the roll is at or below the chance of continuing, the precipitation goes on in some form; roll d10 to see whether it changes:

d10Result
1Up one line on Precipitation Occurrence Table
2-9No change; roll for duration of continuation
10Down one line on Precipitation Occurrence Table

Step 5: Wind Chill

Whenever the temperature is below 35 degrees F, use the Wind Chill Table to find the temperature the characters actually feel. The Climatic Extremes page covers other effects of severe cold.

Step 6: Rainbows

When precipitation stops, check the Precipitation Occurrence Table for the chance of a rainbow.

Step 7: Direction

When you need to know where something is (a volcano, say), roll d8 for one of the eight compass points:

d8Direction
1North
2Northeast
3East
4Southeast
5South
6Southwest
7West
8Northwest

Step 8: Wind Direction

As a rule, winds over the Flanaess blow from the north and northeast in autumn and winter, and from the east and southeast the rest of the year. Mountains and other features can change this locally.

Step 9: High Winds

Strong winds can do harm much like the druid spell control winds. The High Wind Effects Table lists more of what fierce winds do.

Worked Example

A party is camped 3,000 feet up in the Yecha Hills, at 48 degrees north, in the month of Patchwall. The base temperature is 57. The DM rolls d10 twice, getting 5 and 3, so the day's high is 65 and the low is 49. Latitude (8 degrees north of the baseline) takes 16 degrees off each, and the elevation takes off 9 more, for a high of 40 and a low of 24.

A roll of 48 gives partly cloudy skies, and a roll of 23 means precipitation. The first roll on the Precipitation Occurrence Table is a monsoon, which is thrown out because the day never reaches the 50 degrees a monsoon needs. The second roll gives heavy fog.

The Standard Weather Table and further rolls show the fog lasting eight hours, with 12 mph winds. While it lasts, vision drops to 2 feet, movement is one-quarter speed, rangers cannot track, and a travelling party is 50% more likely to get lost.

When the fog's time is up, the DM rolls 33, so the precipitation continues. A d10 roll of 10 moves it down one line: the heavy fog thins to light fog, and the DM rolls its duration and effects.

Finally, the DM sees that the temperature will drop well below 35 by late afternoon. The Wind Chill Table shows that an afternoon temperature of 30 will feel like 12 degrees, and the night will likely be worse.

These are suggestions for what extreme heat and cold can do to a party. They are not a complete list.

Cold

In cold places, always use the Wind Chill Table to find the real temperature.

Heavy cold-weather clothing gets in the way. A suggested penalty is -1 to dexterity, armor class and to-hit rolls for every 10 degrees below 0 degrees F.

Heat from spells or magic items can change the land around it. After a fireball, snow melts and refreezes as slick ice; strong heat cracks ice floes apart; in the mountains it can set off a snow or rock avalanche.

Deep cold affects gear. Oil may stop flowing. Liquids can freeze and burst their containers. A potion left in extreme cold may lose its power or change.

Remember the cold when describing animals, pets, familiars and summoned monsters travelling with the party. Creatures from the Elemental Plane of Fire are furious at being called into a cold land: double their chance of rebelling when summoned. Extra food is often needed in the cold.

Drinking something hot at temperatures below -20 degrees F may crack the drinker's teeth from the sudden change.

At -40 degrees F and colder, frostbite destroys an exposed body part in 10-30 minutes. A part lost to frostbite can only be restored by regeneration, such as the cleric spell regenerate or a ring of regeneration. Frostbite is most likely when:

  • clothing is tight;
  • hands, feet, ears and other extremities are kept still;
  • the character has a long-term disease of the blood vessels;
  • the air is both cold and damp.

The DM decides whether spells with somatic components can be cast in gloves and heavy clothing. One option is a chance of spell failure tied to the temperature, such as 5% for every 10 degrees below -20 degrees F.

On a sunny day in snow, each character has a 2% chance per hour, adding up through the day, of going snowblind for d4 turns. This works like a light spell cast on the character's face. Monsters native to snowy lands are immune.

In hot lands most mammals need extra salt to replace what they sweat away. Extreme heat affects gear and animals about as much as extreme cold does, sometimes in the opposite way. Very high heat can make things burst into flame by themselves, especially very flammable items such as oil in glass bottles left in the sun. Allow for evaporation, spoiling (wine turning to vinegar) and similar trouble. Creatures from the Elemental Plane of Water, or ones with cold-based attacks, deeply resent being brought into a hot land. Metal left in the hot sun soon becomes painful to touch.

Wildfires

When the temperature is above 75 degrees and there has been little or no precipitation, wildfires become possible. Within one hex of a coast or lake (not a river), wooded and farmed land has a 1% chance per day of catching fire, adding up day by day. Ordinary forest or grassland has 2% per day, rising to 3% per day within one hex of a desert. Lower the chance by 1% for each quarter inch of precipitation in the past week, and reset it to zero after any rainfall of more than two inches.

A forest or grass fire starts with a radius of a quarter mile, centered 1/3 to 4 miles from the party (roll d12 and divide by 3). With no wind it spreads slowly, growing another quarter mile in radius every six hours, and only fire breaks or rivers at least 180 feet wide stop it. With wind, it runs downwind faster: for every 5 mph of wind, take one hour off the time it needs to spread another quarter mile, and add 30 feet to the width of river or fire break needed to stop it. In a melee, treat the fire as moving 1" per round, plus 1" for each 5 mph of wind.

Fire can spread into any terrain except water and desert. Creatures living near a fire flee at full speed. With no wind they scatter along any path that avoids the flames; with wind, the fire may drive them ahead of it. They arrive d10 tenths of a mile ahead of the fire and always attack, without checking morale, anyone who gets in their way.

Sunburn

Sunburn can happen in any climate. It is most likely at high altitude and where sunlight reflects off ice, snow, sand or water.

The Migrations

Wandering bands began settling the Flanaess, the eastern part of Oerik, more than a thousand years ago. The first were the Flan: tough, able hunters, not especially warlike, living in small scattered groups that built no real civilization.

Then came the Suel, most of them fleeing the great wars of the Suloise Empire. They came north through the Kendeen (Harsh) Pass at the southern end of the Crystalmist Mountains, a range now called the Hellfurnaces, and spread in every direction. The fierce Oeridian tribes moved east at the same time, shoving Flan and Suel aside. The Oerids were fleeing the same wars. Both the Baklunish and the Suloise hired hordes of Euroz and other humanoids as mercenaries, and those hordes raided north and east, driving the Oerids ahead of them.

When the Invoked Devastation fell on the Baklunish, their own wizards answered with a final dreadful curse, the Rain of Colorless Fire, which turned the Suloise Empire into what is now the Sea of Dust. Enough Baklunish survived to hold the northern plains, keeping their small states against every attacker, including the humanoid peoples called Euroz, High Jebline, Jebli and Celbit.

Oerid and Suel

For two hundred years the Oerids and the Suel fought each other, and the breaking humanoid hordes, for the middle of the Flanaess, clashing with the Flan and the demi-humans along the way. In a few places the two peoples mixed. The main one is the Sheldomar Valley: apart from the Hold of the Sea Princes, the people of Keoland, the Gran March, the Ulek States and the small lands nearby are of mixed Oerid and Suel blood. Far to the north, four of the strongest and fiercest Suel clans kept large territories. Most of the Suel, though, were pushed into the far south: the Amedio Jungle, the Tilvanot Peninsula, the Duxchan Islands, and across the narrow Tilva Strait into Hepmonaland.

The Oerids came to rule so much of the Flanaess partly because they were friendly to the demi-human peoples already living there, the dwur, noniz, hobniz and olve. Their help made the Oerids much stronger. The Flan were also willing to join Oeridian armies. The Oerids' greatest advantage, though, was how vile most of the Suel were: they lied, stole, killed and took slaves whenever they wanted and could. There were exceptions, such as the Houses of Rhola and Neheli, late arrivals who settled and held the Sheldomar.

The Great Kingdom

The strongest Oeridian tribe, the Aerdi, settled the rich farmland east of the Nyr Dyv and founded the Kingdom of Aerdy. After some decades of growing wealth and power, Aerdy began a series of conquests. The greatest was its victory over the cavalry of Nyrond at the Battle of a Fortnight's Length, and from then on it was called the Great Kingdom. Its monarch ruled from the swamps of Sunndi in the south, west along the Telfic Gulf and the Sea of Yar to the Nyr Dyv, and north from there through the Shield Lands and past the Tenh. In time the Overking's authority stretched to Furyon and to Voll (now Veluna), and across the northern prairies to Perrenland. For three centuries the empire changed little in size. After the third Celestial House (dynasty), its borders began to shrink back toward the old lands of the Aerdi.

Nomad bands of mixed Oerid and Baklunish blood slowly moved into the steppes beyond the Yatil Mountains and claimed them, reaching as far east as the Griff Mountains. These wild horsemen inevitably skirmished with the nations to the south as they pushed into the Flanaess. The civilized states might have stopped them, but they were busy fighting the Aerdi for their freedom. One after another, in a string of small but bloody wars, the Perrenders, Velunans, Furyondians and the people of Tenh won their independence.

The Fall of the House of Rax

The ruling Aerdi dynasty, the House of Rax, was then split by a feud. Its junior branch, known as Nyrond, declared its lands free of the Overking. The senior branch, worn down by wars in the rebel provinces, could not stop it. The Overking still gathered a large army to crush the new kingdom, but just then a coalition of Fruztii, Schnai and hired barbarians raided the Great Kingdom's North Province in force. The Overking turned his army northeast and crushed the invaders, at great cost in men and supplies. By then the campaigning season was over. Nyrond used the time to raise troops and grow stronger, and the next year saw only skirmishes and feints. From then on Nyrond was its own kingdom, bitterly hostile to its eastern neighbor and ready to help any of its enemies.

This is when evil began to take hold among the rulers of the Great Kingdom. The House of Rax grew decadent, its policies weak and aimed at keeping the peace at any price. The great noble houses took the hint: they set themselves up as near-independent palatinates and ruled their fiefs like kingdoms.

The last heir of Rax was assassinated during the Turmoil Between Crowns. When the demon-worshipping House of Naelex took the Malachite Throne, the whole South Province refused to swear loyalty and joined the Iron League, alongside the Free City of Irongate, the Szek of Onnwal and the Lord of the Isles. The South Province strengthened the League's hand and let its members make a treaty of mutual defense with Nyrond, which still holds.

It is widely agreed that every Overking of the House of Naelax (spelled so here in the book) who has sat on the Malachite Throne since about 450 CY has been insane, possessed by demons, or both.

The Flanaess Today

Evil is on the rise everywhere, while the Great Kingdom gives itself over to debauchery. Vicious humanoid tribes have banded together to rule whole regions: the Bone March, Iuz (clearly led by humans) and the Pomarj. The Bandit Kingdoms keep growing stronger, and thieves, assassins and orders of evil clerics are taking over cities and states alike.

There is still hope. Nyrond has not fallen to evil, and Furyondy and Veluna in the middle of the Flanaess stand firmly for justice and good. The demi-humans have mostly kept out of human wars, but the founding of Celene and Ulek shows they will resist invasion by the humans of a state. When a realm turns oppressive or evil, demi-humans respond in one of two ways: they wall off their own lands and make them dangerous for intruders, or they move somewhere that suits them better. The many small states of the Flanaess, and the friendly humans in many of them, give them plenty of places to go. Large alliances of humans and demi-humans are no longer unthinkable.

The Battle of Emridy Meadows

This battle showed how much humans and demi-humans now have in common. Men-at-arms and cavalry from Furyondy and Veluna, dwarves from the Lortmils, gnomes from the Kron Hills, and an army of elven archers and spearmen fought side by side against a huge horde of evil men and humanoids, mostly orcs, gnolls and ogres. The armies met on the grassy fields south of the Velverdyva River, several leagues below the city of Verbobonc.

The allies had been closing on the evil creatures' stronghold, the great walled Temple of Elemental Evil near the unlucky village of Hommlet, when elven scouts reported a huge army coming up from the south. The Marshal of Furyondy, who led the allies, pulled back north to ground scouted earlier. Light cavalry screened the withdrawal, and there was no real fighting that day.

When the horde marched out at the next dawn, it found the allied army drawn up and waiting. The pikes of Furyondy and Veluna stood with their flank against the Velverdyva, the cavalry banners held the center, and dwarves and gnomes held the left, with small units of elven archers placed in the gaps. The humanoids threw themselves at the allied left, while the evil men rode against the center and right. The orcs, gnolls and ogres pushed back the dwarves and gnomes they hated and rushed on to surround the rest of the allied army. That was the trap. The whole allied line wheeled; squadrons of knights crashed into the rear of the charging horde, and squares of elves marched out of the Gnarley Forest on the left. Caught in a pocket with the bend of the river behind them and the allied army across the open side, the packed mass of evil men and humanoids fought on without hope.

After the slaughter, the allies laid siege to the Temple of Elemental Evil, which fell in two weeks. The demoness Zuggtmoy (also written Tsuggtmoy) was imprisoned in its ruins behind special wards to keep her from escaping. Only a few of the Temple's evil leaders got away, and they are suspected of the later kidnapping of the Prince of Furyondy, who has never been found.

The Lost Prince

The Prince mattered greatly to the cause of good. He was Marshal of Furyondy and Provost of Veluna, and he was engaged to Jolene, daughter of the Plar of Veluna. Their marriage would have joined the two states, with the Archcleric ruling in spiritual matters and the Prince, crowned King, ruling in worldly ones. Allied with the demi-humans, such a state would surely have made constant war on the evil nations, and its record of victories made that a grim prospect for its enemies.

His disappearance wrecked those plans and left the Flanaess in its present confusion. Humankind is split among realms that keep to themselves, nations that do not care, evil lands, and states striving for good. The Baklunish countries of the northwest have grown more powerful. Nomads, bandits and barbarians raid south every spring and summer. Humanoid strongholds are firmly established all across the continent, and wicked madness rules the Great Kingdom. No one can say how it will all end.

The Human Peoples

Few pure human strains are left in the Flanaess, except perhaps on its edges. The demi-human races have stayed fairly unmixed, but humans, as usual, have mingled freely in the central lands, and the resulting mixed type is now the norm.

Baklunish. Golden skin. Eyes usually gray-green or green; gray is uncommon and hazel rare. Hair from blue-black to dark brown. Ekbir, the Tiger Nomads, Ull and Zeif are the clearest examples of the pure Baklunish strain. The Wolf Nomads have married into the Rovers of the Barrens and show darker Flan blood. Ket is so mixed with Suel and Oeridian blood that it is the least typical Baklunish land: its people range from pale yellow or golden brown to tan, with almost any hair color except the lightest yellows and reds. The Paynim tribes and Tusmit also show some mixing.

Flan (Flannae). Bronze skin, from a light, almost copper shade to a very deep brown. Eyes, from most to least common: dark brown, black, brown, amber. Hair black, brown-black, dark brown or brown, and often wavy or curly. The people of the Duchy of Tenh are pure Flan and proud of their bronze color. Geoff and Sterich, though mixed, show strong Flan influence. The Rovers of the Barrens are the copper-toned kind of Flan, though their western tribes have the golden skin of the Baklunish from marrying into the Wolf Nomads. The Hold of Stone Fist is mostly a Flan and Suel mix, and the Theocracy of the Pale a Flan and Oeridian mix; the people of the Pale are notably good-looking.

Oeridians. Skin from tan to olive. Hair anywhere from honey blond to black, most often brown or reddish brown. Eye color varies a great deal, with brown and gray common. Whatever the Great Kingdom claims, unmixed Oeridians are most common in Furyondy, Perrenland and the Shield Lands, and in the east and south in North Province, Medegia, Onnwal and Sunndi.

Suel (Suloise). The fleeing Suel were scattered all over the Flanaess, so most of them mixed with other peoples. They are very fair-skinned, some nearly albino, with light red, yellow, blond or platinum hair that is often curly to tightly curled. Eyes run from pale blue or violet to deep blue, sometimes gray. The people of the Duchy of Urnst (printed "Ernst") are nearly pure Suel. The Frost, Ice and Snow Barbarians are completely unmixed, and the near-albino Snow Barbarians are the purest of all. The Suel are the main people of the islands off the east coast and of the Tilvanot Peninsula, where the Scarlet Brotherhood rules. Those who went into the Amedio Jungle and Hepmonaland have changed so much that they no longer look typical: they are tan to brown and heavily freckled.

Mixed Complexions and Attitudes

Flan ancestry mixed with Oeridian, Suel or both shows as a coppery or bronze tone. An Oeridian and Baklunish mix gives fairly light skin of a true yellow. A Baklunish and Flan mix gives a golden copper or golden bronze, perhaps the handsomest of all the mixed complexions.

For the most part, skin color matters little. The dark Flan complexion appears often in most nations. The nobles of the Great Kingdom, on the other hand, are proud of light skin, and the rulers of Tenh make far too much of the supposed superiority of their deep bronze. Across the middle of the Flanaess, from western Urnst to Geoff, people pay little attention to skin color or race, whether human or demi-human, and in some places even humanoid. The main exception is the demi-human kingdoms, Celene above all, where humans are thought inferior.

Dress

Oeridians like checks and plaids. The houses of Aerdy and Nyrond wear plaids, while southern and western Oeridians wear checks, often diamond-shaped or some other twist on the plain square. They favor tight trousers, close-fitting tops, and capes or cloaks.

Suel have long worn solid colors. Noble houses use two or more colors, so clothing split into blocks of color is common. They also like to wear emblems or badges in a color that contrasts with the main one. Their original dress was loose pantaloons and a baggy blouse, since changed to suit each climate: northern Suel barbarians wear furs and hides, and the southernmost Suel wear a vest-like top in place of the blouse.

Flan once painted their bodies in bright colors, yellow ochre and vermilion above all. The Rovers of the Barrens still paint whatever their high boots, loincloths and leather chest and arm pieces leave bare. More civilized Flan dress in the local fashion, but in solid primary colors, mostly very bright ones.

Baklunish dress in two styles. The northern branch likes bright patterns and loud colors: gowns and robes, or short breeches with flowing coats. Even the poor wear loud prints, usually a one-piece coverall with whatever else they can add. The southern branch likes split colors in softer pastel shades. Their festival dress is elaborate, full of puffs and slashes. Traveling or at war, they wear rough hide and cloth, with shields and banners in clan colors.

Dwarves love browns, reds and grays set off with one bright splash of color and as much precious metal as they can carry. They favor leather, and wool is popular too. Their clothing is cut much like the Oeridians'.

Elves. Sylvan elves dress much like the Suel, but in pale greens, fawn, ecru and dove gray. High elves dress the same way and add blues, lilacs and purples to the forest shades. For hunting and war, both wear brown, russet or tan. Gray elves wear elaborate flowing clothes of pure white, sun yellow, and silver and gold lamé, set off with polished leather in contrasting colors and jewels. All elves wear cloaks, especially when traveling, in neutral gray or gray-green.

Gnomes and halflings dress alike, often wearing knee breeches instead of trousers. Gnomes prefer sober colors: brown breeches, a tan blouse, green boots and belt, and a dark brown jacket or coat. A halfling in the same outfit might add a yellow shirt and a green cap with a bright yellow feather. Both often wear stripes. For hunting and war, both wear mottled clothing of mixed greens and browns.

Where People Live

In most states the bulk of the people live around the capital and the other large towns. Population is also thickest in the middle of a region and thins out toward its borders.

Settlements almost always sit on a river, road or shore. A few small ones lie in the wilderness, where some crop or resource gives people a reason to live there. Settlements are thickest in farming country.

Forts and castles usually serve as seats of noble power or as defenses against attack. A state therefore has several kinds: the ruler's, those of the ruler's vassals, and military forts guarding coasts and borders. Independent nobles, petty lords, bandits and the like also build fortified places, in borderlands, unclaimed ground and other remote spots.

In any area of 100 square leagues that is reasonably fertile and flat, it is safe to assume there is some settlement or stronghold. The harsher the land, the less likely that is, though robber forts and the castles of petty nobles may still turn up there.

Humanoids have mostly been driven into the poorest land: mountains, barrens, marshes, swamps and forests. Now and then they band together to try to win back better land, as they did in the Pomarj and the Bone March. Something similar is now building around Furyondy and Highfolk.

Only Iuz, the Horned Society and parts of the Great Kingdom let the more civilized humanoids live among humans in any numbers. The large free cities are also known to let various humanoids come and go freely.

Roads

Each state has roads linking its major cities. Their condition depends on the state, but most are fairly wide and well kept, and they carry on through the borderlands where trade routes run.

A second network of poor roads and cart tracks links small towns and border forts to the main roads. Such tracks are usually the only links between states. The notable exceptions are the Ulek States, the two Urnst States, Furyondy and Veluna, and Keoland and the Gran March (the book spells it "Keoghland" here).

Roads are kept up by local governments and communities. In some places travelers pay a toll, part of which goes to road upkeep.

Eastern Oerik has countless dialects, but most scholars agree that only five have ever had enough speakers to count as true languages: Common, Ancient Baklunish, Suloise, Old Oeridian and Flan.

The Five Languages

Common. A new and widely used tongue built on Ancient Baklunish and the Great Kingdom's dialect of Old Oeridian. Almost anyone who crosses borders has to learn at least a little Common or be badly handicapped. Because its roots are so broad, one language often has to be translated into Common before it can be turned into another.

Ancient Baklunish. One of the parents of Common, though after nearly a thousand years of change the two have little in common. The Paynim tribes still speak it; some of their traders and educated people learn Common to deal with outsiders.

Suloise. Once old and widespread, it nearly died out when the Rain of Colorless Fire destroyed the Suloise Empire. Today it is seldom spoken, even by the few scholars who know it. It survives mainly in writing, for those who study the remaining magical books of the Suel.

Old Oeridian. A younger language that had no outside influence at all until a few centuries ago. Its parts are so distinctive that translating it into anything but Common is close to impossible.

Flan. Surely the oldest language still widely spoken. The people of Tenh speak a version worn down by time of what was once the tongue of the whole Flanaess. It has stopped developing, so modern ideas are hard to put into Flan.

Dialects and Minor Tongues

Ferral. A secret Oeridian tribal language now spoken only by officers of the Iron League. It is used just for commands and identification, so it is not really a living language. (The book spells it both Ferrel and Ferral.)

The Cold Tongue (Fruz). Mostly Suloise with some Flan mixed in, spoken by the Ice, Snow and Frost Barbarians. It is unrelated to Common, and even Suloise speakers find it hard to follow.

Keolandish. A widespread dialect of Old High Oeridian with local additions, spoken in and around Keoland.

Nyrondese. A High Oeridian dialect of Common spoken in parts of Nyrond. It is the first language of peasants, shopkeepers and the like; educated people nearly always speak Common too.

Velondi. An Old Oeridian tribal language spoken mostly by country people near the border of Furyondy and Veluna. Someone who speaks only Common cannot understand it.

Lendorian. A little-known dialect of Suloise spoken in the Spindrift Isles. It is unrelated to the Cold Tongue. The book calls it a secondary language for those who speak Common.

Social Rank

The social order of the Flanaess, from highest to lowest. Ranks the book groups together share a line.

  1. Imperial royalty (holding office)
  2. Royalty and heads of state (holding office)
  3. Dependent royalty and heads of state (holding office)
  4. Independent nobility and lords mayor of free cities (holding office)
  5. Greater nobility; major clergy; lords mayor of great cities; free lords
  6. Lesser nobility; guild masters; clergy; great knights; lords mayor of towns; military officers
  7. Lesser knights; petty clergy; sages; minor officials; landed gentry; wealthy merchant gentlemen; freeholders; petty lords (lairds)
  8. Esquires; master craftsmen; merchants and tradesmen who own property; socmen (large landowners); heads of small communities; gentlemen; scholars
  9. Petty landlords; merchants; craftsmen; tradesmen; freemen; professional soldiers; village elders
  10. Mercenaries; students; laborers; masterless men; apprentices; bondsmen; indentured servants; beggars and vagabonds; slaves

Orders of Knighthood

Knighthood comes in many forms in the Flanaess: granted by sovereigns, by greater and lesser nobles, or by the leading clerics of certain states. They are not held in equal regard. Some states grant no knighthoods, a few hand them out cheaply, and in others a knighthood carries great prestige. The Knight Protectors of the Great Kingdom, for example, are very formidable, while those of Medegia are held in near contempt, since everyone knows the title is for sale. Only three are true orders of knighthood.

Knights of the Shield. Described under the Shield Lands.

Knights of the Watch. Hardy soldiers of Bissel, the Gran March, Geoff and Keoland are invited to join this order, sworn to guard the east against the Paynims and other westerners. They hold castles, keeps and strongholds along the border with Ket and elsewhere in the western mountains. The Watchers live almost like monks under very strict discipline. Their Grand Commander is Hugo of Geoff, and the order is said to number 5,000. Their arms: sable, an owl displayed argent.

The Order of the Hart. A far less warlike order in three branches, founded to keep the central states (Furyondy, Veluna and Highfolk) free and true to their purpose. These lands are loosely governed and keep no large standing armies, so each is open to sudden attack by its neighbors. To the east and north are the humanoid hordes and barbarian nomads. To the west are the Baklunish states, the scarcely less threatening marches and military orders in between, and Perrenland with its pushy trade policies and well-drilled soldiers to back them. There is little danger from the south beyond the odd pirate on the Nyr Dyv and some troublesome humanoid raids. Every lord of these nations has guards and men-at-arms, and every ruler a small body of troops, but most of their strength takes a long time to gather. The Knights of the Hart are sworn to be ready at a moment's notice to act as the vanguard. They hold strongholds, serve the allied nations in many roles, and send roving troops to watch trouble spots and hostile borders.

  • Knights of Furyondy: 200 knights, commanding many men-at-arms. Arms: azure, a pair of antlers or.
  • Knights of Veluna: said to be only 80, each of great renown and each leading many sergeants and men-at-arms. Arms: sable, a pair of antlers or.
  • Knights of the High Forest: said to be open only to elves, with perhaps two dozen knights. Arms: vert, a pair of antlers or.

Any branch knights only freemen and gentlefolk devoted to the good of the states they defend. Each candidate must be a proven fighter who has done some deed of exceptional honor, courage and service. Iuz and the Horned Society hate the Knights of the Hart, and so, it is said, do the people of Dyvers. There is no love lost between them and the Watchers, the rulers of Perrenland, or some of the nobles of Nyrond, and there is a strong rivalry between the Hart and the Shield.

Its petty nobles and the Lord Mayor of the town of Innspa all swear loyalty to the reigning prelate, who is usually a high priest. The Bandit Kingdoms are a patchwork of petty holdings founded around 300-350 CY. These small personal domains run from the southern Shield Lands to the Bluff Hills and the northern edge of the Fellreev Forest, and from the Ritensa River east to the Artonsamay. Each is ruled by a robber chief who calls himself Baron, Boss, Plar, General, Tyrant, Prince, Despot or even King.

Borders shift quickly with every sudden war, defeat or victory. There are 17 states in all. Four to six strong lords rule; the rest are trying either to rise to the top or just to survive. The arrangement lasts because no bandit lord is strong enough to conquer the rest, and all of them together are often needed to fight off punitive expeditions from neighboring states. So the bandits stick together out of self-interest. No kinglet, however ambitious, has seriously tried to rule them all, for fear that the threatened lords would call in a neighboring state out of spite, even at the risk of being destroyed by that "ally." Their combined military strength is considerable, since every ruler keeps a large force for raiding and looting; recent scouting suggests about 10,000 regular troops in all.

Around 400 CY the March of Bissel, then called the Lirtlemark (as printed), was Keoland's northernmost frontier. Furyondy took it in the Small War between Furyondy and Keoland, which ended Keoish influence in Veluna in 438 CY. For a few decades Bissel paid tribute to Furyondy. Then humanoid invasions swept over Furyondy, and Margrave Rollo won his land's independence through courage in the King's service: the men of Bissel wiped out a horde of Jebli (goblins) lying in ambush for King Hugh III, who had only a small escort. The King rewarded Rollo with palatine status, and Bissel has governed itself ever since.

The March is now a wall between the hordes of Ket and the rest of the east, and it also shields Keoland and the south. Because of its strategic position, Furyondy, Veluna and Keoland all support it, and adventurers and mercenaries from across the Flanaess serve in the "Border Companies" that form the Margrave's standing army. There are four regular and four reserve companies of 1,000 each, with horse, foot and archers. Favored weapons are lance, crossbow, pike, fauchard-fork, flail and sword. Bissel's soldiers are very well equipped and armored. On border duty each company has a squad of 30 to 50 scouts attached.
