Only a little lower than the Corusks, they are just as unwelcoming to settlers, though there are a few settlements here and there because the mountains hold valuable minerals. A small and beautiful land is said to lie in the heart of the range, ruled by a powerful prince and guarded against all invaders by magic and might, where roofs are of copper and silver, gold is used the way lead is elsewhere, and jewels lie on the ground.

Hellfurnaces

Part of the Crystalmist range, named differently because it is volcanic in many places. Like the northern part of the chain, it is a hive of evil, full of monsters of every sort, especially those that like heat, such as fire giants. Whole labyrinths of passages are said to run beneath it, underground highways stretching scores, perhaps hundreds, of miles in every direction.

Yatil Mountains

These mountains crowd together for many leagues west and south of Lake Quag. With the Barrier Peaks, they divide the Baklunish part of the continent from the rest, except in the north, where western nomads have pushed over the top and beyond. They form the western borders of Ekbir, Tusmit and Ket. Perrenland's cantons and the elven lands of Highfolk lie in and along their eastern slopes. Many humanoids and monsters live in the range, but so do some hardy demi-humans and mountaineers. The Yatils are rich in ore and gems, though these are hard to find and mine.

Minor Mountain Ranges

Barrier Peaks. This range runs from the southwestern edge of the Bramblewood Forest to the Crystalmists. Its northern hills are so rough and steep that they are counted as part of the mountains. The Valley of the Mage is hidden in the central Barriers, and their southwestern end forms the western border of the Grand Duchy of Geoff. These mountains are notorious for their strange inhabitants. Some dwarves live in hidden places in the range, of course, since it holds many precious minerals and gems.

Clatspur Range. This small group of mountains below the Sepia Uplands borders the Vesve Forest on the west and funnels the southern end of Lake Quag. The peaks hold some valuable minerals, and Perrenlanders live in small villages on the lower slopes and in the valleys. There are few demi-humans in the Clatspurs proper.

Drachensgrab Mountains. These small mountains are crowned by several towering peaks in their center. The whole area is known to be full of precious metals and fine gems, but many strange and hostile creatures live in its hills and mountains. Some think a terrible curse lies on the area, and legends say one or more powerful beings will rise in anger if their resting place is ever disturbed. The mountains are now the main stronghold of the humanoid invaders who hold the whole Pomarj: orcs, hobgoblins, bugbears, and many ogres and ogre magi.

Glorioles. Another small range, at the northwestern end of the Hestmark Highlands, with the Rieuwood to the west and the Grayflood and Thelly Rivers to the north. Its peaks and valleys are home to perhaps 10,000 or more mountain dwarves. Although they dislike elves, these dwarves have lately helped in the Iron League's war against the invading forces of the Great Kingdom.

Jotens. The largest spur of the Crystalmists, named because these mountains are very high and imposing, and because many hill giants, and more than a few stone and cloud giants, live there. Otherwise the range is like the Crystalmists.

Lortmil Mountains. A low chain, often worn down into hills by age, though it has several very imposing peaks. It is home to many kinds of demi-humans: dwarves, gnomes, mountain dwarves, a few adventurous halflings, and scattered aarakocra tribes. These peoples have worked together before to drive most of the humanoids and many vicious monsters out of the Lortmils, and they are subjects of the small states that grew up in the shelter of the range, such as the Ulek realms and Celene. The Lortmils hold some of the richest gem and precious metal deposits known, and the dwarves, gnomes and halflings there are said to be as rich as princes.

Rakers. A southern arm of the Griff Mountains running down into the middle of the eastern Flanaess, named because its tall, sharp peaks seem to rake the sky. Their end, the Flinty Hills, is described under Hills and Highlands. They are infested with humanoids and fearsome creatures, but several groups of dwarves and mountain dwarves live there too. How much valuable ore they hold is unknown.

Sulhaut Mountains. This range runs west from where the Crystalmists and Hellfurnaces meet, separating the Dry Steppes from the ghastly Sea of Dust. What they hold can only be guessed, since there is no reliable information. Reports of drow are not uncommon. A twisting pass is said to lead from the Dry Steppes into the Sea of Dust, or east into the kinder lands of the Flanaess.

Ulsprue. The Baklunish name for the lower peaks of the Crystalmists that reach northwest and north into the Plains of the Paynims, possibly after the people who live in the bowl these mountains and the Barrier Peaks form on the plains. Nothing else certain is known about the range.

Source: Guide p.54-55. Rewritten in plain words.

  • Artonsamay River: one of the longest rivers on the continent, navigable from Redspan Town in Tenh all the way to the Nyr Dyv.
  • Att River: a tributary of the Velverdyva, navigable by small craft well beyond Littleberg.
  • Blackwater: a tributary of the Dulsi.
  • Blashikmund River: a tributary of the Tuflik; it now forms the border between Ekbir and Tusmit.
  • Cold Run: a tributary that flows south to join the Artonsamay west of the town of Rookroost.
  • Crystal River: a tributary of the Veng.
  • Davish River: a very cold, fast tributary of the Javan.
  • Deepstil River: a tributary of the Dulsi flowing east through the Vesve Forest.
  • Dulsi River: a broad, deep river feeding Whyestil Lake, navigable up to the fork of the Blackwater.
  • Duntide: rises in the Flinty Hills and flows south into the Gnatmarsh, where it joins the Nesser.
  • Ery River: a tributary of the Selintan flowing south of Greyhawk City.
  • Fals River: a tributary of the Velverdyva marking the northern border of Veluna.
  • Flanmi River: the greatest river of the eastern Flanaess. Its basin drains nearly all of the Great Kingdom, and most of the river and its tributaries can be sailed by ship all the way to Rauxes, and by barge beyond.
  • Fler River: the main river feeding Lake Quag, flowing from the Burneal Forest and the Land of Black Ice beyond. Much of it is thought to be passable by large craft.
  • Franz River: a tributary of the Nesser, navigable to Trigol; it forms the border between Nyrond and the County of Urnst.
  • Frozen River: a swift river running mostly north from the Griff Mountains through the lands of Stonefist into White Fanged Bay.
  • Grayflood: a tributary of the Thelly; it now marks the limit of the land claimed by the Iron League (Sunndi).
  • Harp River: one of the longest rivers on the continent. It rises in the Rakers and empties into Relmor Bay near Chathold in Almor, and is navigable for about half its length.
  • Hool River: a broad tributary of the Javan with swampy banks.
  • Imeda River: a tributary that joins the Flanmi at Rauxes.
  • Javan River: the longest river on the continent. It begins high in the Barriers, runs south for hundreds of miles, then turns east to empty into the Azure Sea above Monmurg in the Hold of the Sea Princes. Large vessels can use it only as far as the town of Cryllor in the Good Hills of Keoland.
  • Jewel River: rises just south of the Kron Hills and flows south through the Gnarley Forest, the Welkwood and the Suss Forest into the Azure Sea, dividing the Principality of Ulek from the Pomarj. About 150 miles of it can take large craft.
  • Kewl River: a tributary of the Sheldomar dividing the Duchy from the County of Ulek.
  • Lort River: a tributary of the Sheldomar dividing the Gran March from the Duchy of Ulek.
  • Mikar River: a tributary of the Flanmi that rises in the Lone Heath and flows through the Grandwood Forest.
  • Neen River: a broad but shallow tributary of the Selintan.
  • Nesser River: a long, very broad and deep river that drains the Nyr Dyv. Despite many islands and channels, it is so wide (over three miles on average) that seagoing ships can sail its whole length with a good pilot. It forms the border between Nyrond and the Duchy of Urnst.
  • Old River: a tributary of the Sheldomar between the County and the Principality of Ulek.
  • Opicm River: the eastern river feeding Whyestil Lake, also rising in the Cold Marshes; it forms the border of the lands of Iuz.
  • Realstream River: a tributary that flows through the Dim Forest to join the Javan just below the town of Hochoch.
  • Ritensa River: a tributary of the Veng dividing the Shield Lands and the Bandit Kingdoms from the Horned Society.
  • Selintan River: a fairly broad, deep-channeled outlet of the western Nyr Dyv. It flows past Greyhawk City into Woolly Bay and carries much traffic.
  • Sheldomar River: divides Keoland from the Ulek States and is navigable from its mouth to the city of Niole Dra.
  • Teesar Torrent: a very fast river that rises in the North Province of the Great Kingdom and feeds the Harp below the Blemu Hills.
  • Thelly River: a tributary of the Flanmi, navigable to the town of Nulbish.
  • Trask River: flows east through the North Province to the Solnor Ocean. The town of Atirr at its mouth is a busy seaport.
  • Tuflik River: a long river flowing west from the northern end of the Barrier Peaks to the Dramidj Ocean. It divides Ket and Tusmit from the Plains of the Paynims and is also the border between Ekbir and Zeif.
  • Velverdyva River: perhaps the second longest river on the continent; some argue the lower Fler should be counted as part of it. It is the border between Veluna and Furyondy. Large vessels can go up to a point north of the Veluna City area, and barges can travel all the way to Thornward in Bissel (by the Fals River) or, with some difficulty, to Lake Quag.
  • Veng River: the outlet of Whyestil Lake and an inlet of the Nyr Dyv, deep and broad and navigable its whole length. It forms the border between the Horned Society and Furyondy and is closely patrolled by river craft, cavalry and infantry.
  • Yol River: a tributary of the Artonsamay that rises in the Troll Fens and divides the Phostwood from the Nutherwood, forming the border between Tenh and the Pale. Barges from Wintershiven, and those heading there, use it.
  • Zumker River: a tributary of the Artonsamay, said to rise in a large mountain lake in the Griffs. It forms a border between Tenh and the Bandit Kingdoms.

Source: Guide p.56-60. Rewritten in plain words; figures as printed (the Gamboge and Vesve figures were checked against the page images).

Adri Forest

Population25,000- (as printed)
Demi-humansFew
HumanoidsFew

This great ancient forest lies mostly inside the Great Kingdom, though its northwestern tip, west of the Harp River, belongs to the Prelacy of Almor. It teems with game and is carefully managed and tended by those who live in it. Its wood is used mostly for shipbuilding, spear shafts, bows and arrows. The people usually carry longbows, battleaxes and short spears.

Amedio Jungle

PopulationUnknown
Demi-humansUnlikely
HumanoidsPossible
Resourcesfoodstuffs, rare woods, spices, ivory, platinum, gems (III, IV)

Little is known of the Amedio Jungle except that tribes of cannibal savages live there, some said to be of Suel blood or mixed with it. Expeditions have sometimes come back with great wealth and tales of mines full of gems. A large lake is said to be where the tribes gather when they prepare for war and raids. Contact has come through various Sea Princes. The savages use darts, javelins, spears, clubs and short bows. Some use blowguns: a hollow tube 5 to 7 feet long that sends a wooden sliver coated with poison 10 to 30 yards on a breath (30 yards being long range). The slivers cannot get through armor, so they threaten only exposed skin. Poison is common but usually weak.

Burneal Forest

The trackless Burneal stretches more than a thousand miles, from just past the shore of the Dramidj Ocean to the bogs of Blackmoor. This huge forest of pines and firs is nowhere less than 100 miles wide and in places more than 200. South of it lie the prairies of the Tiger and Wolf Nomads, and these fearless horsemen often ride into the Burneal for sport. They do so at their peril, because little-known savages live in the depths and lurk among the thick trunks to attack by stealth and surprise. Reports say these hunting tribes are human, aboriginal Flan, living in huts of green boughs in summer and burrows dug into the ground in the cold months. They hunt with pits, snares, bows and spears, using huge wolf-dogs to find prey and corner or bring it down. They must be extremely tough and strong to survive the Burneal's bitter winters and the creatures that share it.

Celadon Forest

The spreading oaks and mighty elms of the Celadon grow from the edge of the Duntide out over the rolling knolls of the Abbor-Alz, and yews and ashes older than memory grow from the Gnatmarsh north to Nellix Town and the Franz River. Many sylvan elves and treants roam beneath these ancient trees; the Celadon is almost a realm of its own. The Nesser cuts through it, with a third of the forest in the Duchy of Urnst and the rest in Nyrond, but neither state cuts timber or otherwise upsets the forest's natural balance, except to hunt. Some humans live here too, hunters, woodsmen and the like, in harmony with their surroundings. Both rulers expect their loyal service, which they give by guarding the forest ways against raiders and hostile creatures coming up from the hills or marshes to the south and using the trees for cover. Fierce creatures, some outlaws and humanoids turn up in the Celadon from time to time, but it is not a healthy place for them. Raiders on the water are the worst problem, and the Duke sends patrols along the Nesser to help the wardens. In time of war the forest provides companies of archers and light infantry.

Dreadwood

Population5,000
Demi-humansSylvan Elves (8,000), Gnomes (1,000), Halflings
HumanoidsSome

This large forest lies north of the Hool Marshes of the lower Javan River in Keoland. It runs some 200 miles from the Good Hills in the west to the Azure Sea coast in the east and is about 70 to 100 miles deep. The Dreadwood is a place of constant war: monsters and humanoids fight the elves who guard it for the King, in return for Keoland's protection of the forest. Large efforts to clear out the evil creatures have been made again and again, but the enemy retreats into hidden places and out into the trackless Hool Marshes, and comes back when the woodsmen and elves withdraw. The Sea Princes are suspected of working with certain bandits and humanoid bands who slip through the Dreadwood to raid Keoland and the Yeomanry.

Gamboge Forest

Population7,000
Demi-humansSylvan Elves (11,000), Gnomes (3,000), High Elves (1,500), Halflings
HumanoidsSome

The Gamboge lies between Nyrond and the Pale, east of Midmeadow Town, along the Flinty Hills and the lower Rakers. It is an old and very dense forest. Neither state has a firm claim to it, so it is practically a nation of its own, and its people deal and trade with the gnomes, halflings and even the dwarves in the hills and mountains to the east. They have no love for Nyrond, but they think far better of it than of the Pale, so they usually swear allegiance to Nyrond, and the kingdom's banners are shown in the forest now and then to discourage any takeover by the Theocrat's servants. The demi-humans (and humans too) of the region are rumored to be seeking an alliance with their kin in the Flinty Hills to form a demi-human realm, but with the humanoid hordes and the Overking threatening, this is very doubtful. The Gamboge can be dangerous, since humanoid bands and monsters from the mountains use it as a route when they go raiding the lands around it.

Gnarley Forest

Population12,000
Demi-humansSylvan Elves (7,000), Gnomes (3,000), others
HumanoidsSome

Celene, Dyvers, Verbobonc and Greyhawk all claim parts of the Gnarley. Most of it, though, is counted as part of the Wild Coast region, and its people are free spirits, so no formal government is likely ever to rule it while there are deep woods to shelter those who resist. The folk of the northeastern Gnarley like the Viscount of Verbobonc, and those in the south favor the Queen of Celene. Many fierce creatures live in the forest too, and many humanoid bands roam it to murder and loot. These invaders work their way up from the Pomarj through the Suss and the Welkwood, and some come down through the mountains and hills from the north.

Grandwood Forest

Population25,000
Demi-humansSylvan Elves (7,000), some others
HumanoidsSome

It is lucky for the people and elves of the Grandwood that no abler ruler sits on the Malachite Throne. It is just as lucky that the Holy Censor of Medegia wants the part of the forest south of the Mikar, while the nobles of Rel Astra try to stop him without actually going to war. Though it lies barely 25 leagues from Rauxes, the Grandwood is a refuge for those fleeing oppression: outlaws good and bad, demi-humans, and anyone who hates cruelty and tyranny. The western third is fairly empty, because the Overking's troops are many there, but deeper in, his servants do not go for fear of attack. Halflings wait in impassable thickets, elven archers hide in the high branches, and woodsmen lie in ambush along the tracks. Now and then the Censor's troops push into the heart of the forest, but they come back fewer than they went, often without ever seeing the enemy who harried them. Men of Rel Astra also enter the Grandwood and post notices claiming it for their city, but they never seriously try to hold any of it.

One tale says the free folk of the forest once led separate groups of intruders into battle with each other, so that the Overking's men-at-arms killed and were killed by troops of his vassals from Rel Astra and Medegia. It is certain that the woodsmen sometimes wear their enemies' colors, so those who enter the forest cannot tell friend from foe. To counter this, the Overking has lately enlisted humanoid troops to clear his opponents out of the woods; the results remain to be seen. The move has angered the Censor, whose troops are said to have orders to cut down all humans and humanoids on sight, whatever colors they wear, which certainly helps the rebels of the Grandwood.

Suss Forest

The Suss is a dreary place, full of thorn trees, brambles, briars and thickets. Its huge trees are black with age and seem to whisper among themselves when an intruder passes beneath. Some claim that ripples of waving leaves and moving branches can be seen along the path of anyone who enters, but this is unproven. The western end is different from the rest: where it grows on the Lortmil Mountains the woods are open and clean, but east of the Jewel River the forest turns gloomy and hateful. The farther south one goes, the worse it gets, until it is filled with an oppressive, evil feeling where it climbs the Drachensgrab Hills.

The humanoid bands of the Pomarj, especially kobolds, orcs and gnolls, seem to love the Suss, and many hundreds are known to live deep within it alongside its native gibberlings, ettercaps and susserus. They also use it as a highway north to raid the Wild Coast, Celene, or even the Ulek states and Verbobonc. The Wild Coast folk once made a determined effort to clear the Suss and pushed its edge back several leagues, but logging parties disappeared and humanoid raiders made it too dangerous, so no such work is done anywhere anymore. The petty nobles and lordlings of the Wild Coast keep a close watch on its edges. A lost, ruined city of the Old Suel is said to be hidden somewhere in the Suss, but few dare to search for it, especially now.

Vesve Forest

Population20,000
Demi-humansSylvan Elves (10,000), Gnomes (6,000), High Elves (3,000), Halflings
HumanoidsHobgoblins (5,000), Gnolls (3,000)

The Vesve is the largest hardwood forest in the Flanaess. Its southern half, and the strip along the Sepia Uplands (printed "Sepia Hills" here) and the Clatspurs down to Highfolk Town, are fairly free of evil creatures, though they have their share of predators. Since Iuz returned, however, the northern quarter has filled with hateful settlements of evil humanoids, and these tribes and bands press on the human and demi-human folk everywhere else in the forest. Rangers and light troops from Furyondy join the Highfolk in organized expeditions to stem the flow of humanoids and drive them out, but Iuz's breeding grounds seem to supply endless fresh hordes to replace those killed, and a war of attrition will doom the good folk of the Vesve. Both sides are expected to make a major attempt to settle the matter soon.

Welkwood

Population10,000 +
Demi-humansMany
HumanoidsSome (raiding parties)

The Welkwood's edges are easy to see, because its trees are so much bigger. They tower over the Suss to the south and the Gnarley to the west and north. Ipts grow 100 feet tall and more, the mighty roanwoods taller still, and even its locusts, elders, maples and the like grow unusually large, so the whole forest is very imposing. The eastern part belongs to the Wild Coast, and many of its folk live in the shelter of the trees. The Welkwood west of the Jewel River is part of Celene and home to elves, faerie creatures of every sort, and unicorns. The woodsmen of the Welkwood are brave and sturdy, famous across the land as hunters, trackers and bold adventurers.

Minor Woodlands

Axewood. A fairly small wood on the border between upper Keoland and the Duchy of Ulek, said to be home to treants and some elves.

Bramblewood Forest. A large, dense forest in the plains between the Barrier Peaks and the southernmost arm of the Yatils, spreading east and west in Ket. It has only one main road and perhaps a few lesser tracks. Its southern edge is guarded by the walled city and castle of Thornward. Dakon are known to live there.

Dim Forest. The huge old trees of this vast forest are so broad and leafy that the ground beneath is dim on the brightest days. No tracks are known, though some must exist to let travelers through its leagues of woods. Elves are said to live in the part west of the Javan; terrible creatures live in the rest.

Fellreev Forest. Once a hunting ground of the Rovers of the Barrens, the whole Fellreev is now held by the Bandit Kingdoms or the Horned Society. Many strange creatures roam its trackless heart, including, it is said, a few small bands of sylvan elves and human tribesmen.

Forlorn Forest. A fair-sized evergreen wood just south of the Icy Sea, whose eastern edge marks the border of the Rovers of the Barrens. Even those fierce nomads avoid the quaggoth tribes that prowl it.

Hornwood. A fair-sized wood in the Grand Duchy of Geoff and the Grand Duke's favorite hunting ground, despite (or perhaps because of) the fierce creatures often found there, many having come down from the Crystalmists. Several groups of sylvan elves live in it. It is named for the hornwood tree, whose straightest limbs are specially treated and seasoned to make the finest elven bows. Hornwood is very tough and springy, but first-grade wood is uncommon and hard to prepare for bows.

Hraak Forest. A largish pine and fir wood in the lands claimed by Stonefist's descendants, bordering the Corusks north of Hraak Pass.

Loftwood. A smallish pine forest on the coast of the Bone March between the Raker foothills and Grendep Bay. Its tall trees are prized as masts for large ships. The humanoids are surely ruining it now.

Menowood. A fair-sized wood in the far southern corner of Idee, said to be home to many treants and elves, with the Hollow Highlands running through its eastern part. The forest is untouched, and few humans go there.

Nutherwood. South of the Yol River; its southern edge marks the end of the Theocrat of the Pale's authority. Few people go there, and many monsters and bandits are reported to hide in it.

Oytwood. A smallish wood, also in Geoff, home mainly to elves.

Phostwood. The forest on the north bank of the Yol belongs to Tenh, though bandits from the neighboring states constantly dispute it. Certain trees found only here glow faintly when they die and start to rot, giving the place an eerie look at night; a branch of phostwood gives enough light for a 5-foot radius.

Rieuwood. This forest caps the northern end of Sunndi, its mighty trees stretching from the middle of the Hollow Highlands to the slopes of the Glorioles. Sunndi's forces patrol it, and elves and rangers make it dangerous for enemies, but raiders and even humanoid marauders still turn up there.

Sable Wood. An evergreen forest in the realm of the King of the Ice Barbarians. Its most interesting feature is a fir whose wood turns a deep, glossy black when cut in the dead of winter and rubbed with hot oils. The barbarians prize it greatly and will not export it.

Silverwood. A smallish forest in the Duchy of Ulek, home to many sylvan elves. Certain trees that elves love grow thickly here, and its people are said to prize them more than silver.

Spikey Forest. A smallish wood dividing the lands of the Frost and Snow Barbarians. Both peoples use its tall pines for masts and spars.

Tangles. A small, jungle-like wood in the Bandit Kingdoms above Riftcanyon.

Timberway Forest. This vast stretch of pines, firs and other northern trees runs from the lands of the Frost Barbarians to the Barony of Ratik, and from the shores of Grendep Bay to the shoulders of the Rakers. Its timber is not as fine as the Loftwood's but is still very valuable for shipbuilding.

Udgru Forest. A large, very dense wood in Ekbir and Tusmit, full of game and, of course, less welcome creatures. Discontented citizens of both states often take refuge there.

Source: Guide p.60-61. Rewritten in plain words.

Bright Desert

PopulationUnknown (scattered nomads)
Demi-humansDoubtful
HumanoidsDoubtful

Since the start of recorded history in the Flanaess, the Bright Desert has fascinated and challenged people. It is said to be full of riches: copper, silver, gold and gem minerals. But the harsh climate, wild swings of temperature and hostile inhabitants (Suel peoples) who fight every intruder with savage determination and bloodlust discourage anyone from exploiting it. The dervishes said to live in the bordering Abbor-Alz also turn explorers back, though if they exist they are probably of Flan descent and hostile to the Suel nomads. One or two organized forces have tried to push into the Bright Desert, and none ever came back to tell what happened.

Dry Steppes

The vast prairies north of the Sulhaut Mountains and west of the Crystalmist and Ulsprue ranges. Rain is scarce and few rivers flow there. The region was once well watered and fertile, the homeland of the Baklunish padishahs and sultans, but the Invoked Devastation destroyed it in the war with the Suel. The middle of the steppes is said to be pleasant and rich still, and large hordes of Baklunish nomads certainly still roam there under various khans. Otherwise this edge of the Flanaess is unknown to the chronicler. Invading tribesmen from the Dry Steppes are usually light cavalry with composite bows, light lances and curved swords.

Land of Black Ice

Those who have gone far into the north beyond the Burneal Forest tell of something strange. Instead of ordinary white snow and clear blue-white ice, there is an endless landscape of deep blue-black ice, with only a little ordinary snow here and there. Strange arctic monsters prowl these fields of black ice, and the few humans living nearby are afraid to go in, because of the beasts and because of what is supposed to lie beyond. Stranger still, they are said to tell of a warmer land past the ice where the sun never sets and jungles grow. Whatever the truth of such tall tales, the place is mysterious indeed. Somewhere between the Land of Black Ice and Blackmoor is said to be the City of the Gods, where iron buildings tower and it is summer all year round, though the snow lies deep in the fields around it. A land that gives rise to such legends deserves further exploration by daring adventurers.

Rift Canyon

North of the Artonsamay, among the rough, broken ground and jutting crags of the badlands, lies a deep canyon of tremendous size. This rift in the ground is more than 180 miles long, from 10 miles wide at its end to about 30 in the middle, near the bandit town of Riftcrag. Tales say it is more than a mile deep and riddled with caves and caverns. Much of it has been cleared of monsters, though they are said to still come out of the tunnels. The Plar of the Rift, as the bandit lord calls himself, reportedly uses humanoid troops and monsters to hold the canyon against their kin and takes rich loot by doing so. The floor of the rift at its western end is avoided, though, because especially fierce monsters live there, and attempts to clear it have ended in disaster. Parties from the Shield Lands on punitive raids against the bandit kinglets confirm this: trying to surprise the brigands by moving through the Riftcanyon from its western end has proved impossible.

Just south of the Riftcanyon stands the lonely volcanic cone of haunted White Plume Mountain, which knights and bandits alike avoid.

Sea of Dust

A land of unknown size lies behind the Hellfurnaces, south of the Sulhaut Mountains. This bleak desert is the Sea of Dust, once the Suel (Suloise) Empire. History says it was once a fair and fertile realm stretching a thousand miles to the west and south as well. Its cruel, arrogant rulers fought the Baklunish for mastery over all of Oerik, and in return for a terrible magical attack, the Suel lands were drowned in an almost invisible fiery rain. It killed every creature it touched, burned every living thing, set the land alight with colorless flame and burned the very hills to ash. Whatever the truth, the place is certainly a desert now: an endless view of dust and fine ash in gentle rises and shallow hollows like ocean waves. It looks far less lovely when the winds howl and tear the surface into choking clouds that strip flesh from bone and rise to the sky, making it impossible to see and very dangerous to live. Add to this the rains of volcanic ash and cinders blown from the Hellfurnaces onto the forsaken lands of a once terribly mighty empire. Legends tell of strange ruins near the feet of the Sulhauts, and say that somewhere in the heart of the desert the nearly intact remains of the Forgotten City, the lost capital of the Suel Imperium, still stand.

A few mountain tribesmen of the Sulhauts are said to go into the Sea of Dust now and then for treasure from the cities and towns buried under the dust. These tales cannot be proven, but people certainly live deep in that mountain range. Reports of firenewt raiders and other horrors are not uncommon but may be unreliable. Similar stories tell of a secret expedition sent by the Sea Princes to find and bring back the loot of the Forgotten City; if it was ever organized and set out, nothing has been heard of its return. That story, however, led the officials of the Yeomanry to try exploring the far side of the Hellfurnaces, and reliable reports tell of at least one party coming back from such a trip with half its members lost but carrying strange art objects and jewelry from the edges of the Sea of Dust. The Freeholder, of course, is giving out no more details, and it happened too recently for rumors to have spread.

Source: GA p.89. Rewritten in plain words.

Little is known of Oerth's geography, because travel is so bad for one's health. Only the rich and powerful can pay for the armed guards, wizards and clerics that make long journeys possible, so people who cannot travel freely are always eager for tales of distant lands.

The strange places in this entry are among the most notorious and best known in the lands people travel. Besides being interesting in their own right, they were chosen to make a point: a place does not have to be packed with monsters, tricks and traps to interest players and DMs alike.

Source: GA p.89-90. Rewritten in plain words.

The Pinnacles of Azor'alq have haunted Baklunish legend for more than three thousand years. They have been called the ancient homes of the gods, the spires of a gigantic drowned city, the great tombs of the half-legendary First Dynasty of the Baklunish, and the nesting place of phoenixes, rocs or the many dragons of the Dramidj Ocean. The epic hero they are named for is said to sleep there with his paladins. The last royal house of the Baklunish Empire is said to have fled there from the Invoked Devastation, and the Cup and Talisman of Al'Akbar is rumored to be there. So much guesswork shows how few have seen the Pinnacles even from afar, and (perhaps tellingly) how fewer still report coming close or landing. Sailors think sighting them is a bad omen, rarely talk about them at all, and then only on shore.

Accounts suggest the Pinnacles lie no more than 50 leagues from the mainland, somewhere in the corner of the Dramidj between Ekbir and Zeif. They are found less often than one might expect, perhaps because they are off the usual shipping lanes and because of the thick fogs peculiar to the Dramidj. Indeed, fog banks often hide them even when the rest of the sea is clear, perhaps because the water around them is unusually warm and the air oddly calm. That is what merchant captains believe, at least; they keep well away from fog banks even in open ocean, and most ships carry oars just to get out quickly if becalmed.

The Pinnacles are huge spires, at least 40 of them (some say 100), in an irregular cluster with none more than two miles from its nearest neighbor. Each is perhaps a quarter mile across at the base, round, and rises steeply in a regular series of cliffs. How deep they go below the sea is unknown, but they stand more than 1,000 feet above it. Their lower parts are covered in forest, including huge conifers that can top 200 feet, mixed with smaller trees (some clinging to the cliffs) and a wealth of ferns, mosses and flowers. Above that is a cloud forest of strange fleshy-leaved plants and rare orchids. This fragrant, silent world contrasts with the highest levels, which are noisy and stained white by countless seabirds: puffins, eiders, albatrosses and others less familiar. On rare clear days the Pinnacles can be spotted from far off by the plume of birds above them.

Landing is seldom easy. The ledges between the cliffs are broad but rarely close to sea level, so a landing party usually has to climb tens or hundreds of feet up from the water. The rough ground, the mists, many waterfalls and thick plant life hide at first the fact that the Pinnacles are not natural, or even carved, but built of gigantic blocks. Now and then one finds openings into their interiors. No one has reported what lies up or down the broad stairways that lead from these bat-haunted cave mouths, or rather doorways.

Whatever else lives among the Pinnacles, dragons of every kind and size certainly do, from tiny ones that play among the lovely and unique forest birds to huge coiled reptiles.

Notes for the DM

Gold, faerie, pseudo-, silver and mist dragons all make fitting residents, and rocs, giant eagles and a phoenix or two can be added. They live in fair harmony, ranging out for fish, whales or even food on the mainland. All of them want to keep any word of the Pinnacles from reaching the outside world, and will strand or kill intruders if they possibly can, depending on alignment and circumstances. Treasures include not only valuables gathered by the intelligent residents but also certain orchids and birds of paradise; some of the birds were bred by the longer-lived dragons and are considered their personal property. The guardians and treasures of the interior should be powerful, possibly undead, and the outer residents do not want them disturbed. The island may have human inhabitants.

Source: GA p.90-91. Rewritten in plain words.

No one has accurately described the whole wasteland made by the Baklunish wizards. Reports are sometimes contradictory and always incomplete, since few are tough enough to go in and fewer still willing to study it. Still, some broad regions can be made out.

The Ash Sea

The Sea of Dust was first named for how it looks just west of the Hellfurnaces, where volcanic ash lies in gray waves over ground now buried deep. Every year the Hellfurnaces add more fine gray dust. What little water gets this far west seeps down through the limestone bedrock. Unwholesome creatures from the Hellfurnaces live in this lifeless waste and have passages leading up through the ash, sometimes disguised as outcrops of the old limestone. Whatever treasures the Suel here once had are buried deep. The only ruins reported are a few old mountain towns in what is really the western Hellfurnaces, and the many fire newts and fire giants there must have looted them long ago.

The North

The northern Sea of Dust has less ash and shows more clearly what Suel civilization was. Here stand the forts that guarded the passes over the Sulhauts into Baklunish lands, and farther into the desert, the ruins of walled cities. Bold scavengers seem to have stripped the nearest of these, close to the Sulhauts, over the past thousand years, but those farther in are less disturbed, partly because harpies live there. The architecture here shows the tall, angular buildings still favored by peoples such as the Sea Princes and the Lendorians.

The Center

The middle of the Sea of Dust is the most forbidding and alien part. There are dunes of white, powdery, caustic material, and the air is so dry that an unglazed jug empties in a day or two and anyone who does not cover the mouth with a damp cloth coughs blood. The white dunes and glassy bare rock cause sunblindness in those who do not shield their eyes with slitted masks or visors. No wonder the so-called Forgotten City is still, if not forgotten, at least unfound in such a harsh place; some would say it is a fable. Strange glassy hollows dot the central Sea of Dust, and some claim they mark the sites of Suel cities.

The Southwest

Oddly, the farthest part, the southwest, is the best known. A little rain falls there, and nomads live in it. Some show Suel ancestry, but most come from farther south: a tall, slender, curly-haired people with blue-black skin and slanted eyes. They are not otherwise hostile, but they guard their wells from every outsider and will not let a drop be stolen or sold. Water is hard to reach and tends to dry up or turn salty as a well is used more, so the nomads move from site to site looking for new sources. When they find a well they use animal strength or, in some tribes, windmills to bring the water up.

When water does reach the surface here, from wells or the rare rains of the "wet" season, the results are wonderful. The dust in these parts is not alkali or barren ash but true soil heaped into great hills, perhaps the once fertile earth of the Suel Empire, and it is extraordinarily productive for wild and farmed plants alike.

Unfortunately the rich dust also supports monsters that burrow through it, chiefly a nameless wormlike beast that can exceed 50 feet in length and an insectlike creature, something like a cross between a mantis and a centipede, up to 20 feet long. Moisture in the soil and the vibrations of people and livestock draw them, making them a great danger. Luckily they are rare and keep away from the nomads' arrows and spears.

Poor as they are in other ways, the southwestern nomads are rich in gems and gold, the gathered fortune of the Suel Empire. They treat these as minor ornaments and value cattle and vegetables far more. How they get their trinkets is most interesting: young men dive for them as part of the rite that makes them adults.

Dustlakes

Scattered across the region are ktosor-hep, or dustlakes, from half a mile to six miles across, where magic makes the dust behave like water. The grains form a kind of fluid that lets air pass between them but holds together as one body that supports waves, boats and swimmers like a real lake. Unlike water, it can be made somewhat breathable with a fine cloth mask over the mouth, though hard exertion is impossible that way. So one can go down to the ground beneath the dust and explore, in the dim, dusty air, the ruins of towns and cities; every dustlake seems to have been such a site before the Rain of Colorless Fire.

If the dim, choking depths were the only obstacle to manhood among the nomads, there would not be so many "boys" of thirty and forty. Other creatures live in the soup of particles too. The burrowing worms seem to like these places as lairs. Water collects there in small amounts, attracting certain odd fungus creatures. Worst of all are the loathsome osid-mrin, a manlike race that, by local legend, first built the cities beneath the dustlakes and (again by hearsay) wants to recruit others into their new race through some horrible operation or transformation. Still, the rewards match the dangers: full manhood in the tribe, gems and jewelry for decoration, and the more prized trophies of a dive, civilized treasures such as artworks, books or even magic items.

The southwestern ruins are known for large domes and tall onion-topped minarets, which sometimes poke above the dust and give a way down.

Notes for the DM

Each southwestern nomad has type Q treasure. The osid-mrin are meenlocks. Purple worms and ankhegs also live in the fertile dust. Movement in the water-dust works like movement in water. The bottoms of the dustlakes can hold many kinds of fungus creatures, including myconids in lakes not infested with meenlocks. The dust of the central regions makes a strong lye when mixed with water.

Source: GA p.91-92. Rewritten in plain words.

In the middle of Flocktime (printed "locktime") in CY 198, the Great Kingdom was amazed by a ball of fire that appeared over the Oljatt Sea, crossed Sunndi, Idee, Ahlissa and Onnwal, and vanished somewhere beyond the Sea of Gearnat. It was seen as far south as the Olman Isles and as far north as Eastfair and Rel Mord, and it caused wonder and worry even in those prosperous, confident days. Selvor the Younger traced it back to where it came from among the stars and declared that the shooting star meant "wealth, strife, and a living death." This caused panic in some of the larger cities, above all Rauxes, where several leading nobles took it as a sign of the end of the world, or at least of an era, and stirred up trouble. When years passed and nothing of the sort happened, Selvor was dismissed from his post and the court and became a laughingstock among his colleagues. There matters rested for more than 300 years, while chaos swallowed most of the Flanaess and few had time or patience for a disgraced astrologer's work.

In 514, Jemrek Longsight, a dwarven sage who had been deeply struck by the fireball as a child, made the opposite kind of study. Using records of its flight, she traced it not back to its source but down to the ground. Her calculations put the landing on the eastern wing of the Abbor-Alz, between the Bright Desert and the Nesser River. Based on earlier shooting stars and what they left behind, she predicted a great deposit of pure metal at the site: iron certainly, and possibly gold and mithral too. Her approach is often cited as proof that dwarven habits of mind persist even in those with the least dwarvish callings.

Her announcement set every power in the region scrambling. All over the Iron League the dwarf clans and other groups made, broke and leaned on alliances as they prepared expeditions. The Herzog of the South Province sent a large band of warriors and prospectors, reportedly told to come back with news of the deposit or not at all. The Principality of Ulek took an interest, as did Almor, Nyrond, the Duchy of Urnst, and trading houses from the Wild Coast and even Greyhawk and Dyvers. Even the rulers of the Pomarj, then new to power, sent a badly prepared company of orcs, goblins and ogres. As these forces closed on the area Longsight had marked, chilling tales of murder, treachery and massacre began reaching the outside world. The weaker groups soon turned back for lack of supplies or men. A temporary alliance of dwarven interests slaughtered the Pomarj force. The people of the Celadon Forest, who did not want such goings-on near their lands, unexpectedly blocked Nyrond and Urnst. The Herzog's troops vanished into the Bright Desert and were never seen again. Everyone was harassed by the natives of the Abbor-Alz, who as always resented intruders, and by the Sea Princes, who were drawn by the supply ships.

After five years of struggle, the House of Highforge, one of the leading dwarf clans of Irongate, came out as finder and holder of the starstone's wealth. It built a port on the waterless coast where the Abbor-Alz meets the Bright Desert and laid a secret trail inland. Highforge and its allies kept everything secret, and with good reason: iron, platinum, gold, mithral and adamantite began pouring out into the world through the closely guarded harbor. Few have reported on the mine itself, but scattered remarks suggest the dwarves found a broad hollow of fused, shattered rock where the star had landed and set themselves up in a nearby mesa, from which they ran a well-planned mining operation. They dug deep artesian wells and built cisterns. They called the mine and settlement Azak-Zil, or Pureheart.

For five years Highforge grew rich, upsetting metal markets as far away as Rauxes. Then the flow suddenly stopped. The port city of Zarak was still there, but word from the mines ceased, and those sent inland found the roads wiped out and the dust storms unbearable. Members of a powerful expedition vanished suddenly and silently in the night, even from guarded tents. After spending much of its great fortune trying to find and retake the mines, Clan Highforge heeded bad omens and gave up. Zarak was abandoned.

Since then most southern dwarf clans have declared it folly to meddle with "things from the sky." Many think the mine was cursed, either by something that came from the heavens or by something woken by the star or by the miners. Many point to nomad legends of an ancient nonhuman people who lived in the mesas of the southern Abbor-Alz and still guard them.

Only one person has claimed to find the mines since they were abandoned: Pont Sandmorg of Narwell. His account puts the mesa on the eastern slopes of the hills, facing the Bright Desert, about a hundred miles or more inland. A poisonous salt lake filled part of the nearby hollow, there were hills of tailings from large mining works, and clear signs of a dwarven cliff city could be seen on the mesa's south face. Sandmorg and his men settled for raiding a few ingots from an old roadside depot. Native tribes and packs of unusually fierce and cunning ghouls had thinned their numbers, and they turned back after "a most horrible howling, like a thousand jackals" came from the city that night, along with "a most foul apparition" that appeared to the men on watch. Those who have tried to follow his route have either failed to find the mines or failed to come back.

Notes for the DM

Around the port city there are only a few hardy, surly nomads. Inland the ground is extremely treacherous and dust storms are likely. Signs of earlier expeditions grow more common near the mines, though most of what those doomed groups carried is now in the lairs of desert monsters. Undead are unusually common, especially ghouls and ghasts, many of them dwarves.

If the player characters reach the cliff city or the diggings, they find that the mining still goes on, and so does the fighting that always came with it. Each miner, now undead, wants all the treasure for itself. There are many of them, mostly ghouls and ghasts, and no incorporeal undead in the city and mines. They attack on sight, looking for food or treasure.

The cause is an egg-shaped lump of bluish metal about 2 feet long and 1 foot thick. Anyone who dies within 5 miles of it rises as an undead creature at the next full moon unless the body is blessed first. Undead within one mile of it are turned at -5, within two miles at -4, and so on to the edge of its area. It also fills its owner with consuming greed and slowly turns the owner into something like a lich. It is now held by a lich who was a 16th level dwarven cleric. Besides raising one main ability score by 2, the stone should have other powers chosen from the DMG; it is an artifact.

Source: GA p.92-93. Rewritten in plain words.

It is generally believed that the Flan of eastern Oerik were simple tribesmen before the events that set off the Suel and Oeridian migrations. That leaves certain ruins in the Griff and Corusk Mountains to be explained. Massive stone foundations, straight level roads, and leveled or terraced mountainsides seem, from the few doorways that survive, to have been built for creatures of human size, and elves or humanoids are unlikely to have built such things. Jade carvings and green ceramic figures found at these sites, and now and then in rivers flowing out of the mountains, show people with Flan features and dress, and the Duchy of Tenh and the Coltens still tell stories of a powerful mountain state of Flan blood. The dwarves of the region may know more, but if so they keep the usual demi-human silence about ancient times. One of the greatest works of this lost people, whoever they were, is the mountain called Tostenhca in Flan and, more commonly, Skrellingshald, the name the Suel barbarians gave it. It has been found many times and lost again just as often.

Skrellingshald stands among the Griff Mountains, but unlike the wild crags around it, its peak has been leveled flat. On this plateau sits a city of heroic size carved out of the living rock, with many grand houses and large pyramids and ramps of unknown purpose. There are big water tanks, and water was evidently once piped all through the city. The broad avenues are lined with tall statues of the same greenish-black stone as the mountain, all with typical Flan features, which is where the city's name comes from. Some houses are three or more stories high, and inside are murals, their colors still fresh, showing the lives of the people. One block covered in such painting was taken to the town of Calbut in Tenh and shown as an example of ancient Flan skill, though some think it a clever forgery. Beneath the city, tunnels lead down to openings lower on the mountain, most ending in terraces that must once have been farm fields. The climate must have been kinder in the city's day, for now it is wrapped in snow for much of the year.

For all its mystery, Skrellingshald might be little known if not for stories of great treasure there. It does somewhat resemble the land that legend places in the Griffs, where the buildings are "roofed in gold." But no human race lives in the citadel, and whatever treasure it has is not on open display. Its inhabitants are said to be especially vicious and cunning kobolds, and perhaps some devilish allies, who haunt the tunnels beneath. Griffons and giant eagles hunt the skies, and the statues are said to guard the city. If it ever had gold roofs, they were looted long ago. What remains is a wealth of jade jewelry and statues scattered over the region, and a great store of gold in a very odd form: balls about the size of two fists together. The hoards of golden balls are somewhere inside the pyramids, but meddling with them is said to be unhealthy; stories say those who carry them off catch a horrible wasting, rotting disease.

The citadel is protected by more than its remoteness and fierce inhabitants. Deep gorges or high mountains surround it on every side, and the altitude saps the strength of lowlanders. It is cold and windy in every season and often so cloudy that one cannot see more than a few hundred yards. No one knows exactly where it is. Few have looked, and those who found it and came back usually say little. A typical case is Hradji Beartooth, a Frost Barbarian chief who led a band in search of it in 520.

Hradji came back later that year with fewer men and far more wealth, mostly the golden balls. Naturally he would not say where the mountain was, since he meant to gather a stronger force and go back the next season for even more. But Hradji and most of his men died within the year, some as soon as they got home, and everyone who spent much time around the gold sickened and died as well. His heir got rid of the hoard by trading it to merchants of the Great Kingdom, and the curse is said to circulate there still as coin of the realm, though this may be a tale invented to undermine the Emperor's currency.

As proof that Hradji really reached Skrellingshald, he also brought back two young griffons and a shield of pebbly, fire-resistant hide that has since been identified as the skin of a devilish creature.

Some dwarf clans of the Griffs are rumored to know where the citadel is. They certainly use the roads said to have been built by its makers, along with their tunnels and roadside fountains, so it would be no surprise if they had learned something of its location.

Notes for the DM

The kobolds of Skrellingshald are well prepared to drive off invaders while spending few kobold lives. They shoot from above and roll boulders down on attackers. They are smarter than typical kobolds and have many shamans and witch doctors. Their chief wears a medallion that lets the wearer summon an ice devil once a year if one intelligent creature is sacrificed. Those who try the hard climb up the outside of the mountain, or come by air, must deal with griffons, white dragons and the uncertain, windy weather (add 15 mph to all wind speeds around Skrellingshald). Lowlanders lose 2 points of constitution at this altitude.

The city is guarded by stone golems, which make up part of the statues, and, if tombs or altars are disturbed, by natural and magical traps and by undead or beings from other planes. Artwork from the city is very valuable if it can be carried away, especially in Tenh.

The curse on the golden balls is permanent, but its effects on one person can be removed with cure disease and remove curse. Each succeeds with the same chance as dispel magic against a 12th level enchantment. The curse strikes anyone who owns the balls or stays near them for more than four hours. It takes the form of a chronic severe disease of the blood and skin that strikes within 1d4 weeks and becomes terminal once it has run its full course as a severe illness.

Source: GA p.93-95. Rewritten in plain words.

The Sinking Isle has haunted the waters near the islands of the Sea Barons since time out of mind. The first Oeridian tribes to fish the Solnor there knew of it, the Flan before them had legends of it, and the seafaring elves of Lendore Isle have still older tales. Neither our civilization nor even the elves' was the first in the Flanaess; others came in times so long ago that the very shape of the land has changed since, and the Sinking Isle is a reminder of them.

The area around Asperdi Isle, the northernmost of the Sea Barons' islands, has rare but powerful earthquakes. Perhaps one of these long ago sent an island city to the sea floor, and perhaps the same unrest sometimes lifts it back into the air. Local sailors say its movements can never be predicted, but are sometimes heralded by tremors and a boiling and bubbling that stirs up dark mud and releases bubbles of foul-smelling gas. The isle is also said to rise most often in storms or fog. At such times coastal traders and pirates, who normally prefer the sheltered inner passage between Asperdi Island and the Solnor's unpredictable waves, either go the long way round or stay in port. Many northern captains raiding south will not try the strait at all, having no friendly locals to warn them.

The Sinking Isle does not always give warning, nor does it always rise fully above the water. Often only its highest points stick up, as if lying in wait for careless ships. Sailors credit the isle, or whoever controls it, with an evil will and blame it for every disappearance in the strait. More than one tells of nearly running aground, of a suspicious darkness in the water on a clear day, or of breakers where there should be none. A very few claim to have watched the island or even landed on it, but they say so in whispers, since loud boasters are said to vanish from their homes some dark, rainy night afterward. So only faint rumors of the Sinking Isle and its twisted ruins reach the outside world.

One famous man was far less careful than adventurers today: Atirr Aedorich, a hero of the Great Kingdom in its youth. In 155, as a young man, he was sent south by his father to study at the university of Rel Astra, then a great center of magical learning. The isle was less active in those days, but as fate would have it, a sudden squall drove Atirr's ship onto its hidden claws. Atirr was fascinated rather than frightened, as the nobles of the Great Kingdom were in those days. For a full hour, while the crew sweated at the pumps and struggled to patch the single hole in the hull, he studied the strange glowing landscape and made several sketches, until one of the Solnor's strange great waves came rolling into the strait and lifted the damaged ship free. Atirr swore to return and learn the island's secrets.

He did return north some years later, as Herzog of the North Province, but not until middle age did he have the leisure to take up his study. By examining certain ancient Suel books and using the arts he had learned at Rel Astra, he worked out a way to predict or command the isle's movements. This knowledge, like much else, was lost in the Turmoil Between Crowns, but several accounts survive of what he found when he sailed alongside the risen city.

In the short time before the island sank again, Atirr and his companions recovered or recorded a great many objects from among the spiky, heavily decorated ruins. There were many panes of fine stained glass, some still whole and some in shades no modern artist has matched, and a number of twisted ornaments of gold and lead later found to be sahuagin work. Atirr also found a book sealed against the water in a lead casket. All of these were sent to the court at Rauxes in the Overking's honor, and Atirr, a patient man, hoped to study them further in retirement. He called the book especially interesting: among other things, it was written in a lost language and contained "an ancient history together with magical secrets."

Sadly, he never got the chance. Two years after his finds, he and his whole crew went down in a storm off the coast of the North Province that apparently even the Herzog's powers could not calm. The book has since vanished, though it may still be somewhere in the catacombs of Rauxes; it is hard to be sure, since so little news now comes out of that court. Atirr was convinced from his first study that the city was not built mainly by sahuagin but by some land-dwelling race, though sahuagin-like creatures and other sea life appear often in its decoration.

Later observers have searched the coast and sea near the isle's site and, on one dark evening, may have seen its upper towers. The area is cold and forbidding for so southern a place. Fishermen say the catch there is excellent but nets are often fouled, and those who go into the water find it dark and cold. Most are happy to leave the Sinking Isle to the sahuagin, or whatever race of the deep holds it now.

Notes for the DM

The Sinking Isle is held by sahuagin or by krakens, depending on the currents of the moment. When the southern current reaches it, the water around it is clear and warm; when the northern current touches it, the water is cold and dark. Each kind of water has its typical creatures: sahuagin in the warm, krakens in the cold. In any month there is a 10% chance that the current will reverse over the following month.

The island's rising and sinking are controlled by sacrificing intelligent creatures at an altar in the middle of the largest ruin. The sahuagin did not build the city, but it would be fair to suggest that its builders were the once-human ancestors of the sahuagin themselves. In any case they were an evil race by the end. The ruins look much like Gothic architecture, heavily decorated, with many tall pointed arches.

The isle is fairly empty while one current is giving way to the other. It normally rests on the bottom. In each month the characters spend nearby, there is a 15% chance it rises on its own, staying above water for 1d6 hours. Local fishermen have a 10% chance of knowing exactly where it is, local mermen 50%, and neither will be keen to tell or to act as guides. The sahuagin and krakens have a few allies ashore who keep them informed.

The House of Rax may be holding Atirr's book. Besides its history, it is both a libram of ineffable damnation and a book of vile deeds.

Source: GA p.95-96. Rewritten in plain words.

The Drachensgrabs have always been an odd land, out of place among the more settled parts of the Flanaess. Legends say some powerful being sleeps there and that something unclean hangs about certain hills, and the humanoids' seizure of the Pomarj is just the kind of thing one would expect of the region. Rumors aside, there is at least one sleeping, dangerous power in these pleasant-looking lands: the badly named "Twisted Forest."

The Twisted Forest is not a forest at all but a collection of stone pillars, pitted gray shapes that look as much like humanoids as trees. They are scattered over the hillside meadows like so many leafless olive trees, though no one would really take them for plants. They range from the size of a very small goblin to that of a very large ogre, and their twisted upper parts look as much like raised arms as branches. The whole place is unwholesome and unnerving, with a feeling of being watched. The patterns on the trunks look like tormented faces, and despite their great age they carry none of the mosses, lichens and birds' nests that cover the local rock outcrops so thickly.

The flowery ground between the "trees" holds a surprising number of bones and many weathered weapons and pieces of gear. At first they might look like the remains of a battle, but they are of very different ages: some so old they have crumbled away and show only as stains in the soil, others far more recent. Where scavengers have not scattered them, the bones and gear are still whole. The killer is not some danger in the hills around but the forest itself. Those who touch the stone shapes often die or go mad.

The goblins of the Pomarj now know the danger well. Early in their invasion, a large company of goblin scouts looking for new land learned from local herdsmen that the forest might hold treasures somehow locked inside the stone shapes. What happened the day they went in is not known, but it seems to have been worse even than the usual danger, which the goblins and their allies might have known about had they not eagerly killed their informants before pushing on. Later observers who have studied the field of stones think there are rather more of them than older accounts suggest. There is also something that surely was not there in past centuries: a contorted river of stone among the pillars, more than thirty feet long and tapered at both ends. Unfortunately, old and new eyewitness accounts cannot be compared directly, since the region's former natives are now dead or scattered.

The forest would be a complete mystery if not for the records of the Keoish court at Niole Dra. An ancient, much-copied manuscript there claims to be a history of the Suel just after the final disaster of their empire, written by Uhas of Neheli. It tells of a particularly wicked band of Suel who fled east with all their treasures along the north shore of the Azure Sea, looking for new land on which to build a powerful nation. They were as learned and powerful as they were cruel, and all their evil ventures succeeded until they slaughtered a band of innocent Flan tribesmen in an especially vile way in the Suenha Hills. That brought on them a terrible curse from certain Flan gods the tribe had worshipped: that none of them, nor any of their kind, should leave the valley where the massacre happened, and that they should stand as monuments to their own wickedness, "pillars of tortured stone for all the world to see." This seems a clear reference to the Twisted Forest, and historians generally agree that the Suenha Hills were the early Suel colonists' name for the Drachensgrab. The deadly effect of the stone figures still needs explaining, since it was surely not part of the original curse; perhaps the powerful Suel wizards found some way to make sure their malice would go on hurting the world, at least in a small area. As further evidence that the figures were once Suel, the flowers found only in the Twisted Forest are kinds seen nowhere else but the far western Sea of Dust.

As for the treasures some insist are buried in the figures, it is probably best not to look for them, given the forest's terrible effect, but if the figures really are a host of transformed Suel, the treasure must be great indeed. What, if anything, might be gained from what may be the newer pillars is unknown, even by rumor.

Notes for the DM

The pillars are mostly the remains of evil creatures. Any evil creature that enters the Twisted Forest is affected within 1d4 to 1d20 turns, depending on how evil it is. From then on it must save vs. spell each round or be turned, with all its goods and gear, into a twisted stone parody of its own form. Victims stay fully aware and can still hear, see and even feel their surroundings, but cannot move and are practically indestructible. Fire, cold, lightning, acid and nonmagical weapons do no damage but cause excruciating pain. The stone is also immune to common spells such as rock to mud, stone to flesh and dispel magic, though know alignment works on it. Only polymorph any object can free a victim, and its success is checked as if dispel magic were used against a 20th level spell. The release is permanent if the victim survives a system shock roll.

Trapped creatures usually have only one way out: they can try to take over the body of another creature that touches or strikes them, as with a magic jar spell. They get one attempt each round of contact, and may also try against anyone who casts speak with stones on them. Once in the new body, the new occupant must survive a system shock roll or die. Resurrection or raise dead on a body killed this way brings back the new occupant, not the old. Either way, the body's former owner is trapped in the attacker's stone form. Every creature is vulnerable to these effects, but ordinary animals feel an antipathy and avoid the pillars.

Freed creatures vary widely. Some are the original Suel band, including powerful spellcasters. The smaller ones are goblins or kobolds and the larger ones usually ogres. The big snakelike figure is a red dragon. Some are non-evil creatures trapped in new bodies. Their reactions depend on alignment and how long they were imprisoned, and some of the older ones are quite mad. Their gear varies just as much.

Source: GA p.96-97. Rewritten in plain words.

The stretch of land facing the Icy Sea between the Cold Marshes and the Forlorn Forest is one of the least traveled regions of the Flanaess. Even the Rovers of the Barrens see little use in it; they mostly keep to the grasslands farther south, and even these hardy folk call it "the Wastes." But even the poorest parts of the Flanaess have their wonders, and here it is the famous Burning Cliffs.

The cliffs are named for their northern edge on the Icy Sea, where the smoking rocks drop steeply into the water; ships along that coast can see them from a hundred miles or more on a clear day. In fact the burning reaches well inland. It is mostly oily shale and a black flammable rock that give off smoke and steam from a fire that has burned without stopping since the earliest histories, and it may have spread in recent centuries.

One might think the fire would make the local climate easier to bear, but the smoldering, steaming rubble gives off more heat than is comfortable, and in places it is actually in flames. In most seasons one would have to stand right in the blaze to feel it, since the fierce north winds soon carry the heat away, and even then the comfort would come with sooty fumes and steam. Ships passing downwind of the cliffs tend to leave with darker sails than they started with. A warmed traveler would find nothing to eat in that desolate land either, apart from a few scrawny northern deer that feed on the sparse lichens and willows upwind of the burning. The Rovers rarely bother to go there and see it as just another obstacle on their rare trips through the Wastes.

The cliffs seem to have changed somewhat over the past century. Sailors note that the clouds rising from them now hold more soot than steam, and that at night a dull glow covers the whole region, as if there were taller flames near the middle. Both the Rovers and the seamen have noticed the burning area spreading by up to several hundred yards a year, though it shrinks back a little in cold winters; it is already nearly 30 miles across. Shapes are sometimes reported moving behind the wall of cloud and soot. Perhaps most important, the forests, marshes and grasslands at the edge of the Wastes, hundreds of miles away, have begun to sicken and die, which supports the claim of some scholars that the Burning Cliffs caused the Wastes in the first place. Most northerners do not care much; the lands up there are wide and seem endless.

None of these newer reports has moved the practical northern peoples to act or investigate, and what more is known was found by accident. In 523 a man named Storrich of the Hold of Stonefist tried to get ahead by less than traditional means and failed. Poisoners are not well thought of even in that grim country, so Storrich and his followers had to flee. It was summer, and the Ice Barbarians would not let his ship pass in peace, so he and his pursuers turned west. Unluckily for Storrich, his pilot ran the ship aground off the Wastes, and his company had to take to the land with the pursuers close behind. As a last desperate move, Storrich took a stone path he found leading into the smoldering ground. His pursuers turned back there, well satisfied; after waiting some days and seeing nothing of him, they told the Master of the Hold they had driven Storrich to his death. They were wrong.

Two years later Storrich turned up in Dyvers, and being a talkative man he soon told his story, or rather several stories, some contradicting others. A fairly believable account can be pieced together from his boasting. His company stumbled on a city of fire-loving creatures and managed to steal valuable gold and jewelry. The fight that followed, and the flight south through flames and fumes, killed all his followers; only he was protected from the full effect of the cliffs, apparently by magic in some of his possessions. Who he robbed is unclear, since his claims kept changing: at various times they were elementals, devils, demons, harginn and even efreet. These contradictions were never sorted out, because within a month of arriving Storrich choked to death at a banquet. No other survivors could confirm his tale, but he clearly had gained a great fortune in jacinth and gold. He spent freely in his last weeks and still left a sizable hoard behind.

Since his death a number of people have tried the Burning Cliffs. Some have gone in by the paths that can now sometimes be seen across the region; others have tried scouting from the air, or relied on magical protection from the heat and set out across country. None who went deep into the land has come back. Several reports say Iuz and the Horned Society have taken an interest and sent large companies north, for reasons known only to the rulers of Dorakaa and Molag. Someone has built an altar to Pyremius on the northern coast of the cliffs, whether to appease or to worship is not known. Members of that cult have now and then been linked to the region, but they fiercely deny it.

Notes for the DM

Depending on how fierce the fire is at a given spot, the heat and fumes deal 1d3 points of heat damage and 1d4 points of poison damage (save vs. poison to avoid the poison damage), anywhere from once a day to once a round. These effects are halved for anyone standing on a path or otherwise out of direct contact with the burning rock.

The region's inhabitants all come from the Elemental Plane of Fire, and Iuz and the Horned Society have been courting and recruiting evil fire creatures among them. A large town has grown up near the center of the blaze around a gate to the Plane of Fire. Storrich's boasts were entirely true: he went through to the City of Brass itself and got away with some minor treasures, so the residents are now on the lookout for intruding "vermin." Unless the link to the Plane of Fire is broken, the Burning Cliffs will keep growing, to the great delight of the cult of Pyremius.

pages.name: Csipros Erd, the Geysers of Death

text.content:
Source: GA p.97-98. Rewritten in plain words.

In 510 CY the last Euroz and Jebli tribes were driven out of the Lortmil Mountains. One very large horde unwisely tried to reach the Yatil Mountains by crossing the gap from the Lorridges. Smaller bands had gone before it, and the combined cavalry of Bissel and Veluna was ready. Much of the horde was destroyed, but the rest survived by a ferocious counterattack and got into the southern Yatils. There halfling, human and elven forces raised by the locals harried them, being in no mood to let such numerous and ferocious creatures gain a foothold. The horde finally turned south, hoping to reach the Barrier Peaks through the Bramblewood Forest. There it met its last and fatal enemy: Sandor the Headstrong, young lord of Polvar province in eastern Ket.

Unlike the others chasing the goblin and orc horde, the lord of Polvar was not worried about it settling in his lands, which it clearly did not want to do. He was driven instead by rumors that had reached Ket after the earlier battles: that the carts the horde's leader, the half-orc Urgush, guarded so fiercely held a great store of gems and precious metals gathered during the horde's years in the Lortmils. Sandor was determined not to let such a prize escape. He chased the horde in a string of forced marches that wore out his foot soldiers so badly that many fell behind and the rest could not mount a decisive attack against Urgush's resistance. The chase led through the Bramblewood and into the hills, Sandor's force slowly recovering and Urgush's dwindling. In desperation Urgush turned up an unknown valley to make a last stand, and there disaster struck both sides.

The northern Barrier Peaks and the Yatils have many hot springs, well known and well liked by the Ketites, so Sandor was neither surprised nor worried when he began passing through the outskirts of a field of geysers, full of white frothy stone and colored pools and pits. He only slowed his cavalry over the rough ground. Being supremely confident, he was not much bothered either when scouts reported several nearby lakes of a blood-red color that Ketite peasants called unlucky. The horde's wagons were in sight and plainly stuck. Sandor readied his men for a hard-driving attack, hoping to scatter the horde and take its prize, when the ground began to shake.

With terrible speed a powerful wind swept down the valley, knocking the orcs flat and overturning the precious carts, which spilled a wealth of gems. Sandor's men had hardly begun to grasp this when they too were thrown down. Only those on the upper slopes, where Sandor had been placing the crossbowmen, were spared. None of the others even got back to their knees. Farther down the valley the strange wind snapped trees off at the base, and geysers set off by the tremors shot into the air.

Sandor sent a careful group of scouts into the ruined valley, but they fainted long before reaching the floor. He tried the descent himself and had to be dragged out by the rope he had wisely tied to himself beforehand. Sandor and some of the scouts recovered, as did some of those who had been on the middle slopes, but everyone else was lost, and the invisible poison blocked any further entry. After two fruitless days Sandor gave in to his much reduced force and went home to Polvar, swearing every man to keep the treasure's location secret and vowing to return.

As soon as he had recovered he set out again, taking care to bring everyone who had first seen the valley. The sight of the Euroz and Jebli wealth had inflamed his greed, and he was sure that with certain magic treasures he had acquired, he and his men would come back with enough wealth to make Polvar a nation of its own. He never returned.

Many have since looked for Csipros Erd, the Geysers of Death, but none have come back to tell of them. The maze of hills and valleys around the northern Barrier Peaks is large, and quite a few have geysers and hot springs. No trace has been found of the "blood red lakes" in Sandor's account. As far as anyone knows, Urgush's treasure, along with what must be a great many human and humanoid bones, still lies undiscovered.

Notes for the DM

The geysers and hot springs of the Valley of Death are no more dangerous than those elsewhere, which is to say one must be very careful. A geyser blast might deal anything from 2d2 to 2d20 points of damage (a save vs. breath weapon fits), and most erupt and rest at basically unpredictable intervals. The water and mud pools can do similar damage to anyone in them, over anything from segments to hours; even comfortable temperatures sap strength over time.

Small, clear, lifeless lakes in the region sometimes release poison gas. There are two along the approach to Csipros Erd and a larger one at the head of the valley above the geyser basin. The gas has no smell or color and otherwise works like a cloudkill spell. It fills a huge volume, is slow to disperse, and flowing downhill can move fast, like a flood. The lakes usually release gas only when strongly disturbed, as by a small earthquake or a landslide. For 3d8 weeks after a release they turn rust or blood red and will not release any gas.

The gems, jewelry, precious metal and magic items of Csipros Erd are now scattered over a wide area, picked over at various times by locals who braved the geysers, which are now extremely active around the site. Much is still in the hot pools, guarded by steam and mud elementals that have moved in. The rest belongs to ogres, various giants, giant ravens and eagles, and lesser creatures. Sandor's force ran into a coalition of hill giant tribes formed to loot the treasure, which broke up in quarrels soon after. One tribe still lives by Csipros Erd and has learned to throw boulders into the lakes when enemies come up the valley floor, which sets off a release of gas. The valley is remarkable for the number of bones in it, many now crusted with minerals from the hot springs.

Source: GA p.98-99. Rewritten in plain words.
