More than one scholar has noted that while the Baklunish wizards' destruction of the Suel has lasted longer, surviving to this day as the Sea of Dust, the Invoked Devastation that the Suel first loosed on the Baklunish must have been more thorough. A thousand years later, ruins of Suel cities can still be found in the barren Sea of Dust, while the far more livable Dry Steppes seem to hold no remains of Baklunish cities at all. The great exception is Tovag Baragu, known in the east as the Stone Circles, which still stands near the salt lake of Udrukankar at the edge of the Flanaess.

Tovag Baragu ("Navel of the Oerth" in Baklunish) is a set of five broad circles of huge, smooth pillars of extremely hard white rock. The pillars are sometimes fluted but usually completely plain, and they stand on a wide pavement of blocks of the same stone. The whole structure is round, more than a mile across, and perfectly level, though the land around it slopes west toward Udrukankar. On its western side a series of broad, shallow steps leads down from the platform and ends rather suddenly 20 or 30 feet above the salt flats. Its eastern edge is level with the surrounding ground, and dust and plants have crept over its margin.

Moving the pillars, each about 40 feet tall, must have been a huge task. There is no such rock within 200 miles, and where the stone came from is unknown; perhaps it came by barge, if the great rivers that once crossed the steppe still flowed when Tovag Baragu was built. Just as surprising, since so little else survived the Invoked Devastation, is its perfect condition: no erosion, not one tilted pillar or tipped paving stone. The local tribes do not claim their ancestors built it, which is very unusual given their nature and their ancestors' real achievements. Nomads will solemnly swear, for instance, that the rocky pinnacles north of Lake Udrukankar were once a great lighthouse built for the lakeside city that stood there a thousand years ago, and perhaps they are right. Tovag Baragu does look a little like the badly worn ruins found in the Jotens and Crystalmists, which are credited to an ancient civilization of stone giants. Without evidence, though, its origin is uncertain, though the obvious answer is that the Baklunish built it.

The local human and centaur nomads hold Tovag Baragu sacred, and many tribes of the Dry Steppes make a yearly pilgrimage and festival there. They trade, arrange marriages, and gather to celebrate the destruction of the Suel while their priests call down more curses on that land. The event lasts two weeks, and everyone attending or traveling to or from it must give up feuds and war, and is protected from them in turn. For most of the rest of the year the site is deserted, and it is thought bad luck even to see it on the horizon. That is easy to understand, since some of what happens there would disturb even a civilized mind.

One common effect for those who walk among the circles is that distant things seen between the pillars are sometimes magnified, and the other senses can be heightened in the same way. One can learn astonishing things like this, as in the case of Celene, but that is a story for another time. With concentration the view can sometimes be sharpened or aimed. Sometimes, though, things are seen through the pillars that are almost surely distant in time or in planes rather than in space. One of the most common is a glimpse of a great lakeside city, usually at night. Another is a green plain crowded with the strange mammals sometimes found near the Sulhauts. More rarely, one may see or hear places that must be the Outer Planes.

These views would be entertaining rather than frightening, except that now and then a connection forms and things can pass between Tovag Baragu and the place shown. Luckily or not, these openings are brief. They may explain some of the unusual creatures in the southern Dry Steppes.

The locals also believe Tovag Baragu affects the weather, and there is good evidence for it: the few outsiders allowed to watch the yearly ceremonies see the nomad priests' weather-calling powers greatly strengthened. Whether Tovag Baragu works on its own, without guidance, is an open question.

Notes for the DM

Treat Tovag Baragu as an artifact, as described in the DMG. Its powers, and when they work, depend on the movements of Oerth's heavenly bodies. Each circle is linked to a particular moon or planet and works only when that body is in the sky. What people in the circle do at those times can affect the result, but the player characters should not be allowed to learn everything needed to control it properly. The most common full connection is to an Ice Age (Pleistocene) setting. Whether the city seen is the past, an alternate world or the future is up to the DM. The player characters might be allowed to get the impression that Tovag Baragu keeps the Sea of Dust the way it is, but they should not be able to do anything about it until they reach extremely high levels, if then.

If the campaign includes the Cup and Talisman of Al'Akbar (DMG, Artifacts), a number of interactions between it and Tovag Baragu can be set up.

The nearest settlement is a very large community of dervishes sworn to protect the site from foreign meddlers. The human and centaur tribes of the Dry Steppes generally feel the same, if less fiercely, and will do what they can to keep adventurers away. They certainly will not act as guides, except perhaps for an occasional unscrupulous tribesman.

Source: GA p.99-101. Rewritten in plain words.

Any student of nature can see that the fields of black ice covering the northern tip of Oerik are not natural. Like the Sea of Dust, they are almost certainly made and kept in being by magic. Put simply, the towering wall of blackened ice that meets the northbound traveler should not last. Even ordinary snow and ice do not survive the summer on land at those latitudes, as the Icy Sea shows by breaking up every spring. Dark ice is especially weak, since it soaks up heat; merchants in northern cities commonly sprinkle ashes on their doorsteps to melt the ice, which works even in the weak winter sun. Given such a magical nature, it is no wonder strange tales come from the region. One of the odder but more reliable is that of the Rainbow Vale, Rigodruok.

Some years ago a fragment of a document was recovered from Blackmoor Castle that gave weight to the widespread stories of a land "beyond the black ice where the sun never sets." It did not describe the land itself, but it gave clear directions for finding it in the wastes of the Black Ice. The parchment turned up for sale in the bazaar of Eru-Tovar and fell into the hands of Sormod, a merchant and adventurer from Perrenland who was visiting. Being a romantic, Sormod set up an expedition as soon as he could find backers and left Dantredun in Richfest of CY 453.

In CY 460 a book surfaced in the city of Greyhawk claiming to be the personal journal of Henriki Ardand, the expedition's magician. True or not, it is a marvelous tale. Henriki describes the hard crossing of the sooty ice, where hot springs underground, like those beneath Blackmoor, put the expedition in danger. They weaken the ice and make crossing it risky, since a cavern may suddenly collapse under travelers' weight. In places small volcanoes blacken the fresh snow on the ice. Between these dangers, the jumbled fields of collapsed ice, certain "iceworms" (most likely remorhaz) and the hostile dark-furred bugbears of the region, the expedition moved slowly, and several members were lost or refused to go on. At last they reached a range of low peaks just poking above the ice, as their directions had said. What they found on the other side must at first have seemed a paradise to the survivors. Henriki calls it the Rainbow Vale.

Past a band of mist, the explorers saw a green, fertile bowl of land, warmed and lit by a sunlike body floating half a mile above its center. Several large islands of land drifted around it too, some big enough to hold small rivers whose cascades of droplets gave the valley the name Henriki chose. Below the miniature sun lay a central lake, and beside it Sormod's group could see several clusters of broken reddish towers.

Sormod and his band climbed down the steep cliffs into the valley's forests, passing first through birch, fir and sablewood, then oak and beech woods where they stopped to gather uskfruit and yarpick nuts, then magnolias and fig trees, and down to the lakeshore, where palms and deklos thrived in the steamy heat. Curls of vapor rose from the part of the lake beneath the valley's light. They camped by one of the waterfalls falling from the sky near the ruins they had seen from the rim, and were surprised to find the buildings made of deeply rusted iron. Perhaps worn out by the long journey, or drowsy in the unfamiliar heat, the watchmen fell asleep.

Sormod's party was neither weak nor poorly equipped, but without warning they had little chance against the sudden attack: goblins, bugbears and giant spiders, some of astonishing size, speed and fiendish intelligence. The camp was scattered, and Sormod, Henriki and the other survivors watched in horror as their companions were bundled up and hauled on ropes of spider silk to the nearest floating island.

Henriki and the others regrouped, and for some weeks they explored carefully. They found a group of primitive humans who apparently worship the spiders and their humanoid servants, and many baffling constructions of metal and glass in the ruins. Without their gear they did not want to risk the overland journey back, but a friendly caveman told them of a tunnel leading south that eventually reached the surface. With an escape route assured, they used Henriki's remaining powers to raid the sky island where their companions had been taken. They found no sign of their friends, but in a grove beside the spider village they found some very large spider statues with big diamond eyes. They took these and fled.

The long trek south through the tunnels killed more of the group, some from heat exhaustion as they passed the warm springs. Eventually they came out south of the Black Ice at the headwaters of the Fler. From there they crossed the Burneal Forest, where Sormod died from a poisoned arrow in a quarrel with forest tribesmen. The survivors, Henriki, a priest of Pharlagn (as printed) from Schwartzenbruin and two Wolf Nomads, split the treasure and went their separate ways, none willing ever again to face the terrors of the land beyond the Black Ice.

Notes for the DM

The valley's main inhabitants are goblins, bugbears, giant spiders of various kinds, and the subject cavemen. DMs with the Oriental Adventures rules may add bakemono and goblin spiders, and creatures from almost any climate can be added. The whole valley is rich in diamonds, and the spiders and their allies have a number of magic items salvaged from the ruins.

Characters might learn the way there from the expedition's survivors or their descendants. The valley's origin need not be explained, at least in the first adventures. The tunnel at the headwaters of the Fler is hard to find without a long search and probably impossible without directions. It is in hex Y4-56. Rigodruok, the cavemen's name for the valley and the name on any old directions, is in hex W4-51.

Source: GA p.101-102. Rewritten in plain words.

The Lortmils have always been famous for gems and precious metals, and there are many stories of hidden settlements where dwarves, gnomes or halflings are as rich as kings. Some have a real basis, though the wealth is greatly exaggerated: gems and gold are worth much less near where they are found, and shipping them out safely is costly, even since the Hateful Wars (dated CY 520 in this book; the Guide dates them 498-510). Still, one of the wilder tales may be true after all.

In Growfest of 556, the simple folk living on a river that flows into the Jewel south of the Courwood found a beautifully made bronzewood casket on a sandbar. Inside was the body of a young tallfellow halfling with unusually handsome, noble features, preserved in a sweet-smelling resinous liquid. He was dressed in silks and gold brocade set with emeralds and wore armlets, rings and necklaces of gold and emerald, with much other treasure. Perhaps because of elven influence, the river folk there are not like other men. Each took just one ornament, since by their custom pallbearers may claim one item from the grave goods, and they buried the casket in a secret place, each swearing never to tell where. Even so, the story spread up and down the river like wildfire, and soon people as far off as Gradsul and Highport were guessing where the casket came from.

The news revived a long-forgotten tale written by Pontus Hardiggin, a halfling who traveled widely between 350 and 390 before retiring to write his memoirs. Among other stories, some plainly made up, Hardiggin described visiting a happy land where halflings and giants lived together in peace, blessed with fertile soil, good health, a great deposit of gold, emeralds and useful metals, and above all, hidden from the outside world. He placed it in the Yatils, but that may have been a joke, or a way to protect its people. His account and the casket share some striking details: the halflings (tallfellows, unusually handsome), the land's treasures (silk, gold, emeralds, resins), and even burial customs (a bronzewood casket placed in a cave). It seems unlikely that simple river folk could pull off a hoax elaborate enough to copy an old, little-known tale, or costly enough: two of the emerald ornaments have since turned up in jewelers' shops on the Wild Coast, flawless and of a distinctive design.

Still, it is hard to see how the land Hardiggin described could stay hidden so long. By his account the valley is at least ten miles across, and a large settlement that includes giants is hardly easy to miss. Several things may help. He describes the nearby mountain slopes as foggy and covered in dense forest, and the only passes require climbing sheer cliffs or finding secret passages cut through the rock. Either way the altitude is exhausting, and the whole route is guarded. The only other way in is a river that disappears near a whirlpool in Esmerin's eastern quarter and runs through underground caverns, an even harder route. As for seeing it from the air, only giant eagles and aarakocra are likely to, and Hardiggin called them allies. Finally, Esmerin is said to be protected by the magic of a huge emerald "as big as a giant's head," standing in a pavilion at the center of the main settlement. Hardiggin said it could change how the land looks from a distance, and credited it with power over the weather and other things.

According to Hardiggin, anyone who wanders into Esmerin is made to stay; evil intruders are simply killed. Those who seem unwilling are given a geas never to leave. The charming Hardiggin narrowly escaped this, or at least put it off long enough to flee by a dangerous route down the caverns beside the underground river leaving Esmerin, past the burial chambers and through several flooded passages (one wonders how so reckless a fellow lived to write his memoirs). Perhaps, apart from Hardiggin, every outsider has been kept out or kept in.

Whatever protections Esmerin has, it surely needs them. Over the past twenty years hundreds of fortune hunters have crossed the Lortmils looking for it, many of them dangerous and evil. Some well-equipped expeditions from the Pomarj have pushed into the Lortmils through the Suss, for example. None has yet come back with a report, but given the hard evidence of the emerald ornaments, that may be only a matter of time. One hopes, too, that the casket will not be found and its contents, and perhaps the dead halfling's spirit, examined.

Notes for the DM

Esmerin is home to 1,600 tallfellow halflings and 400 stone giants. All are well fed, well educated, healthy, peaceful and handsome, with the maximum number of exceptional individuals among them. Two colonies of giant eagles are their allies. At the center of the main settlement is an artifact, as per the DMG. Besides any other powers, it is intelligent, can use its bearer's senses, and casts spells as an 18th level cleric and 14th level druid. It can also create hallucinatory terrain large enough to hide Esmerin from the air. Within five miles of the emerald, crop yields are doubled and natural mineral deposits renew themselves in 2d10 years. It is very well guarded, naturally, and will defend itself if it must.

This civilization of stone giants and halflings has existed since before the Baklunish-Suel wars and has kept to itself from the start. The two races have influenced each other, so many of the halflings lean toward neutrality and the stone giants toward law and good. They do not like to kill, but they will fight hard to keep their peaceful isolation. By a freak accident the burial casket fell into the river that leaves Esmerin, and they have been on guard ever since (halflings and stone giants live longer than humans, so the memory has not faded).

Good player characters may feel bound to help drive off evil invaders, who will be closing on the settlement at about the time the characters first arrive. Either way, it will be hard to persuade the people of Esmerin to let the adventurers leave.

Source: GA p.102-103. Rewritten in plain words.

The Oljatt Sea is mostly unexplored because of its predatory sea creatures, but bold traders (the book calls them the Sea Lords) have routes along its shallower parts well down the coast of Hepmonaland. One of the main reasons for such a hard voyage is the lacework of islands, reefs, lagoons and lakes called Turucambi.

Turucambi is a maze of limestone rising from the sea floor some 20 leagues off the far eastern tip of Hepmonaland. Captains usually approach along the coast rather than across the deep water, preferring attacks by natives to sea beasts the size of ships. They come for its wealth of precious coral and the odd relic the locals trade.

This tangle of land and water is rich in life above and below the surface, rather too rich for most merchants. It is about 30 miles across and roughly oval, with many small islands made almost entirely of steep ridges. The plant life is dense, and much of it has saw-toothed edges or poisonous sap that raises blisters wherever it touches skin. The branching islands are full of lakes and lagoons, many linked to the sea by underground passages that run through the whole region. All the rock is limestone, riddled with caves large and small, the footing is very difficult, and the main land animals seem to be venomous, bad-tempered snakes and a few crocodiles. Turucambi's wealth is in the water.

Its reefs are among the most complex known and full of surprises. The tides rise and fall a long way, exposing shallows regularly, and there are bottomless sinkholes and fierce tidal races that can toss a ship like a toy. There are plains of white coral, beds of sea grass, mangrove swamps and jumbled gardens of bright coral, all swarming with life from the tiny to the gigantic. The waters teem with mermen, sahuagin, water nagas, sea elves, koalinth, saltwater trolls, ixitxachitl and even a tribe of seagoing lizard men. They fight constantly over territory and to keep out uninvited land folk. Nor are they the only danger: many corals and jellyfish have poison stings that raise painful or deadly welts, as do a number of shellfish and fish, and plesiosaurs cruise the shallows hunting prey large and small.

Turucambi draws the water races for two reasons: it is one of the richest reefs of the Oljatt, and it draws human trade. Precious corals can be harvested in the deeper reef, not only the familiar red and black but the rarer golden coral. In some of the darker, less explored corners there are also ancient treasures, such as small figurines of precious stone or delicately colored bowls, apparently made on land, which are highly prized. In return the reef folk get things hard to make underwater: glass, copper or bronze (they have little use for iron, which rusts too easily), silver and gold jewelry, and much plainer things like wood and stone, obsidian especially. Most have treaties with merchants from civilized lands or with Hepmonaland natives that allow safe passage and free trade.

They may trade even more widely. A ship from Duxchan, blown out to sea and unsure of its position, once approached from the east and saw a huge hulk over a hundred feet long, with many masts and a slender, shallow hull. It seemed to be holed, with its cargo plainly visible under six fathoms of water, but the practical, incurious Duxchaners turned away. Approaching an unfamiliar part of Turucambi is dangerous, not just because of nature but because of the locals, who are quite willing to try piracy instead of trade and resent anyone who might be poaching coral.

Some have suggested that Turucambi may be artificial, in whole or in part, since such twisted islands are found nowhere else in such numbers. That would explain the odd trade goods sometimes found, but the size of the structures strains belief. The hard-headed traders who go there are in no hurry to spend time solving the puzzle, and the residents, even the friendly ones, do not seem eager to answer idle questions.

Notes for the DM

Because these waters are so dangerous, the traders at Turucambi should include the maximum number of exceptional individuals, and so should the various water races.

Some lakes are very warm, above human body temperature; use the heat exhaustion rules if characters explore them. Others hold poisonous dissolved gases below a certain depth (treat as a cloudkill spell). Such water has a sharp smell the characters will not mistake twice.

Minor reef life may carry any of the insinuative poisons, types A to D (see the DMG), or sting like a Portuguese man-of-war, and the locals may have gathered some of these poisons.

Tidal currents and ranges are strongest when Celene and Luna are both full or both new, and weakest when one is at first or last quarter and the other full or new (the range is zero around Growfest or Needfest, printed "Neefest"). Even so, the currents' directions are unlikely to be predictable without local help. Changing tides flood or uncover underground chambers and pull divers into or out of tunnels.

If the player characters explore without a local sponsor, they will very likely be taken for poachers. If they try to find out whether parts of Turucambi are artificial, the coral homes of the present residents will probably confuse them.

The wreck on the east side of Turucambi is a clipper ship (the characters will never have heard of such a thing), carrying china and tea. It may come from another plane, from across the Oljatt, or nowhere explained, as the campaign needs. If the player characters somehow copy its design and find a shipbuilder willing to build such a "monstrosity," and a crew able and willing to sail it (no small tasks), they will find it fast but flimsy, hard to handle (they will probably wreck it experimenting), very expensive to keep up, and of little use in trade or war.

The locals will probably all see the player characters as pawns in their various quarrels.

Sources: Guide p.62-64; GA p.4. Rewritten in plain words; the lists as printed.

The people of Oerth worship many gods. These pages cover only the deities of the central Flanaess, and mostly the lesser gods among them. The greater gods are generally too remote to have much to do with humankind; they are worshipped, but few people take them as patrons.

Gods have been known to step directly into human affairs, but only when those affairs bear directly and crucially on the god's own concerns, and the historians record only a few such cases in the history of the Flanaess. Gods have weighty business of their own and generally cannot be bothered with the petty needs of a band of lowly mortals. Under some circumstances, though, a demi-god or a minor god may well get tangled up in human affairs. Because of the schemes of Iuz and of various demons and evil elementals, St. Cuthbert has become actively aware of events, with indirect help from Beory, who resists elemental destruction. The feud between Iuz and St. Cuthbert may yet lead to open confrontation.

The gods often visit the Prime Material Plane in the form of avatars, to help their worshippers or simply to enjoy themselves, and one way or another they influence every creature on the plane. For some unknown reason the city of Greyhawk gets an unusual amount of their attention, and at least one avatar is usually in the city. Many ballads tell of awe-inspiring clashes between avatars of opposing alignments in its crowded streets, and the streets needed a good deal of repair afterward.

Greyhawk Adventures describes twelve gods in three parts: the deity, the avatar it most often uses, and its clerics. The spells listed with a deity are always available to its clerics. The special spell-like powers are available to the head cleric of any of the deity's temples, granted in times of special need.

The Deity

The deity's name comes first, then its status: greater deity, lesser deity or demigod. Status shows its power relative to other gods and helps decide how strong its avatars are, how many it can use, and what special powers it has when its avatars are at full strength. Only the powers of the avatars are given.

  • AL (Alignment): how the deity behaves. A note in brackets shows a tendency to stray from that alignment.
  • WAL (Worshippers' alignment): the alignment of its lay worshippers.
  • SoC (Spheres of control): the ideas, events or subjects it governs or cares about, and what it is worshipped for.
  • SY (Symbol): the sign it is known by. Clerics must carry a copy to cast spells.
  • CR (Color): the color most linked with it. Its avatars and clerics often wear it, and the visible effects of its clerics' spells are always in shades of it.
  • PN (Plane): where it mainly lives.

Avatars

An avatar is a physical body a god creates by pouring part of its life force into it. Greater deities have used as many as three at once, lesser deities never more than one, and demigods cannot use avatars at all. A deity usually makes equipment to go with the form. Only the most common avatar of each deity is listed, though far stronger ones are known.

Some deities keep several avatars on their home planes in case one is destroyed; destroying an avatar does not harm the deity. When an avatar dies its equipment is usually destroyed too, though the deity may leave it behind if that suits its purposes. Gods send avatars to the Prime Material Plane to influence, help or teach their worshippers, and many of the greatest heroes of every race were avatars sent to help it. An avatar takes great care never to reveal that it is part god. If it dies, its body vanishes after several days and cannot be brought back by magic. Avatars usually appear in lonely places and travel toward the people they mean to protect.

Statistics

  • HD: hit dice.
  • THAC0: the d20 roll needed to hit armor class 0, from which the roll for any other armor class is easily worked out. It does not include strength or magic bonuses.
  • SpA (Spell ability): the class and level at which it casts spells (MU = magic-user, CL = cleric). Its own unique spell-like powers work at a higher level that reflects the deity's true power.
  • MV: movement. //#" is swimming speed, (#") burrowing speed, *# speed in a web.
  • AC: frontal armor class including dexterity, magic and natural toughness; it may be worse from the side or rear.
  • hp: the hit points the deity "lends" the avatar, usually about a third of its own.
  • #AT attacks per round; Dmg damage per attack; MR magic resistance, usually about half the deity's own; SZ size, always a little larger than normal for the race the avatar is sent to help.
  • Str, Int, Wis, Dex, Con, Cha: ability scores.

Clerics

Each god demands a different kind of worship and draws a different kind of cleric.

  • AL: the alignment a cleric of this god must have, always narrower than a worshipper's.
  • RA (Raiment): what the cleric wears for formal rites, and usually at other times.
  • AEx (Additional experience cost): the extra experience the cleric must earn to advance, in return for the special powers the god grants.
  • WPN (Weapons): the weapons the cleric may use. Weapons marked with an asterisk are closely tied to the god, and the cleric must be proficient with them at 1st level. Several gods require their clerics to learn edged weapons, for reasons of their own, breaking the usual rule against clerics using them.
  • SPH (Spheres): the kinds of spells the god grants. This is for an optional rule of the second edition rules and can be ignored.
  • SPL (Specials): special powers, usually spells or spell-like abilities, that the cleric gains automatically each day.
  • ADD (Additional spells): spells outside the god's spheres that its clerics may still use.

Sources: Guide p.64; Glossography p.38; GA p.5-6. Rewritten in plain words; statistics as printed.

Boccob (the Uncaring). Greater god (the Guide's heading says "major god"), neutral. Concerns: neutrality, magic, arcane knowledge, foreknowledge and foresight.

The God

Boccob the Uncaring is Lord of All Magics and Archmage of the Deities. He seems not to care at all whether anyone worships or serves him, and he has few followers. Even so, seers and diviners all over the Flanaess beg him for omens, sages revere him, and those trying to create new spells or magic items often ask his help. He rarely leaves his own hall, preferring to send his servant, the mad archmage Zagyg, in his place.

He always dresses in purple covered with shimmering golden runes that move and change, and he carries many amulets and protective devices. His palace is said to hold at least one of every magic item ever made by a magic-user or illusionist, apart from artifacts and relics. Boccob neither seeks nor avoids conflict; he values balance above alignment, and knowledge above everything.

Worship

His followers are spread across the Flanaess. His services, when held at all, involve complex rituals, incense, the recital of alchemical formulas, and readings from special works honoring knowledge. His clerics wear purple robes trimmed with gold.

Powers

All planes and times are open to Boccob. He can draw positive or negative energy from the matching plane, either to strike fear into undead or to send out a rolling cloud of energy like a huge wall of fire, and he can use a net of negative energy against creatures that draw on the Positive Material Plane. Together these forces can tear apart a demon or devil, a deva or an elemental. No spell of mental control or possession affects him, nor does feeblemind or similar magic. Otherwise he has the usual powers of a greater god.

His favorite weapon is his staff of the archmage, which combines a staff of the magi with a wand of conjuration. It can always absorb 24 spell levels, whatever its charge. He can be hit only by +5 or better weapons, sees twice as far as normal in every spectrum, and regenerates 1-4 hit points a round.

Disc of Concordant Opposition. Boccob can cast this once a round: a 1" square web of force, a plane of mixed energies. Creatures with fewer than 13 hit dice or levels (96 hit points or fewer if dice are unknown), or less than 50% magic resistance, are blasted into nothingness. Creatures above 12 hit dice take 100 points of damage, minus twice their magic resistance. Characters above 12th level take 50 points, minus their magic resistance and minus ten times their magical protection bonuses. Creatures with 50% or more magic resistance are unharmed.

Celestian (the Far Wanderer, the Star Wanderer). Lesser god, N(G). Concerns: stars, space, wandering and wanderers.

The God

Celestian and Fharlanghn are said to be brothers who took similar but different roads: Fharlanghn chose the distances of the world, while Celestian was drawn to the endless reaches of the stars and the Astral Plane.

The Star Wanderer appears as a tall, lean, middle-aged man with smooth ebony skin and eyes of the same color. He moves quickly and in complete silence and seldom speaks; when he does, it is in a cold, unearthly whisper that carries well despite its softness. He dresses in deep black, and somewhere on him is always his symbol: seven "stars" (diamond, amethyst, sapphire, emerald, topaz, jacinth and ruby) blazing with the colors of distant suns, worn as an ornament or worked into the cloth.

His habits and temperament keep him apart from the other gods. He has only a small following among humans, made up mostly of those concerned with the cosmos or the sky: scholars, astronomers, astrologers, navigators, philosophers and dreamers.

Worship

Services are always held outdoors at night, preferably when the sky is clear and full of stars. His shrines stand in the country, away from city lights, on mountain peaks or hilltops with a clear view of the night sky.

Celestian has no one weapon he always carries. He usually has one or more of these: a long bow +3 with 20 arrows +3; a spear +4 that looks only 5 feet long but darts out to 10 feet; a short sword +5 with no special powers; a battle axe +3 he can throw up to 40 feet; and a dagger +6 of unbreakable metal.   • Comet: a flaming missile strikes one target up to 70 feet away, setting fire to everything combustible on it and dealing 5-30 damage from flames and poison gas.

St. Cuthbert (of the Cudgel). Lesser god, LG(N). Concerns: wisdom, common sense, truth, forthrightness, dedication and zeal.

The God

St. Cuthbert appears as a stout, red-faced man with apple cheeks, a drooping white moustache and flowing white hair. He wears magical plate mail, with a crumpled hat on top of his helmet and a starburst of rubies set in platinum on his chest. In his left hand he carries a billet of wood (a bronzewood cudgel) that beguiles anyone it touches, and in his right the fabled Mace of St. Cuthbert.

He hates evil, but his main interest is law and order and the twin work of converting people and keeping "true believers" from backsliding. He leaves his plane only when some great duty calls. On the Prime Material Plane he sometimes appears as a yokel covered in manure, a wanderer in brown and green robes, or a slight, elderly tinker, and in these guises he tests the faithful's grasp of doctrine or looks for new converts. He can gate between Arcadia and the Prime Material Plane at will and otherwise has the powers of a lesser god. There is a great personal enmity between St. Cuthbert and Iuz.

Worship

St. Cuthbert has a large following. He has many large temples, but wayside shrines and small, rough chapels are more usual. His followers are found mostly in the central Flanaess: around Greyhawk, on the Wild Coast, in Urnst and in Verbobonc, where his temples are large, elaborate and well kept. His followers and those of Pholtus of the Blinding Light are great rivals.

Ehlonna (of the Forests). Lesser goddess, NG. Concerns: forests, meadows, animals, flowers and fertility.

The Goddess

Ehlonna of the Forests, honored as a fertility goddess, is said to be the patroness of all good folk, elven, human or otherwise, who live in and love the woodlands, and of animals. She is also the goddess of those who hunt, fish and otherwise make their living from the forest, so rangers, foresters, trappers, hunters and woodcutters worship her. More women than men serve her.

She can take two forms, a human woman or an elven woman. As a human her hair is chestnut or black; as an elf it is pale gold or coppery gold. In either form her eyes are a startling blue or soft violet and her skin is clear and fair. Her clothing ranges from the practical gear of a forester or ranger to the delicate gown of an elven princess.

She carries a longbow that always hits, with arrows of slaying for many woodland creatures such as bears and stags, and she fights with a magic longsword and a magic dagger at once, often parrying with the sword and striking with the dagger. In human form she has special power over horses, and in elven form she commands unicorns. Her high whistle calls either from as far as a league away (Greyhawk Adventures: three miles), and they gladly carry her. She has the usual powers of a lesser god and is personally served by a planetar.

Brownies, elves, gnomes and halflings are especially attuned to her, and she often travels among them. If she asks a service of them, they are very likely to help in any way she asks (90% likely, for any good or neutral member of these races, whatever the task).

Worship

Her worship is centered on the region from the Wild Coast to the Ulek fiefs and from the Kron Hills to the sea. Her temples always stand in woodland settings, though small shrines are sometimes found in villages. Services use wooden and horn vessels and various herbs, with music from pipes and flutes. Her clerics wear pale green robes, are excellent trackers and can befriend animals.

Erythnul (the Many). Lesser god, CE(N). Concerns: ugliness, hate, envy, malice, panic and slaughter.

The God

Erythnul, called the Many, is the god of fickle malice, hate, envy and panic. Humans and humanoids alike follow him, for he is said to reward his faithful richly for their faithlessness and wicked deeds. He stalks every battlefield to spread fear and rout wherever he can.

He appears as a brutal-looking man seven feet tall, red-faced, hairy and muscular, with mad, darting eyes of dull green that are horrible to look at. He usually wears red furs and russet-dyed leather and carries a huge stone-headed mace. The head is pierced, so that it gives off a shrieking whistle when swung; the sound has sent hearers fleeing and screaming in terror until they collapsed from exhaustion.

In battle his face shifts from human to gnoll to bugbear to ogre to troll, a sign of his special power to make servants from his own blood. He can also spread fear through his eyes and take the shape of a human, gnoll, bugbear, ogre or troll at will. Otherwise he has all the usual powers of a lesser god.

Worship

His clerics dress in rust-colored clothing; their ceremonial robes are often white spattered with blood, and they wear stylized masks for each of his five aspects. Most of his places of worship are hidden. Most towns and cities have a small cult of his followers among the people of the thieves' quarter, and many gnolls, bugbears, ogres and trolls worship him. Services feature shrill reed instruments played out of tune, gongs and drums; major rites involve fire and a sacrifice.

Fharlanghn (Dweller on the Horizon). Lesser god, N(g). Concerns: horizons, distances, roads and travel.

The God

While his younger brother Celestian wanders the roads of the stars, Fharlanghn roams the four corners of the world; he is the god of travel and distance. He sometimes enters the Elemental Plane of Earth, seldom that of Air, and shuns those of Fire and Water, though he can travel to any inner plane. His name is invoked across the Flanaess whenever a road is built or seriously repaired, and his symbol hangs over the doors of inns and stables throughout the continent.

He appears as a middle-sized man, elderly and weathered, with brown, leathery, deeply wrinkled skin and bright green eyes that seem far younger. His movements look slow and measured, but he is actually quick and spry, especially when traveling. He talks readily with fellow travelers, politely but never at great length, and wears plain clothing of leather and unbleached linen, always travel-stained but seldom dirty.

His symbol is a wooden disc with a curving line across its upper part for the horizon. He wears an ornate one, the Oerth Disc, made of many kinds of wood inlaid with jade and turquoise, with a bright golden sun (Greyhawk Adventures: an amber gem) set into it.

He reads languages and magic; detects charm, evil, good, illusion, magic, snares and pits; speaks every tongue of Oerth; and talks with other creatures by telepathy. He pays closest attention to those on roads and paths and in long tunnels. His iron-shod staff never misses the creature he chooses to strike. He can curse an enemy so that any journey of more than a league takes twice as long; the curse lasts a month and can be removed only by a high priest of Fharlanghn (10th level) or by some other god able to do so. He is never surprised on the Prime Material Plane, and spells of earth do not affect him.

Worship

His worshippers are most active in the central and southwestern Flanaess, and are usually adventurers, merchants, wanderers and the like. Services are held outdoors whenever possible, under a sunny sky with a clear view of the horizon.

His priesthood has two branches. Urban priests wear brown robes and keep small chapels in towns and cities. Pastoral priests wear green and minister on the road, wandering from one small wayside shrine to the next and preaching as they go.

Heironeous (the Invincible). Lesser god, LG. Concerns: chivalry, honor, justice, valor and daring.

The God

Heironeous is the champion of rightful combat and chivalrous deeds, and the god of those who fight for honor and strive for order and justice. He often leaves the Seven Heavens to roam the Prime Material Plane, aiding heroic causes and championing lawful good.

He is tall, with coppery skin, auburn hair and amber eyes, but he can create an illusion that makes him look like a young boy, a mercenary soldier or an old man, dressed to suit. In every guise he wears a suit of fine magical chainmail. At his birth his skin was soaked in a secret solution that protects him from many weapons, magical and not. His personal weapon is a great magical battle axe that shrinks at his will to a twentieth of its normal five-foot length, or grows back, so it goes unnoticed when he is in disguise.

Besides his normal attacks, he can loose a bolt of energy drawn from the Positive Material Plane. It is more destructive to creatures of the Prime Material Plane than to those of the Elemental Planes or the neutral planes, harmless to natives of the Positive Material and Upper Planes, dangerous to natives of the Lower Planes and to all undead, and especially deadly to creatures of the Negative Material Plane. He has all the usual powers of a lesser god.

Heironeous and his brother Hextor, who chose a different path, are bitter enemies, each trying to destroy or thwart the other.

Worship

His worshippers are found everywhere, and wherever there are soldiers or doers of heroic deeds, a chapel of Heironeous is likely. His clerics are especially warlike and always wear chainmail, with dark blue robes trimmed in silver to show their rank. His temples are usually decorated with blue hangings and silver, and sometimes with stained glass windows showing Heironeous triumphant. Behind the altar there usually stands a copper statue of the god in silver mail, armed with a silver battle axe, with seven silver bolts radiating from behind his head.

Hextor (Champion of Evil, Herald of Hell, Scourge of Battle). Lesser god, LE. Concerns: war, discord, conflict and fitness.

The God

Hextor is the god of many soldiers and fighters who think lawful evil the fittest to rule and who admire war and discord, though others follow him too. He lives on the plane of Acheron and can wander to the Hells or even Nirvana, but he spends most of his time on the Prime Material Plane looking for war, helping lawful evil and opposing good. Above all he seeks to bring down the servants of Heironeous, his half-brother and chief enemy. When Heironeous chose lawful good, Hextor chose to serve lawful evil. He was always the weaker of the two, so the Lords of Evil gave him six arms instead of two, so that he could beat Heironeous and every other foe.

In disguise he looks like a handsome, ordinary man, since he can merge four of his arms into his body whenever he likes. Then his skin is fair and his hair and eyes jet black. He is well spoken and charming, a hearty fellow and a man's man, yet irresistible to women; he can talk with sages, reason with philosophers, argue with clergy and discuss arcane secrets with spellcasters. In his true form his skin is gray, his hair lank, and his red-rimmed eyes bulge from a face horrible to see, and he cares only to fight and kill.

In battle he draws two great bows that fire iron-barbed arrows. At close quarters he uses two spiked bucklers and four weapons, usually a military fork, a scimitar, a flail and a morning star. His armor is made of iron scales with metal strips at the shoulders and cuffs, a corslet of the same guarding his waist and groin, and greaves on his legs, all decorated with skulls. Around his neck, on a chain of crude iron links, hangs the Symbol of Hate and Discord: the six red arrows of Hextor.

Besides the powers of a lesser god, his fighting skill and an assassin's skills, he can stir up discord around him: friend argues with friend, annoyance turns to hatred and petty jealousy to boiling rage. Without the Symbol of Hate and Discord he lacks this power, except through spellcasting. He often carries a magic horn, the Trumpet of Acheron, which can be blown once every six days to call up a squad of skeletons that obey him, and once every six years to summon a horde of skeletons and zombies.

Worship

His places of worship are grim, dark and bloody, and his major shrines and temples are usually built on some field of slaughter. His clerics wear black robes embroidered with white skulls or gray faces. Only the higher clerics wear the arrows of hate and discord in red; lower clerics wear gray ones. His ceremonies are full of chanting, discordant wind instruments, shouts and screams, and the clash of iron weapons. His priests are trained in assassination. Hextor is greatly honored in the Great Kingdom.

Incabulos. Greater god (the Guide's and Greyhawk Adventures' heading says "major"), NE. Concerns: evil, plague, sickness, famine, drought, disasters and nightmares.

The God

Incabulos is the god of evil sendings: plague, sickness, famine, drought, disaster, nightmares and the like. Woe and wickedness are his chief delights, and even the princes of Hades and the dukes of Hell fear him. Being so baneful a god, he has no large following, yet common folk all over the Flanaess make him offerings, usually foul-smelling, guttering black candles, to turn aside his wrath, and despicable people of every sort revere his power and malice.

He is horrible enough to make anyone shudder, with a nightmarish face, a deformed body and skeletal hands. He wears dead black robes lined with sickly orange and nauseating moss green, and roams the Astral, Ethereal and Prime Material Planes, the last only in darkness. He often rides a huge nightmare, attended by six of the strongest night hags, also mounted.

Among his many powers, he can cast a permanent sleep that only exorcism can lift. His usual weapon is a staff that causes terrible wounds to any creature, plant or animal it strikes, and he is believed to use a venomous bastard sword at times. In need, he gates in night hags or hordlings, which arrive one at a time and serve him willingly.

Worship

His worshippers and servants are very secretive, fearing the anger of everyone, even other evil folk, who loathe what he stands for. Yet many call on him, and hidden temples exist underground and in forsaken wilderness. His priests dress in black, with the eye of possession symbol in verdigris-covered bronze, repeated in dull orange on the robes of higher clerics; they are masters of disguise. His services are held in secret against a background of weird humming and droning chants, lit dimly by flickering, smoky black candles, while the faithful celebrate many kinds of wickedness. All the vessels are of old bronze, carnelian or bloodstone.

If not, it falls feverish and confused with plague for six turns, losing 10% of its original hit points and one point each of strength and constitution, with -2 to saves and to hit, and +2 to be hit. Every creature within 10 feet of a victim must make a constitution check or catch the plague too; no one can have more than one case at once, and someone near several victims checks only once. When the attack ends, the penalties end, but the lost hit points and ability points take 1d6 days to come back. Before that, there is one last attack: the victim makes a constitution check against the lowered score, dying on a failure and recovering everything on a success.

Sources: Guide p.70-71; Glossography p.43; GA p.13-14. Rewritten in plain words; statistics as printed.

Istus (Lady of Our Fate, the Colorless and All-colored). Greater goddess ("major" in the Guide and Greyhawk Adventures), N. Concerns: fate, destiny, predestination and the future.

The Goddess

Istus is honored and feared as the one who decides what will be. She has few true devotees, but many people call on her in times of want or need; she may answer or not, and no one knows which. Some seers and fortune-tellers revere her. Because fate is so often cruel or unreliable, mostly cynical or unfeeling people serve her, though some worship her because fate has been unusually kind to them.

No one knows where (or when) she lives. Some scholars think it is a pocket universe, or a demi-plane of the Deep Ethereal, that only she and her strands of fate can enter or leave. She certainly visits other planes, the Prime Material among them, sometimes as an old crone, sometimes as a noble lady, a lovely gentlewoman or a shepherd girl. In any form she carries no obvious weapon, since she can use any object as one. She is said to be served by a strange companion, a creature of time something like an elemental prince (the Glossography says it is a time elemental).

She casts her strands and webs with a spindle (Greyhawk Adventures calls it the Spindle of Fate, a golden rod wound with silver-gray thread) that answers to her alone. While she has it she knows all times, places and planes and moves freely among them. If she loses it she returns at once to her own plane, the lost spindle crumbles to powder, and until she makes a new one she cannot control fate. The Guide says this may take up to a year; the Glossography says 30-300 days; Greyhawk Adventures says 3d10 x 10 days.

She can never be surprised. Once a day she can jump into the future and back in an instant, which heals her. Time-related spells, such as augury, divination, time stop and tempus fugit, are useless against her however they are used.

Worship

Her worship is centered in Dyvers, Greyhawk, Rauxes, Rel Mord and Stoink, places where people tend to rely on luck to carry them. Services feature gauze hangings, clouds of incense, woodwind music, chanting and group meditation.

Strands and Webs

Istus can cast one strand or web a round. Strands reach 60 feet and webs 30 feet; the Web of Stars is always centered on her. All are cast at 24th level. The figures below are from Greyhawk Adventures; where the Glossography differs, that is noted.

  • Strand of Binding (3 a day): the creature struck must save vs. spells or be held as if wrapped in heavy iron chains for 100 rounds minus its hit dice or level, however strong it is.
  • Strand of Cancellation (2 a day): any nonliving object struck is treated as if it had never existed. Magic items save at 5% per plus or equivalent; artifacts at 50% and relics at 75%, plus 5% per plus (so an artifact sword +4 saves at 70%).
  • Strand of Death (1 a day): any creature struck, even a god, is turned to dust and gone forever unless magic resistance or a save vs. spells protects it.
  • Strand of Hostility (2 a day): the creature struck (save vs. spells negates) turns against anyone or anything that opposes Istus and does whatever it must to defend her, even turning on old friends, because fate wills it. The effect is permanent and only Istus can remove it.
  • Strand of Passage (2 a day): links the plane she is on with any plane she wishes. Anyone touching it is carried to the other plane at once. It lasts three rounds and works in one direction only.
  • Strand of Sending (at will; the Glossography says 3 a day): sends the creature struck (save vs. spells negates; willing creatures need not save) to the place and time, up to 200 days ahead, where the DM thinks its freedom or life is in greatest danger. She can also send a creature to the time and place of its greatest coming opportunity.
  • Web of Enmeshment (1 a day): everyone caught in the 30-foot web is lost in a misty labyrinth of unlimited size where they can see only 10 feet, filled with nameless dread and 50% likely to attack any creature they meet, friend or foe. The web lasts one turn. Prisoners not fighting may save vs. spells on the second round and each round after until they escape. A creature with magic resistance rolls when struck: on a success it is not caught; on a failure it is trapped until it saves. Creatures killed or knocked out inside stay there until someone carries them out.
  • Web of Entropy (1 a day): an invisible 30-foot web that lasts one turn. Each round, magic items in it must save as if struck by a Strand of Cancellation, and spells cast from, into or through it are negated.
  • Web of Stars (1 a day): carries Istus and every creature within 15 feet to a boundless time-space, perhaps her own home. It is a pathway beyond dimensions to anywhere and anywhen, for those who know the way, and Istus does. Others see endless starry space hung with silken strands; distances are warped, and a single step may carry one a vast way. Creatures more than two "steps" off look like glowing stars of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet or white. The web lasts one hour, or 600 "steps." The stars are doorways to other times and planes, impassable unless their nature is known. Creatures of supra-genius intelligence can find their way back to where they started. Those above supra-genius can locate other points along the web (10% per point of intelligence over 20) and use it to travel to other planes and times. Creatures of genius intelligence can also learn the nature of the time-space (1% per point of intelligence) and find points along it, but must study each doorway for one turn (100 steps) first, and may try to understand the place only once per visit. Points along the web are 3d8 steps apart. Anyone still inside when the web fades is teleported to a random spot on their home plane.

She has often granted strand casting to her high clerics, but never more than two strands a day.

Iuz (the Old). Demi-god, CE(N). Concerns: oppression, deceit, wickedness and pain.

The God

No mortal knows whether Iuz is a human who has grown demonic over the centuries or a half-demon, a cambion, perhaps (as some suggest) a bastard son of Orcus. He is the first known minor god of chaotic evil, and his wickedness and treachery are infamous across the Flanaess. He appears either as a huge fat man, seven feet tall (ogre-sized, says Greyhawk Adventures), with demonic features, reddish skin, pointed ears and long steely fingers, or as a wrinkled old dwarf of a man barely five feet tall. Either or both may be his true form.

He rules part of Oerth, a dreadful land that bears his name, and plots to conquer the whole world. The Guide and Greyhawk Adventures both name his court as the city of Molag; the Guide's state entries give Dorakaa as the capital of Iuz and Molag as the Horned Society's town. Few creatures outside his domain will speak his name, let alone worship him.

In his demonic form he prefers a great magic two-handed sword, though he can use other weapons. In any form he can claw, strike and strangle with his long, sinewy fingers. In his small form he can spit a disgusting spittle that ages whatever it touches and withers the flesh or limb it hits, and his wrinkled face revolts most creatures who see it.

He is rumored to keep a soul object hidden on the Abyssal plane ruled by the demoness Zuggtmoy (printed "Zuggtoy" here), whose consort he is known to be, so he can roam beyond his land without fear of lasting harm. If he is slain, he is banished to the Abyss like a demon prince. He wears an old, short cape that protects him against physical and magical harm.

Iuz and St. Cuthbert are bitter enemies, and their servants carry on the feud.

Worship

His clerics dress in rusty black, his favorite color, or in white streaked with rust-red bloodstains. His ceremonies feature foul-smelling incense or burning dung, great drums, gongs and clanging bronze bells, and blood sacrifice whenever possible. His places of worship must be old, filthy and dark, and his altars are usually made of bone and decorated with many skulls.

Nerull (the Reaper). Greater god ("major" in the Guide and Greyhawk Adventures), NE. Concerns: death, darkness, the underworld and covert activity.

The God

The dreaded Nerull is the Foe of All Good, Hater of Life, Bringer of Darkness, King of All Gloom and Reaper of Flesh, the god of all who seek the greatest evil for their pleasure and profit.

He appears as a skeletal figure with a dull, rusty-red body. His skull-like head has thick, ropy locks of black-green "hair," and his glowing eyes, his teeth and his taloned nails are all the green of verdigris. Wearing a cowled cloak of rusty black and carrying a staff of red-veined sablewood, he stalks the planes, the Prime Material above all when it lies under night. He cuts down any living thing he meets, and sends any undead of lawful leaning howling to its doom. His staff is the Life Cutter, a magic scythe only he can use: at his whim a huge blade of red force appears at its tip. It is especially deadly to creatures of, or drawing energy from, the Positive Material Plane, can strike creatures in astral, ethereal or gaseous form, and drains even undead of their negative energy.

He likes to carry and use evil magic items such as a necklace of strangulation, a bag of devouring and a rug of smothering, using them as an assassin would, silently and from behind. He can summon three demodands of the greatest strength whenever he finds them useful; they hate him, but fear of him outweighs everything, so they obey at once or attack his obvious foes. He can also create a large clump of blackness from which tendrils shoot out, groping for any living thing within their long reach; their touch means almost certain death, and corrosive injury to those who survive. Only holy water, blessings or dispelling their evil destroys them.

He can travel all the lower outer planes, the Astral and Ethereal Planes, and the Elemental and Prime Material Planes, but mostly leaves Tarterus only to wreak havoc on the Prime Material Plane. He can fly at will, so he usually travels alone and seldom rides anything. Magical darkness and vision-blocking clouds do not hinder his sight.

Worship

Many evil humans and some humanoids honor Nerull, and assassins and thieves often take him as patron. In wicked lands, such as the Great Kingdom, his temples and cathedrals operate openly; elsewhere his rites are held in underground shrines and sacred vaults. Worship takes place in total darkness, with a ghastly litany of death and suffering, and human sacrifice is common. Altars are of rust-colored stone, and service pieces usually of copper and malachite. His clerics wear rust-red or blackish-rust clothing, carry staves, and bear the unholy skull-and-scythe symbol somewhere on them.

Obad-Hai (the Shalm). Lesser god, N. Concerns: nature, wildlands, freedom, hunting and wild beasts.

The God

Obad-Hai, the Shalm, is an archaic god of nature and the wildlands, one of the oldest known; the Flan worshipped him before the Aerdi invaders came.

In human form he is a lean, weathered man of great but uncertain age, usually dressed in brown or russet and carrying a hornwood staff, looking like a pilgrim, a hermit or just a country fellow. At other times he appears as a dwarf, gnome or halfling. He can also instantly take the form and nature of any of these creatures, and often roams in such a guise: centaur, leprechaun, pixie, satyr, sprite, treant, badger, brown bear, boar, giant eagle, giant goat, giant lynx, giant otter, giant owl, giant pike, giant porcupine, giant stag, wolf.

His weapon is the Shalmstaff. When he lets go of it, it flies at once to the nearest hornwood tree and stays there until he calls it. Its bearer can walk tirelessly without food or water for as long as he likes; animals never harm him, and plants part to let him pass.

The Shalm loves nature and wilderness. He is a patron of druids and a friend to all who live in harmony with the natural world. Because of his particular kind of neutrality, there is rivalry and dislike between him and Ehlonna of the Forests, so most of his followers are men and most of hers women.

Worship

His clerics are usually druids. A few are ordinary clerics, most of whom wander as pilgrims in russet clothing, carrying staves. His churches and chapels always stand in country settings and are built of rough timber. Services are brief and not very ritualized, decorated with living flowers, earth, water and fire.

Olidammara (the Laughing Rogue). Lesser god, NC (as printed; the Glossography gives neutral, tending to chaotic). Concerns: music, revelry, roguery ("rougery" as printed), tricks and jokes, wine and spirits.

The God

Olidammara, the Laughing Rogue, minstrel and scoundrel, is the favorite god of many thieves, and bards, jesters, vagabonds, beggars and common folk worship him too. He wanders the Prime Material Plane in many disguises, stealing from the rich, the proud and the wicked and giving wealth to those who have none, often by spending his loot on great revels. His favorite haunts are city slums or their very opposite, country glens and woods.

He always looks young, but he may pass as a tinker or peddler, a foppish wastrel, or often a green sellsword, changing his looks to suit the moment. His true appearance is said to be middling height and slender build, with chestnut hair and a rakish beard, an olive complexion and merry, sparkling emerald eyes, much given to laughter and petty tricks. His favorite colors are green and gold.

He wears only a leather vest and high leather boots, but their enchantments and a special ring protect him very well. He also has a mask that lets him completely change his appearance as long and as often as he likes; it cannot be seen while worn. And he has a stringed instrument of great power, the Kanteel of the Oldest, usable only by very experienced bards or certain other gods. It lets its holder charm creatures or people, make a fog cloud, dispel illusions, project emotions, create nonliving things, create programmed illusions and seek supernatural guidance through visions.

Zagyg once trapped him for trying to steal the Mad Archmage's treasure and turned him into a shelled animal as punishment. Olidammara escaped, but kept the ability to grow a horny shell on his back. Under it he can use his spells to escape, leaving the shell behind to cover his getaway; he is said to have gone back and looted Zagyg's treasury, using the shell to foil the Mad Archmage's attempts to catch him. The discarded shell is a dome about 2 feet wide and 3 feet long that welds itself to stone and must be smashed or otherwise destroyed to be removed or passed.

Worship

Few chapels are dedicated to Olidammara, and those are always in large towns or cities, though shrines are fairly common in towns and the countryside. Two rustic hostels are said to exist in the central Flanaess, one on the Wild Coast and one in the Kron Hills, and his clerics are often found at both. His clerics learn to hide in shadows like thieves and are taught music, and many can magically change their appearance, build and so on. They dress in brown, green, green and brown, or green and black. Services feature much singing, chanting and feasting, with libations of fermented berry drink.

Pholtus (of the Blinding Light). Lesser god, LG(N). Concerns: light, resolution, law, order, inflexibility, the sun and the moon.

The God

It is said that the regular rising and setting of the sun and the cycles of the moon are as fixed as Pholtus's resolve to show every creature the One True Way, a strict path that allows no straying but gives absolute certainty of being right. Some of his followers even claim that Pholtus set the sun and moon in their rigid courses and keeps them there, but this is not official doctrine.

He appears as a tall, slender, pale man with flowing white hair and bright blue eyes burning with devotion to his cause. He always wears a silky white gown and a cassock trimmed with gold and silver and embroidered with suns and moons. In his hand is the Staff of the Silvery Sun, an ivory staff shod (or covered) in silver and topped with an electrum disc. It can serve as a weapon, but its main power is magic: it gives off light as a wand of illumination, causes or cures blindness by touch, fires a pulsing flash of radiation from the infrared through the visible to the ultraviolet that holds the gaze of anyone it strikes and makes them obey the wielder's every command, and releases a globe of great brilliance that expands from the staff and can blind everyone in it except Pholtus permanently (curable only by the staff, a wish, or a god able to cure blindness or grant a wish).

He can also dispel darkness by touch, make any nearby creature glow brightly by pointing at it, and turn his body mirror-bright so that it reflects all radiation: gaze attacks bounce back on their users, heat does not affect him, and even creatures with infravision or ultravision can be struck blind by looking at him. The Ethereal, Positive Material and Prime Material Planes are open to him, though he usually stays in Arcadia. He can summon monadic devas through gates.

Worship

Like their god, Pholtus's clerics are inflexible and constantly try to show the light to unbelievers. They will not tolerate argument, and resisters are quickly shown the way of the Blinding Light (usually, says Greyhawk Adventures, with a continual light square between the eyes). The priesthood is most active in cities. Its consecrated buildings are white, and services feature many brightly burning candles, long sermons and choruses of the worshippers' anthem, "O Blinding Light." His followers and those of St. Cuthbert are great rivals.

Ralishaz (the Unlooked For). Lesser god, CN(E). Concerns: chance, randomness, bad luck, misfortune and madness.

The God

Ralishaz is the god of chance, ill luck and misfortune, seen as the one who brings about unforeseen events that cause woe more often than good. As god of chance and randomness he is also the patron of gamblers and those who take unusual risks, though no one ever hopes for his help.

He usually appears on the Prime Material Plane as an ancient, oddly dressed beggar, sometimes male, sometimes female, who begs or gambles; at other times as a jester or an idiot. His true form is awful to see: one moment the face and body are handsome, the next wrinkled and ugly, then a scabby beggar's, then a lovely maiden's, and throughout, his randomness spreads a deeply disturbing unease. The only weapon he uses is wooden, sometimes a club and sometimes a staff, though both are the same item.

Besides the powers of an 18th level high priest and a spellbinder (illusionist), he can put a person to sleep with his gaze, age a person with his touch, and curse a person.

Worship

Few formally worship Ralishaz, though there are a handful of small shrines and modest temples in large cities and remote places. His clerics wear robes of many colors, cuts and materials. Oddly, they seldom suffer bad luck, but when they do it is very, very bad. They avoid taking chances whenever possible; "Tempt not Chance" is their motto. His ceremonies involve random notes on musical instruments, babbling hymns, frequent casting of fortune-telling devices, and wildly changing light and darkness, noise and quiet, heat and cold.

Raxivort. Lesser god, CE. Concerns: xvarts, rats and bats.

The God

The tale goes that Raxivort was born an ordinary xvart centuries ago. His superior abilities made him leader of all xvarts, and for great service to a demon (some say Graz'zt) he was given certain powers and made the demon's Master of Slaves. Raxivort pretended to be grateful and waited. In time the cunning xvart gained enough knowledge and power to loot the demon's strongroom, and with this new arsenal he tried to seize the Abyssal plane from its lord. The struggle was titanic and lasted for months, with neither side able to win. At last Raxivort sought a truce and left for the ever-changing planes of Pandemonium, giving back the part of the Abyss he had taken but carrying off great plunder. He now lives in luxury; demons shun him, and at least one plots dark revenge.

Raxivort is Lord of Xvartkind, Packmaster of Rats and Night Flutterer. He can take the form of a xvart, a rat or a giant bat (mobat), or use magic to look like a human, demi-human or humanoid. His normal form is a xvart, of course, with bright blue skin and burning orange eyes, extremely gross and ugly. He wears silk over blue mail, the whole shimmering as if on fire.

He prefers small bladed weapons such as knives, daggers and short swords, which he can throw with great accuracy, and he seldom carries fewer than a dozen throwing knives and daggers. He also has a small falchion of great magical power called Azure Razor, which in his hands can paralyze one chosen kind of creature on command. He can also make a blue flame blaze from his left hand that burns like both fire and acid. Many companies of xvart fighters serve and guard him, and packs of the largest giant rats and scores of mobats come at his call.

Worship

Raxivort's shamans always show the blue-flaming hand of their god and can rise to the level of lama; his witch doctors, who use magic, can rise to the level of theurgist.

Trithereon (the Summoner). Lesser god, CG. Concerns: individuality, self-protection, liberty and retribution.

The God

Trithereon, the Summoner, is the god of individuality and of the right to protect oneself. His symbol, the rune of pursuit (see Runes and Glyphs), stands for many things, among them the need to strive for liberty and to bring down those bent on cutting short life or freedom.

On the Prime Material Plane he appears as a tall, well-built young man with red-gold hair and gray eyes, usually dressed in pale blue or violet, often with a shirt of golden chainmail showing. He carries a broad-bladed spear and a broadsword, with a scepter in his broad belt of gold-studded leather.

  • Krelestro ("the Harbinger of Doom"), the spear, flies swiftly back to his hand after he throws it.
  • Freedom's Tongue, the sword, can make all its wielder's foes afraid.
  • The Baton of Retribution, the scepter, can find any enemy anywhere, unless very powerful magic guards against location, and lets its wielder summon certain creatures. Merely having it lets its owner travel to any place on any plane not magically barred. When wielded, it can also, at will, turn the surrounding area into a strange plane unknown to the wielder's foes: perhaps a barren desert of purple rock under a green sky, a swamp of milky water with red plants, or a featureless plain of gray and black whose ground glows like see-through fire under an opaque black sky. In each such place a creature must answer Trithereon one question truthfully or be left in that strange world for 100 years, unless it has some way to escape.

As the Summoner he can call up three creatures, one at a time, to hunt and fight those guilty of enslaving others, curbing liberty and similar crimes: Nemoud the Hound, Harrus the Falcon and Ca'rolk the Sea Lizard. Each follows orders as well as it can. He can also summon any kind of deva through gates, but only to fight great evil.

Worship

His priests wear dark blue or purple robes trimmed in silver or gold, and for special ceremonies golden-red cassocks bearing the rune of pursuit. Curates and above may use spears, and patriarchs and above broadswords. His followers are common in large towns and cities and in certain states of the Flanaess, notably the Yeomanry and the Shield Lands. Services feature ceremonial flames, bells, and iron vessels and symbols of various kinds.

Ulaa. Greater goddess ("major" in the Guide and Greyhawk Adventures), LG. Concerns: hills, mountains and gemstones.

The Goddess

Whether Ulaa is closest to humans, gnomes or dwarves is debated. She is as tall and broad as a dwarf and has a gnome's features, but her husband Bleredd certainly looks human. Being who she is, she can appear as male or female, dwarf, gnome, human or nearly any creature she likes, though all her guises tend to have a dwarf's build and a gnome's face. She lives mostly on the Prime Material Plane and the Elemental Plane of Earth, where she is most at home, loving rolling hills and craggy peaks, earthen burrows and stony vaults.

She usually wears adamantite mail, with many gems decorating her harness and weapons, and always carries her military pick and her hammer of thunderbolts, whose name means "Skull Ringer." She can throw the hammer, and it is especially deadly to humanoids, killing as many as 25 in one pass. Ogres, ogre magi, trolls of every kind, ettins, all giants except cloud and storm giants, and all golems except iron ones die instantly if Skull Ringer hits them.

Because of her bond with earth and minerals, all earth elemental creatures except evil ones respect her. Good ones serve her when asked, and those hostile to her flee in terror at the sight of her. She owns many gems and jewels, some magical, with powers ranging from commanding elementals to commanding earth and minerals. Those who win her favor usually receive one or more magic jewels mixed in with a reward of gemstones. She can pass through earth and rock very quickly and has many magical powers tied to earth, and no earth-based spell can harm or hinder her.

Worship

Many demi-humans (dwarves, gnomes and halflings) serve Ulaa, as do fair numbers of humans, mostly hillmen, mountaineers, miners and quarrymen. Her shrines, chapels and temples are found only in hills or mountains, often underground. Services are always held in stony places, with earth and gemstones on display; rhythmic hammering on stone and deep chanting serve as hymns. Her clerics wear green and brown at first, then brown, then brown and gray, and all gray at the highest levels.

Wastri (the Hopping Prophet). Demi-god, LN(E). Concerns: bigotry, self-deception and amphibians.

The God

Wastri, the Hopping Prophet, Hammer of Demi-humans, lives on the Prime Material Plane, now in the region of the Vast Swamp. He preaches that humankind is supreme above all. Humanoids may serve, but demi-humans, dwarves, gnomes and halflings above all, are fit only to be killed, and with his gray-clad "servants" and his toad packs he hunts and wipes them out wherever he can.

Somehow Wastri has changed into something both less and more than human. His froglike features and odd gait make him unmistakable, yet he moves quickly enough and can hop long distances easily and accurately. He wears no armor, relying on speed and nimble dodging, and dresses in split colors of gray and dull yellow. He is famous for his great glaive-guisarme, with which he hounds his prey; he especially loves to catch small demi-humans on its long end spike.

Besides his normal attacks and spells, he can give a croak that confuses, or cast an enchantment that covers the victim in huge, knobby warts. He can also cast a dampness over a square mile that shortens the range of archery, limits sight to 60 yards, puts out ordinary fires and weakens even magical ones. He can speak with any amphibian and command it as he likes, and can summon bullywugs (up to 40), giant toads (up to 20), poisonous toads (up to 8) and ice toads (up to 4), always the biggest of their kind and fearsome fighters.

He is normally attended by his "Immaculate Image" (a high priest and master monk), three "Greater Servants" (high priests of various levels) and a pair of huge toads.

Worship

At his Sacred Polystery the Hopping Prophet has scores of "Hopefuls" trying to become his clerics, dressed in dun, and dozens of "Lesser Servants" (acolytes, adepts, priests and curates), robed in gray. All help breed and care for superior toads. Some of these monsters are rumored to look remarkably human, just as some of Wastri's followers look like toads. All of his clerics can speak with amphibians.

His worship is uncommon, though it is said to have spread to the Hool Marshes and perhaps elsewhere. Ceremonies involve sacrifices, strange musical instruments and croaking chants, in places of worship that are always dim, dark and chilly. The creed of human superiority, and the rights and duties it demands, is always stressed.

Xan Yae (the Perfect Mistress). Lesser goddess, N. Concerns: mental and physical mastery of mind over matter, twilight, shadows and stealth.

The Goddess

Xan Yae is one of the few Baklunish gods to win any following across the Flanaess. Those who serve her through the martial arts sometimes call her the Perfect Mistress; she is the very model of grace, speed and perfection in that discipline.

She always appears in human form, but of either sex and any age. In every guise she is slender and graceful, but only in her true form can she be recognized as the Lady of Perfection. Whatever the guise, she usually dresses in dove gray, dusty rose or golden orange.

She has been known to use every weapon associated with monks, but prefers her pair of magic falchions. They are no bigger than table knives until she wills them to grow into full falchions about three feet long, one for each hand. Their magic shifts during a fight, so that her right side is stronger at first and the balance gradually moves to her left. She can also fight barehanded as the "Supreme Mistress of Petals." Besides all this she is a powerful psionic.

Hostile surroundings that are not magical, such as airlessness, cold or heat, do her no harm. She can travel to any of the Inner Planes and on the Astral Plane, but must use her psionic powers to reach the Outer Planes.

Worship

Those who seek mastery of mind and body, and those who love twilight, tend to serve her, so her followers include monks, thieves and less savory sorts, as well as young lovers and cautious people. Her clerics wear gray cloaks over robes the colors of sunset. Her places of worship are usually secluded; those in cities are large but built so as not to look like a monastery or temple. Services include dance-like exercises, meditation, reading, chanting and prayer, always in dim, shadowy light, with breezes ringing chimes and bells for background "music."
