SASpells: 5-1st, 5-2nd, 3-3rd, 2-4th
SDspells

Guiliana Mortidus was born to members of the Horned Society, an evil fighter mother and an evil priest father, who dedicated her to the Society before she was born. When she was old enough she was tested exhaustively, showed the makings of a cleric, and began training at the earliest possible age. She was not popular: her sneering contempt for the less gifted and her talent for holding a grudge left her few friends. She moved through the school exactly on schedule without showing any special talent, doing the menial tasks given to pupils without complaint but without enthusiasm, and on finishing was invested as a cleric.

She hid her burning hatreds from her superiors and teachers, judging that they would betray her to her enemies, and raged in secret that she could not yet crush everyone who had ever offended her. When she was given a low-ranking post in the Society's temples, she smiled politely, accepted and bided her time. After several years she was made a clerical "adviser" to the Society's armies, which were preparing for war, and went off happily, watching for ways to advance. She gained experience quickly, and a few magic items of no great worth; the valuable ones always went to the high command, and seeing them flaunt things she wanted made her blood boil.

At last, after a battle against the Shield Landers, her patience paid off. Searching among the dead and wounded for those needing healing, she found a ring of human influence on a dead Shield Lands officer and a talisman of pure evil on a wounded, unconscious Horned Society cleric, whom she promptly killed to take it. She has used both ever since, but carefully, since she does not want anyone to know she has them; she has seen many colleagues stabbed or smothered in their sleep for their magic items and does not mean to share their fate. With the ring she has suggested to her equals that they should not stand in her way, and she has been experimenting with suggesting to her superiors that she deserves promotion.

Owning these items has made her vainer and even less popular than before. She used to be merely unbearable, with her disagreeable ways and her well-founded touchiness about her plain looks. Now she has alienated nearly everyone of equal or lower rank, and her superiors, who rightly suspect her ambition, watch her carefully. She is a thin, slovenly woman with stringy brown hair, weak features, bad teeth and faded blue eyes, who wears a battered suit of banded mail and carries a shield in battle. She does exactly what her superiors tell her and nothing more.

She has started a small spy network of her own, mostly hobgoblins who believe the Society has approved it, and plans to use what they learn to incriminate her enemies and take revenge. She does not know that a lowly potboy she recruited is really an assassin in disguise spying on her. Her superiors have no present reason to worry about her schemes but want to make sure they do not endanger them. If her plans are consistently clumsy she will be charged, condemned and executed; if they show promise she will be quietly encouraged to fit them into her superiors' larger plans.

She is now a cleric of middle rank at the Society's main temple in Molag and has gone on several minor missions to its allies, such as Iuz. She rules her few underlings by threats and abuse, and everyone unlucky enough to rank below her hates and fears her. Besides the ring and talisman she owns a staff of withering that also works as a staff sling +2, and a mace +1. She is bargaining for a set of chain mail +2 that some hobgoblins captured in a recent fight, but their shaman knows its worth and is asking a high price.

Apart from her lust for revenge, she is completely loyal to the ideals and goals of the Horned Society. Having seen so little of the outside world, she barely understands that any other view of life is possible, let alone reasonable. Secretly she thinks anyone who refuses to accept the Society's teachings is at best willfully fooling himself, if not mad. The few times she has spoken with prisoners, she could not grasp how they could hold views so opposite to hers. She will gladly argue philosophy and alignment, but nothing will convince her that the Horned Society is anything but a paradise on earth for wise souls who work hard and obey its laws.

Water

Rivers. Travelers on foot or horseback can swim a river. Anyone carrying goods or armor must build floats, which takes about half a day. Fords, bridges and barges let a party cross with no delay.

The DM sets the speed of barges, boats, ships and rafts on rivers. As a guide: rowing upstream goes at the fast afoot rate for a road; poling (a raft or barge) goes at half that; halve again against a very strong current. Going downstream, double the rate, or triple it for craft under sail or oars. Watch out for rapids, cataracts and falls when heading downstream.

Lakes. Barges move at the road rate for afoot, unencumbered, and rafts at the road rate for afoot, encumbered. Sailing merchant craft move at the road rate for carts and wagons, and sailing warships at the road rate for horses. Galleys move at the same speed as warships; the book adds that they "can move at 10% for one hour," without saying more, so the DM must decide what that means (perhaps a short burst of extra speed under oars).

Oceans and seas. Only ships are allowed normal movement at sea, using the lake rates.

Source: Glossography p.4-7 and 16. Rewritten in plain words; figures as printed.

The Glossography gives encounter tables for every major region of the World of Greyhawk; they are in the Greyhawk Tables compendium, one table per region or terrain. Where a table says "Standard Encounter Tables," use the DMG tables (p.179-194). For monsters, see the MM or FF entry. Many results are patrols or other armed parties of men or demi-humans, described below.

Throughout, armor class figures leave out dexterity and magic bonuses unless noted. Where a party has a "chance for magic," it is usually 5% per level of the character's highest class: a 5/6 character has a 30% chance.

Elves, Knights

Elven and half-elven Knights of the Hart of Highfolk, usually mounted: knights on medium barded warhorses, esquires on medium warhorses, serjeants on light warhorses. A party has 7-10 knights: 1 commander (F/C 7/7), 1 lieutenant (F/C 6/6) and 5-8 knights (F/C 5/5). With them ride 2-4 elven spellcasters: 1 master (F/MU 4-6/8-11) and 1-3 assistants (F/MU 3-5/4-7). Each knight has 1-4 esquires (F/C 3-4/3-4) and 3-12 serjeants (F 2).

Elven clerics can and do use every kind of edged and piercing weapon. Dexterity bonuses average +2. Arms and armor: knights AC 3 with shield, lance, long sword and mace; esquires the same at AC 4; serjeants AC 5 with bow, long sword and mace. The magic-users are armored like esquires, usually without shields, and use bow and long sword. Magic-users may also have potions, scrolls, rings, rods and the like. Elves with bows carry one +1 arrow per (highest) level.

Elven Patrol

Elves and half-elves, mounted on medium or light warhorses or on foot as suits the ground: 1 captain (F/MU 4-6/5-7, AC 4), 2 lieutenants (F/MU 3-5/4-6, AC 5), 1 half-elf scout (C/R 5/5-7, AC 5), 4 serjeants (F 3-5, AC 4), 4 scouts who may be half-elves (R 1-2, AC 5) and 13-18 ordinary 1st level elves (AC 5). All carry bow and long sword. Magic as for Elves, Knights.

Hobgoblin Soldiery

Well-trained humanoid bands, usually with human officers: 1 captain (F 6-8, AC 2), 1 lieutenant (F 5, AC 2), 4 subalterns (F 3, AC 4), 8 hobgoblin serjeants (AC 4, 9 hp) and 90-160 hobgoblins (AC 5, 5-8 hp each). They may be supported by a cleric of 4th-7th level (AC 2, 50% chance), a magic-user of 3rd-6th (AC 10, 30%) and a thief of 5th-8th (AC 8, 70%). Chances for magic apply to the humans only. The humans ride medium warhorses with lance, whip, long sword and/or mace as fits. Hobgoblins carry composite bow and short sword (20%), fauchard-fork and short sword (50%) or morning star (30%). They march and fight in close order as heavy infantry, with excellent morale as long as their human leaders survive.

Men, Characters

A typical party of human characters has 2-5 major characters with enough henchmen to make 7-9 in all. Most (90%) are mounted on suitable warhorses, carrying weapons such as lances, crossbows and two-handed swords; the rest are on foot. Alignments: lawful good or neutral good 10%; chaotic good or chaotic neutral 30%; neutral 30%; chaotic evil or neutral evil 20%; lawful evil or lawful neutral 10%.

Men, Patrol, False

Scouts or raiders disguised as soldiers of the state they are invading. Scout groups have fewer than 42 members. Raider groups have 42 or more but hide some of their number so as to seem 25-30 strong. A false patrol matches a normal patrol (heavy, light and so on) of its nationality, with any extra members (40+) as raiders. There is a 30% chance it is a raiding party.

Men, Patrol, Heavy

21-40 members, usually on heavy or medium warhorses (on foot where the ground demands), all trained to fight in close order and heavily armored: 1 officer (F 5-6, AC 2), 2 subalterns (F 3-4, AC 2), 6 serjeants (F 2-3, AC 3), 7-10 veterans (F 1, AC 3, 7-12 hp) and 9-24 regulars (F 0, AC 3, 4-7 hp), plus one of: a cleric of 5th-6th level (AC 2), a druid of 5th-6th (AC 8) or a magic-user of 4th-5th (AC 10). Chance for magic is 5% per level, from these items: fighters, armor and shield, sword, miscellaneous weapon, potion, scroll; clerics, armor and shield, miscellaneous weapon, miscellaneous magic, potion, scroll; magic-users, potion, scroll, ring, rod and the like, miscellaneous magic. Weapons suit the patrol's nation, with broad or long swords common to all officers and serjeants.

Men, Patrol, Knights

11-14 knights and their retainers, always mounted, knights on heavy warhorses and retainers on medium ones: 1 commander (P 8-9 or F 9-10), 1 lieutenant (P 6-7 or F 7-8) and 9-12 knights (F 4-6), with 1 chaplain (C 7-9) and 1-3 assistant clerics (C 3-5). Each knight has 1 esquire (F 2-3) and 5-8 serjeants (F 1). Knights: AC 2, lance, bastard sword, mace. Clerics: AC 2, flail, hammer, mace. Esquires: AC 3, lance, long sword, mace. Serjeants: AC 4, light crossbow (50%) or spear, and short sword. Magic as for a heavy patrol.

Men, Patrol, Levies

Usually foot soldiers raised locally and led by regulars: 1 captain (F or R 6-8, AC 4), 2 lieutenants (F 4-5, AC 4), 4 serjeants (F 3, AC 5), 8 veterans (F 1-2, AC 5) and 41-50 levies (0 level, 3-6 hp, AC 6-7). Magic as for a heavy patrol. Officers and their assistants ride light warhorses. Weapons are typical of the area; levies usually carry pikes, long spears or polearms, and up to 50% may have missile weapons where that is usual. In some areas the levies may be non-human; adjust to suit. In troubled areas a levy patrol may add 1-4 scouts (R 3-5, AC 5), a cleric of 4th-5th (AC 4), a druid of 4th-6th (AC 8), a magic-user of 3rd-5th (AC 10) or an illusionist of 3rd-5th (AC 10). Normally there is a cleric or druid and a magic-user or illusionist, but danger may change that.

Men, Patrol, Light

As a heavy patrol, but on light warhorses, with armor class two steps worse and missile weapons, and 17-24 regulars.

Men, Patrol, Medium

Also like a heavy patrol, with officers and leaders on medium warhorses and troops on light ones, armor class one step worse, and weapons typical of the patrol's nation.

Men, Patrol, Slaver

Like a levy patrol or a light (horse) patrol, but with prison wagons or carts fitted with special chains: 3-5 wagons or 5-7 carts with teams and drivers, and 1-100 slaves.

Men, Patrol, Warband

90-120 strong, following the general rules for nomads, with arms typical of their homeland. A roll showing them "in lair" (15%) just means they are carrying special loot; adjust the amounts to suit.

Men, Raiders

Raiders always come from neighboring hostile lands, and what kind of men they are depends on where they are met. Whether they ride or walk depends on where they come from, the ground they are crossing and perhaps how well their raid has gone: Hool marshmen might steal horses in Furyondy, use them for speed and sell them in the Hold of the Sea Princes. Their number is always the maximum for a suitable patrol plus 5-30, or the MM number plus 5-30; Hool marshmen are tribesmen, so they raid in groups of 10-120 plus 5-30 (15-150). Raiding can pay, so if the roll shows them "in lair" they carry suitable (or type A) treasure. Raiders may be bandits, brigands, knights, soldiers and so on. In hostile land they are always alert and suspicious; at home, if undisciplined, they may relax and carouse.

Men, Rhennee

The wandering barge folk of the lakes (see Geography: Bodies of Water) are nearly always found within a few hundred feet of one of the three great lakes or the navigable rivers that feed or drain them. About 10% of the time they are met at their secret camping and meeting grounds, up to five miles from water. They never go inland except in groups of 7-12 barges.

Each barge carries 1 chief (F/T 4-6/5-7), 2-4 guards (F/T 3-5/2-4), 13-24 "folk" (F/T 1-2/1-4), 1 "wise woman" (I/T 4-7/1-4) and 1-2 "advisors" (I/T 1-3/1-2). Guards and folk include both sexes: 75% of guards and 50% of folk are male, and advisors are always female. There are also 7-12 children aboard (roll d12 for a child's age); those over 9 are 1st level thieves with some weapon training (0 level fighters).

Barges always have ballistae fore and aft, about 12 heavy crossbows, and a supply of harpoons, throwing spears and javelins. Every Rhennee learns the crossbow (ballista included) from childhood, and knife and dagger from the earliest years, on top of their four starting fighter weapons; harpoon training covers spear and javelin. Short-range missiles and polearms come second to manning the ballistae and heavy crossbows.

Aboard: chiefs and guards wear leather and shield and carry harpoon, battle axe, long sword, sling and bullets, and dagger(s). Folk wear leather and carry a dagger plus glaive-guisarme and short sword (30%), trident and sling (30%), or javelins and battle axe (40%). Children of 10-12 carry club and dagger.

Ashore: chiefs wear chain and shield with battle axe, long sword, sling, dagger and 6 darts. Guards wear scale and shield with spear, battle axe, long sword, sling, dagger and darts. Folk wear leather and carry a dagger plus light crossbow and short sword (30%), trident and sling (30%), or spear, javelins and battle axe (40%). Children of 10-12 carry club and dagger.

Harpoons are 6 to 8 feet long, with a range of 30 yards (as a spear), dealing 2-8 to small and man-sized foes and 2-12 to large ones. A hit buries or snags the head in the target. A line is attached; a creature of intelligence 2 or more can pull the harpoon out or cut the line and save vs. poison to free itself. On a failure it takes 1 more point of damage a round and can be hauled on the line if the harpooner wishes (see the kuo-toa in the FF).

Magic: armor or shield and miscellaneous weapons, 5% per level of fighter ability; sword, potion, scroll, ring and miscellaneous magic, 5% per highest level; rods and the like (illusionists only), 5% per illusionist level.

If 12 barges or groups are met, there is a 50% chance that 1-4 more are with the fleet. One barge is larger, with maximum numbers and levels and a noble aboard: a fighter/thief of 8th-9th/10th-13th level, always with magic armor and at least one magic miscellaneous weapon, one miscellaneous magic item and one ring. Rhennee met more than a mile inland have a 50% chance of a bard of 3rd-8th level with them, or a bard of 7th-12th level in a group with a noble; their barges are hidden and guarded by 2-3 folk from each. Each individual carries 1-3 coins of each type per level. A barge holds treasure types O, P and Q, plus the Q chance for 2-5 pieces of jewelry.

The Rhennee are neutral and live by a strict code of their own. They always seem open and friendly but are really very cautious, suspicious and scheming. They gladly lie to, cheat and rob anyone who is not Rhennee, and will kill if they must. They do a little cargo shipping, ferrying, trading, craftwork, fishing and hunting, and know such trades as tinkering, but they will never work when they can steal or deal fairly when they can cheat. Among themselves, and with those adopted into the folk, they are usually honest. When they need to, they steal young children to fill their ranks, and these are raised as true Rhennee. Outsiders who do them some great service may be taken into the folk and sometimes given high standing, perhaps equal to a noble's.

A typical barge is a junk-like boat with a keel about 60 feet long and a 15-foot beam, with keel boards for full speed under sail, a 10-foot forecastle and a slightly higher sterncastle. Its sides slope outward, with about 6 inches of freeboard when fully loaded (drawing about 8 inches). The low middle deck is home to the men, women and children aboard. It has one or two lug-rigged masts, is steered by tiller and can be rowed with sweeps, usually two a side. The wise women and their families live in the forecastle, the chief, his guards and their families in the sterncastle, and the rest of the folk below decks with the animals and cargo. The sides are rigged to mount heavy crossbows every 4 feet, eight a side. Each barge carries a small dinghy aboard and tows a longboat, and can be chained or cabled to others at bow, stern or either side.

Rhennee look like Oeridians but tend to have dark brown or black curly hair. They are shorter than average (about 5'6") and slender but wiry and strong. Their legends say they came to Oerth by accident from a very different plane, where they roamed on horseback and in wagons; here, conditions were so dangerous that they took to the water to survive. Their nobles claim descent from the legendary leaders of that lost tribe, and ordinary Rhennee from its common folk. A third kind of Rhennee, very rare, are land wanderers who claim to be the only "true" Rhenn-folk, since they have not changed their way of life since coming to the Flanaess from Rhop, the lost homeland.

Men, Tribesmen

The MM describes tribesmen as primitive, but in the Flanaess this is not always so. Some hillmen, marshmen and mountain tribes are quite civilized, especially those who are refugees from a neighboring civilized land. Primitive tribes have shamans and witch doctors as usual; civilized ones have clerics or druids and perhaps illusionists. Civilized tribesmen number 20-120 plus leaders and clerics, with a 10% chance per 10 men of an illusionist of 4th-6th level. Their arms and armor are like bandits', adjusted for the area: hillmen might be slingers with spears, mountaineers might carry crossbows and polearms, and marshmen short bows and long spears. Magic is 5% per level: fighters, armor, sword, miscellaneous weapon, potion; clerics, armor, miscellaneous weapon, potion, scroll, miscellaneous magic; illusionists, potion, scroll, ring, miscellaneous magic.

Rovers of the Barrens tribesmen usually carry spears, light lances, short bows, clubs and daggers, with wooden or bone breastplates and hide shields. Their woodcraft and stealth let them surprise others 50% of the time. Tribesmen in general lean toward chaotic alignment; many are neutral, but refugee and outlaw bands need to be.

Men, Woodsmen

Woodsmen are met in groups of 30-100, armed as follows: ring mail, small shield, battle axe and short sword (10%); ring mail, bow or crossbow and short sword (10%); leather, small shield, short spear and hand axe (20%); leather, bow or crossbow and hand axe (30%); leather, spear and battle axe (30%). They have leaders and clerics like tribesmen and surprise opponents 50% of the time. They are experts at ambushing intruders and evade pursuit as if they were a party of fewer than six moving in darkness, whatever their real number.

Orc Soldiery

120-150 orcs plus their ever-present orc under-officers and serjeants, normal orcs in every respect, with human and/or half-orc officers: 1 captain (F 5-6, AC 3), 3-5 lieutenants (F 3-4, AC 4) and 1 half-orc cleric (C/T or C/A 3-4/3-4, AC 4). There is a 20% chance that the captain or a lieutenant is a half-orc, a fighter/thief (70%) or fighter/assassin of 4th-5th/4th-5th level (captain) or 2nd-3rd/2nd-3rd (lieutenant). Orc soldiery often includes some half-orcs and hobgoblins. All are surly but well trained, with poor morale once their leaders fall or flee. Magic as for levies.

Soldiery

A company of 150-200 mercenaries, usually on foot, with officers, serjeants and scouts mounted: 1 commander (F 6-8, AC 2), 5 lieutenants (F 3-5, AC 3), 2 serjeants per 10 soldiers (F 2, AC 4), 10 scouts (F 1, AC 5) and 140-190 soldiers (F 0, AC 5 or 6; polearms 50%, side arms 30%, missile weapons 20%). Troopers' arms suit their region. Magic as for levies. In hostile land a cleric of 4th-6th level (AC 2) or a magic-user of 3rd-5th (AC 10) goes with them.

Sometimes the DM will want to know where a non-player character was born and raised. The birthplace tables assign a home region at random, and players may use them too if the campaign does not tie their characters to a particular area. The human table favors the mostly non-evil states, since where an evil character comes from is likely to be more obvious.

The tables are in the Greyhawk Tables compendium: Greyhawk Birthplace: Human, Elves, Dwarves, Gnomes, Halflings and Half-Orcs. Each result names a broad area; the DM or player may pick an exact spot within it. The most common alignments and main languages given with each result are suggestions, not rules, and the DM may change either for good reason. Every player character speaks at least the Common tongue.

Source: Glossography p.26-30 ("Adventures on the World of Greyhawk" and "Adventure Locales"). Rewritten in plain words; figures as printed.

These six wilderness scenarios are meant to capture the feel of the Flanaess. The book calls them apocryphal: they grew out of notes scribbled in the margins of the original manuscript. Each is an outline only, and the DM must fill in the details, the encounters, and the treasure to suit the party's levels and the campaign.

Quest of the Mist Golem

Background. Fifteen years ago the city of Greyhawk (or another city of the central Flanaess) suffered a string of strange disappearances among the children of its noble families. They vanished at night and were never seen again, though sometimes a simulacrum took a child's place, committed vile blasphemies and had to be destroyed. After both magical and ordinary investigation, the city magistrate named the wizard Murq as the culprit; his purpose was never learned. When a grim band of high-level guardsmen went to arrest him, he had already fled, leaving only another simulacrum, which died swearing vengeance on the magistrate and the city.

The hook. Murq was all but forgotten until the magistrate began having nightmares. In them, Murq stands in a cold fen and threatens the magistrate and the city with doom. He boasts of finding an ancient book of great power whose secrets let him build a mist golem, a creature that can kill but cannot itself be killed. When the stars are right the golem will be finished and sent out to kill, first the magistrate and then anyone it finds, until everyone in the city is dead or gone.

The court magicians, clerics and astrologers have studied the dreams, the threats, and the place Murq "broadcasts" from, including the stars in the sky behind him. They have searched their histories and star charts and communed with Celestian. All agree the threat may be real; if so, the golem will be finished in only 63 nights. They place the source of the dreams near the headwaters of the Dulsi River, in the Cold Marshes.

The player characters are hired to track Murq down and stop him before the golem is complete. Success brings a large reward, plus whatever they win from evil foes along the way.

The journey. The first leg is easy: across the civilized Kingdom of Furyondy to the town of Crockport on Whyestil Lake. Past that the land is wild. Going up the Dulsi by boat looks fastest but is too risky, since it would surely draw the notice of Iuz's evil creatures. The party must go north overland, dodging or beating humanoid bands from the northern Vesve Forest, Iuz's scouts and spies, and bold Wolf Nomads. Then comes the dangerous crossing of the Howling Hills: the eastern part breeds evil creatures for Iuz, and the western part is the sacred burial ground of the savage, cunning Wolf Nomads. Beyond lie the frozen, monster-filled Cold Marshes.

Murq is guarded by trolls, gnolls and invisible stalkers. Even if he is beaten before the 63rd night, the party must still get back south to collect the reward. The DM creates the encounters, Murq and the mist golem to suit the players' levels and experience.

Werewolves of the Menowood

The Menowood was once a safe haven for elves, pixies and their kind, but lately evil has crept in from the south and east. Most pressing, a savage band of werewolves seems to have settled in the far north of the woods. For several months they have raided the human settlements along the river and the dwarves and gnomes of the Hollow Highlands. The locals have had enough and have pooled their money to hire the party to end the threat.

The employers seldom enter the Menowood and have no idea where the lair is. In the forest the party is likely to meet several of the following:

  • Trolls from the Vast Swamp, who find forest creatures easier prey. They camouflage themselves with green branches and leaves and wait by game trails, surprising on 1-4 (d6). They leap on their prey and rend it, or try to chase it into hidden pits.
  • Bandits, 20-30 of them, newly arrived in the last few weeks after the elves and rangers of the Rieuwood drove them out. Hearing of the werewolf raids, their leader had a clever idea: the bandits wear wolfskins when they raid, and their victims, already terrified of the wolf-men, flee instead of fighting. It has worked twice, bringing a good haul and no losses. Their only fear is meeting the real werewolves. The party will most likely meet them in their wolfskins on the way to another raid. Along with the usual fighter leaders, the band has a 5th level magic-user and a 7th level thief.
  • Treants, 2-5, angry and suspicious of all intruders and wanting every outsider gone. Treated with respect, they may point the party in the general direction of the lair, but will help no further.
  • An owlbear and an ogre that hunt as a team but know to keep away from the elves and treants.
  • Sylvan elves (11-20) on patrol. They can tell the party where not to look, that is, which areas the elves hold. They know of the werewolves only secondhand, since every raid has been outside the forest.
  • Minions of Wastri, two dozen, from the Vast Swamp, with a pack of giant toads, hunting demi-humans to kill. Eight are 1st level clerics and one is 7th level.
  • A blighted elm treant whose disease has rotted its heartwood, so that it hates all animal life (people included) and attacks on sight.
  • The werewolf band, staying near its lair until the time is right for another raid. The lycanthropes have taken over a series of caves in a ravine and set up a small camp, posing as simple woodsmen. They welcome any party of humans and demi-humans, waiting until the visitors are off guard and surrounded before changing shape and attacking. Deep in the caves is the treasure room, holding the loot of every raid. It is also the lair of their leader, a powerful werewolf who is also a vampire. The others accept this and even count it an advantage, since the vampire dislikes their curse-tainted blood. The vampire will not come out by day, even during a battle, unless disturbed in person.

This adventure calls for fairly high level characters; even ordinary werewolves are hard for low and middle levels to handle.

The Lost Passage of the Suloise

The legend. When the Rain of Colorless Fire ended the Age of Glory and brought down the Empire, the tribes chose to seek their fate in the east, in the lands of the Flan. To speed the migration, Slerotin, the Last Mage of Power, had a great tunnel made by magic through the northeastern mountains. One by one the tribes passed out of the Empire into the East. When none were left in the Sea of Dust, the Last Mage sealed the tunnel at both ends with a spell meant to last a thousand years.

The hook. Where the Crystalmists border the Yeomanry, humans and demi-humans brave the mountains for their gems and precious metals. A band of dwarves prospecting for silver recently found a huge cave mouth where none should be. Being dwarves, they went in, but were chased out by a huge, thundering black creature with glowing red eyes that seemed unharmed by their crossbow bolts. It looked like an unbeatable evil monster from dwarven legend and frightened them so badly that they refuse to go back. They have told almost no one, but one night a tipsy dwarf tells the tale to a certain party of adventurers.

The tunnel. With the dwarf's directions the opening is not hard to find. Brush and large trees hide it, but not well enough to stop determined searchers. The opening and the passage behind it are 30 feet high and 300 feet wide, and the tunnel runs straight through the mountains at that size for its whole length of over 200 miles.

The northeastern end is guarded by a large black juggernaut that "sees" through glowing red gem eyes. Its low armor class makes most missiles bounce off. Over the centuries its magic has run down, so an unencumbered man can now outrun or outmaneuver it, but anyone it catches is crushed flat. It was placed there to destroy anyone who found and dispelled the magical seal.

The truth. The seal did last a thousand years; it has been weakening for decades and is now gone entirely. The legend is mostly true, but it leaves out one thing that Slerotin never knew: one Suloise tribe, the Lerara, had not quite left the passage when it was sealed. Trapped in the tunnel, they and their animals adapted, and a whole underground ecology grew up.

Most of the tunnel is dry and empty except for dust, but some stretches are damp or even wet, and fungi of every kind grow there, including edible and glowing kinds. After about 25 miles, travelers reach the first outposts of the Lerara. Fair to begin with, they are now near-albinos with pale bluish-white eyes and silver-white hair. These degenerate, inbred Suloise farm many kinds of fungus for food and use giant millipedes as draft animals. Noble warriors ride the millipedes, and this cavalry makes up about a quarter of their troops. All Lerara weapons are coated with a paralyzing fungus poison.

The Lerara have not been wholly cut off. When the tunnel was made it crossed a much smaller tunnel about halfway through the mountains, and strange boring creatures have dug more since. The smaller tunnel leads to the deeper maze beneath the Hellfurnaces to the south, and the Lerara now trade with the Drow there, swapping fungus poison for weapons, goods and animals (such as the millipedes). Even so, they might have died out had they not found something in the tunnels below the main passage, in a place untrodden for an age: a thing to worship and a reason to exist, the Mother.

The Mother is all but evil made flesh, giving off a wickedness that is somehow strangely attractive. It looks like a huge, white, glowing ooze covering the walls and ceiling of its large cave, with complex ripples and waves always flowing across its surface. The floor of the Cavern of the Mother is strewn with the ancient treasure the Lerara were carrying when they were trapped, offered to the Mother when they found her divine evil, along with the bones of earlier sacrifices.

Meeting the Lerara. The Lerara do not yet know the seals are open. On meeting intruders they are first astonished and retreat down the tunnel. After a while they change their manner and welcome the party, seemingly delighted to meet people from the outside world at last, and offer to lead them to their chief, a trip of many "sleeps." Those who go along are shown every sign of hospitality. In truth the warriors are leading them to the tunnel crossing and then down to the Cavern of the Mother, always pretending to head for the chief's cave. Near the Cavern they plan to attack, paralyze the party, and throw them into the Mother's body, which slowly drains their life levels.

The DM decides how tough to make the juggernaut, the Lerara and the Mother, based on the party's levels, numbers and experience, and creates the Mother's treasure to fit the campaign.

The Jungle of Lost Ships

The offer. In Sulward, capital of the Lordship of the Isles, an aging merchant approaches the party with a business proposal. One of his ships on the regular run to Hepmonaland, he says, was caught in a sudden storm and blown hundreds of leagues east. When the wind died, a strange current drew the ship to a great mass of dense, tangled seaweed, some of it formed into huge floating mounds. Drifting closer, the captain saw that the mounds were derelict ships, trapped and overgrown by the weed: ships of every nation, some of kinds out of use for decades or never seen before. Most important, he recognized two from the legendary Lost Treasure Fleet of the Sea Princes. Another storm let the ship escape before it was stuck for good. The captain reported all this and retired, since that voyage was to have been his last anyway.

The merchant plans a voyage to the sea of weeds to loot the treasure ships and wants to hire the party to deal with the many strange monsters in and around the weed if they interfere. As payment the adventurers may keep any treasure they find and can carry themselves. The mission must be kept secret to avoid rivals; in fact their ship leaves tonight at midnight, from a spot a few miles down the coast, before word can spread.

The truth. Most of the story is true, except that the teller is no merchant but the Sulward Guildmaster of Assassins in disguise. Pirates robbed and sank the merchant ship, and its captain tried to buy his life with the tale; all he bought was a quick death. The pirates needed money for repairs and joined forces with the Sulward Assassins' Guild, whose leader was once a pirate himself. The Guild paid for the mission with a large fee just received from the Sea Barons for assassinating the Lordship's Grand Admiral. For that deed the Prince of Duxchan is now trying in earnest to destroy the Guild, so most of the assassins, the Guildmaster included, are going on the voyage, hoping things will have cooled down by their return. The ship waiting down the coast is the refitted pirate vessel, disguised as an armed merchantman.

The job offer is real, but the Guildmaster has not mentioned that once the treasure ships are looted, the assassins (disguised as sailors) will try to kill the party under the best conditions they can get, at night with all or most of the party asleep. All the pirates and assassins are ordered to act like ordinary rough sailors and have been threatened with dire punishment if they give themselves away. If sea monsters attack on the way, the crew is to let the adventurers do most of the fighting.

The weed sea. The seaweed jungle sits at the center of a giant, slow whirlpool of ocean currents. Because the huge weed patch turns slowly, the ship will not find the treasure ships at once. The edges can be sailed, but the crew must work very hard not to be trapped. Most of the trapped ships were crippled by storms first; a sound ship should stay clear with hard work, and oars help.

The first thing the characters notice is that the weed swarms with life: fish, birds, crustaceans, eels. It is a floating reef and a haven for creatures of all kinds, including predators such as octopi and squids (some quite large), Portuguese men-of-war, barracudas, giant sea snakes, sharks and sea crocodiles. The weed itself is dangerous, full of strangle weed waiting for the unwary.

Across several square miles are dozens of great weed mounds, each the corpse of a trapped ship. They all look much alike, so several will probably have to be searched before the treasure ships are found. Reaching the center is hard, since no ship's boat can push through the matted plants. Once inside, the party finds that many of the ships are inhabited:

  • a ship occupied by a hunting band of lizard men;
  • a ship haunted by lacedons (sea ghouls) and drowned zombies;
  • a ship that serves as a kelpies' lair;
  • kopoacinth lurking just under the surface, ready to snatch stragglers;
  • a ship made of metal, with no mast or oars, holding charts of unknown seas;
  • eight ships that are home to a strange society of half-mad humans, a mixed people descended from centuries of shipwrecks.

The weed people live by fishing through holes cut in the weed and travel across the mat on snowshoe-like footgear made of light planks. Most carry spears. They worship a spirit of the ocean and believe all land beyond the horizon has sunk beneath the waves, leaving a world of water. Every newcomer must swear to this belief or be killed as a blasphemer. Their leader is their high priest, Narawa, best known for intolerance and insanity (and high charisma).

How much treasure is left in the Lost Treasure Fleet is up to the DM; the reward should match the difficulty of the adventure.

The Copper Raider

The Voormann of Perrenland is worried. The Cantons export a great deal of copper south, but for ten weeks no copper caravan has reached the town of Highfolk safely. Three caravans were wiped out, their caravaneers killed and the copper and other goods stolen; the third had 24 men-at-arms as guards, and all of them were killed and looted. Plenty of other trade has passed between Schwartzenbruin and Highfolk without trouble, but the copper trade has stopped. No local will risk a copper shipment, so the Voormann seeks outside adventurers to take the copper through to Highfolk. If they destroy whatever has been attacking the copper caravans, they will be richly rewarded, and no one will complain if they keep some of the loot from the earlier caravans.

The road from Schwartzenbruin to Highfolk follows the Velverdyva River through a deep canyon where it cuts through the Yatil Mountains. Humanoid raiders sometimes attack travelers here, though the Perrenlanders have driven most of them off. Rockfalls and landslides now and then block the road and slow travel. The river runs sometimes on the east side of the canyon and sometimes on the west, so the road crosses it on bridges here and there, and sometimes passes through what the book calls "runnels" in the canyon walls.

The raider is Clonoc, a large, old copper dragon who lost a duel with a demon and is now possessed. The dragon's body and mind are too big for the rather small demon to control fully, so its attempts have left him somewhat deranged, with a split personality. The demon's plan to have him attack all passing trade has mostly failed, except when a copper caravan passes, which the dragon's tortured mind somehow takes as a deliberate insult. Then the demon takes over and the caravan is attacked. Once everyone is dead, the dragon's natural greed (made worse by demonic greed) takes over and the loot goes back to his lair. Deep inside, Clonoc regrets what he does but can do nothing about it.

Clonoc is a spell-using dragon. Before an attack he casts invisibility on himself and glides down from the canyon heights, becoming visible only when he rakes the party with his first breath of acid. From then until the fight ends, the demon fully controls his fighting. That loosens its grip elsewhere, giving Clonoc's own personality some room, so even while trying to kill everyone in the caravan he roars "Help me! Save me! I'm possessed!" and the like in Common. He cannot be subdued while possessed. If he is captured or disabled, the demon takes over his speech and answers questions with insults and threats. If the demon is exorcised, Clonoc gratefully hands over the caravans' loot, perhaps with something extra from his own hoard.

As with the other adventures, the DM decides the amounts of treasure to suit the campaign.

The Stolen Seal

Background. The successful alliance of the Barony of Ratik and the Frost Barbarians has alarmed Bone March, and the Baron of Ratik's political enemies in Rauxes. The tribes of Bone March still smart from the beating the joint Ratik-Fruztii armies gave them last year, so their evil leaders have decided the northern alliance must be broken. They contacted certain spies in Marner who usually work for the Overking and struck a deal. In a daring raid, the Seal of the Alliance was stolen from the Baronial Vault. This symbolic parchment was endorsed and blessed by the gods of both Ratik and Fruztii, and the superstitious Frost Barbarians set great store by its safety. Once it is known that the men of Ratik failed to keep it safe, the alliance will probably collapse, or at least be badly hurt. The Seal is now on its way to Spinecastle, to be displayed and the theft publicly announced.

All this was learned, under duress, from a spy captured in the raid. The Baron asks the player characters to ride with a platoon of troops in pursuit, capture the conspirators and recover the Seal, following them into Bone March if need be.

The chase. The party is given fast horses if they have none and hurried off to join the platoon. On the road, bandits hired by the conspirators delay the pursuit just long enough for the thieves to cross the border. The border road, high in the hills, is guarded by two companies of orcs, too many for the platoon. Its officer suggests the party leave the road and slip across the border to the east or west while the horsemen create a diversion. From there it is up to the party to catch the conspirators, recover the Seal, and bring it back to Marner.

Despite the diversion, the party meets a few orc guards; if these are not silenced properly they may bring many more. Once over the border and back on the road, a couple of hours of hard riding should catch the now slow-moving conspirators. Recovering the Seal will not be easy: the thieves and assassins from Marner now ride with an armed group that was waiting for them with the border guard:

  • 24 orcs, including some leader types;
  • an evil human magic-user of high level, with suitable magic items, who now carries the Seal;
  • 5 ogres, all well armed and armored;
  • a charmed minotaur that guards and obeys the magic-user.

The DM should add or remove foes as needed for balance. The minotaur is very alert, so the group is hard to surprise; if they hear the pursuers' horses far enough off, the hunters may themselves fall into a quick ambush.

If the party recovers the Seal, they must still escape through the enslaved countryside back to Ratik. The border orcs could be a real problem: by now they know someone slipped past and will watch for the same trick from either direction. They are commanded by a half-orc fighter/assassin who makes clever use of his savage troops. The reward for returning the Seal is up to the DM.

Source: GA p.117-118 (Appendix 1: Zero-Level Characters). Rewritten in plain words; figures as printed.

Player characters usually start at 1st level, but they need not come from nowhere. By the time a character reaches 1st level, he or she may have studied for years and made the choices that shaped a life. Instead of skipping that time, players may start their characters at zero level, without the skills of any class. This lets a player build exactly the character wanted, even a sword-swinging wizard or a thief who can turn undead. Few adventures are more exciting than these first ones, in which ordinary, untried people must find power within themselves, survive, and grow strong.

Creating a Zero-Level Character

A new zero-level character's abilities are weak and undefined; the only advantages are great curiosity and enthusiasm. Roll only for the things that are fixed from birth: height, weight, and social status if that is used. Record strength, dexterity, constitution, intelligence, wisdom and charisma at a starting value of 3 each. The character also starts with 3 hit points.

Zero-level characters have no experience points and cannot earn any. Their only real resource is aptitude points (AP), which are spent to build everything else. Each character starts with 90 + 1d20 AP.

Raising Ability Scores

Once per game week, the player may put 1 to 8 AP into a single ability score or into hit points. The points come off the AP total at once and are added to the score. A score raised this way never goes down while the character is at zero level; in effect, the character always had the talent and has suddenly developed it. Abilities still take time to reach their full potential, so no more than 8 AP may be spent this way in a week.

Demi-humans must raise every ability to their racial minimum before play begins, spending AP to represent their long childhoods. A zero-level demi-human has all the natural features of the race, including ability bonuses. Racial penalties, such as a halfling's -1 to strength, never take a score below 3; they apply only once the score is raised above 3. For example, a new dwarf has charisma 3 (the -1 cannot apply yet) and constitution 4 (3 plus the +1 bonus). He must spend 8 AP at once on constitution to reach the racial minimum of 12. Later, when he raises his charisma, the first AP goes to cancelling the racial penalty before the score can climb above 3.

No amount of AP can give a zero-level character more than 18 hit points or a score above the racial maximum. Gray elves may have intelligence 19; everyone else is limited to 18. Exceptional strength needs special fighter training (see Fighting Skills). Players should not pour too many AP into one ability, since AP are also needed to learn skills.

Ability scores have all their usual effects at zero level: a character who neglects strength suffers in combat, and one with low dexterity cannot use thief skills. Since any ability can be raised at once, characters will seldom be stuck with a penalty, but a wise player may let some abilities lag to concentrate on others.

Hit Points

A zero-level character's hit points have nothing to do with skill, luck or toughness; each one stands for youthful energy and vitality. The starting 3 points represent body mass. A character who raises constitution gets the usual hit point bonus, as if 1st level. The bonus of 3 points for constitution 17 or 4 points for 18 is a special fighter ability, like exceptional strength, so zero-level characters do not get it. A zero-level character can never have more than 18 hit points at once. On reaching 1st level, the player rerolls hit points in the normal way.

Alignment

Zero-level characters have no real alignment; spells and magic items treat them as true neutral. Instead they have an alignment tendency, which the DM assigns to reflect the character's behavior and attitude. The DM can track it with two scores, one for law/chaos and one for good/evil, on a scale of 1 to 20 where higher numbers mean more lawful or more good and 10 is the middle. Alignment stays true neutral until a score moves more than five points either way. Scores can go below zero.

ScoreMorality (good/evil)Ethics (law/chaos)
5 or lessEvilChaotic
6-14NeutralNeutral
15 and aboveGoodLawful

The book prints these as two separate charts, the Morality Chart and the Ethics Chart.

The DM adds or subtracts points whenever the character does something typical of an alignment. Such acts are easy to spot: love, forgiveness and heroic courage are good; cruelty, greed and treachery are evil. Chaotic characters dislike and disobey rules and decide things on the spur of the moment, perhaps acting differently in similar situations. Lawful characters work toward order and consistency. Neutrality may be a lack of opinion or a deliberate effort to balance extremes. Isolated acts of necessity, such as making friends or defending oneself, do not change the scores. Acts of choice, such as forming close friendships or giving to charity, may. Willful acts such as senseless slaughter by a good or lawful character certainly do.

At creation, a player who does not want to start as true neutral may pick any score from 0 to 20 on each scale, representing what the character's family and friends taught. These scores can change quickly if the character breaks old habits, and adventures may move a character off true neutral.

At the end of each adventure the DM tells players their characters' tendencies, but not the exact scores; characters seldom know exactly how lawful, chaotic, good or evil they are. Every decision is a moral dilemma that may shape a whole life. When a character reaches 1st level, he or she becomes whatever alignment the tendency shows at that moment.

Source: GA p.118-124 (Appendix 1: Zero-Level Characters). Rewritten in plain words; figures as printed.

Once a character has raw abilities, he or she must learn to use them. A zero-level character experiments all the time, perhaps trying to weave spells one day and crossing swords the next. That freedom makes learning new abilities the most exciting part of a zero-level life, and the most dangerous. Whenever the player wishes, the character may study, or simply attempt, an ability normally used by a character class. Characters may try abilities of up to 12th level in difficulty, but will almost never do better than a 1st level character could.

An "ability" here means any of an adventurer's tasks: fighters fight, clerics turn undead, mages cast spells and thieves pick locks, each at some ability level. A zero-level character has two ways to attempt a class task: trust to luck, or take time to study it first.

Study

A class ability must be taught by an NPC who has it; any thief can teach picking pockets and climbing walls. A character may study under several teachers at once to pick up several abilities. When using an ability, the character rolls on the Learning Table below, so the result does not depend on the teacher's level or on 1st level. Zero-level characters have the zest and confidence of people who have not yet grasped the danger. A 1st level cleric carefully presents a holy symbol and speaks the words to turn undead; a zero-level character might rush up, thrust the symbol in a vampire's face and yell "BOO!" The 1st level cleric could not turn the vampire, but the zero-level character might turn it as a 12th level cleric, simply because the vampire was so surprised.

Studying earns one instruction point per week, with at least an hour a day with the teacher; missing a day loses that week's point. The player records the points and what they apply to. The character also spends 1 AP for every 6 instruction points earned.

It is possible, and often wise, to earn more points in a field than the class needs. Learning a fighter ability takes only 2 points, for example, but extra points help with the many different abilities of that class.

Study in one field must not be broken up: a character studying to be a fighter must study two weeks in a row to earn the two points, or lose everything gained. While study continues, nothing is forgotten. If the character stops studying a field, the points earned are kept for three months per point; six points toward magic are remembered for 18 months. After that, study must start again from scratch. Points earned through luck are never lost.

Luck

Trusting to luck means the character has not studied the task but thinks "this can't be too hard, other people do it," and tries to force a way through. The Learning Table gives the result. A specific task can be tried by luck only once a day: a character trying out thief skills may try once to pick a pocket, once to climb a wall and once to hide in shadows, but not two pockets in 24 hours. A successful luck attempt earns instruction points, since the character learns by deduction and intuition; the DM decides how many.

Finding Teachers

Finding a teacher should be one of a zero-level character's first adventures. Clerics and fighters are not hard to find, mages are harder, and thieves and the rarer classes are very hard. Teachers expect work in return, and the odd jobs they need done make good early adventures: fighters always need equipment mended, mages need spell components gathered, thieves need lookouts, and clerics need their temples cleaned.

The Study Time and Learning Tables

Type of skillStudy points for success
Fighter2 points
Mage6 points

Druid6 points
Paladin8 points
Ranger7 points

Thief3 points

01-1001-10NoneTerrible Failure
