86-9788-959Insight
98-10096-10012Great Insight

When trusting to luck, the player rolls percentile dice and takes the result, and the DM works it into the adventure. A character relying on instruction points also rolls percentile dice; if the character has earned enough points for the result rolled, it happens, and if not, the DM uses the Failure result.

  • Terrible Failure: the attempt fails and any equipment used is broken or lost. The DM also invents a penalty to fit: a beginning archer might shoot a friend, or an amateur sorcerer flood the teacher's laboratory.
  • Failure: nothing is learned, but there is no penalty.
  • Partial Success: the character may use this one ability as a 1st level character. If this came by luck and the character later studies the ability, the first week of study earns 2 instruction points.
  • Learning: the character counts as 1st level for this one ability. If this came by luck, the first week of later study earns 3 points.
  • Insight: the novice not only succeeds but uses the ability as a 12th level character. With a weapon proficiency, the character attacks as a 12th level fighter with weapon specialization; non-weapon proficiencies get a bonus of -4 to the die roll. The insight is forgotten after one hour per point of intelligence. If this came by luck, later study earns 4 points after one week.
  • Great Insight: as Insight, but kept for one week per point of intelligence before it is forgotten. The DM should also invent a stroke of good luck: a single arrow might rout a whole bandit gang, or an artisan might make a beautiful item that is also magical. If this came by luck, the abilities are lost after two weeks (four weeks for magic-user spells), and later study earns 6 points after one week. The character can use the very task being attempted at 12th level for those two weeks even without ever studying it: a character who gets Great Insight while turning undead can turn undead as a 12th level cleric, but cannot necessarily do anything else a 12th level cleric can.

The table never allows the impossible: no luck or training lets a character cast spells without a spellbook or pick locks without tools. Each result applies to one skill only; a character who learns to pick pockets still cannot hide in shadows.

Sages as Teachers

Sages make the best teachers, since they can teach any skill they have studied. Their usual fields are given in the DMG. Two more fields exist that sages may know and teach to zero-level characters: Weapons & Warfare and Crime & Criminals, both special categories studied under humankind, demi-humankind and humanoids/giantkind. A sage's chance to teach a skill equals the DMG chance of answering a question about it exactly. Many fields overlap: a sage whose major field is humankind has a 57%-60% chance to understand a cleric spell well enough to teach it (under Theology & Myth) and the same chance to teach picking pockets (under Crime & Criminals), so a student could learn both without finding a cleric and a thief.

Class Skills

Every field has its pitfalls and customs. Advanced studies such as magic need more AP and study, and the DM should play teachers' attitudes accordingly.

A novice may serve a patron as an apprentice, or study at the college of a great religious order or magical cabal. A college may charge up to 500 gp a year, though nobles may grant scholarships to promising students, usually expecting repayment in some form, such as a quest. Some religious colleges are free but open only to worshipers of their deity. Wealthy characters who find no college and scorn apprenticeship may hire tutors at 100 gp a month or more. Characters may need to travel to find teachers. In remote places they are limited to the few skilled people nearby and may soon outgrow them, while city dwellers have more to learn from but tend to lose touch with nature and may need to go into the wilds to learn from rangers or druids.

Clerical Skills

Each deity has its own customs for new followers: many churches eagerly seek worshipers, others are secretive. Zero-level characters may freely mix religion with other pursuits, but no sect knowingly welcomes its enemies. A character cannot use clerical powers unless his or her current alignment tendency matches the god's alignment, and even luck rolls give no clerical power unless the character calls on a deity of friendly alignment. Using clerical powers deepens commitment: each time, the DM moves the character's tendency one point toward the deity's alignment.

A zero-level character may cast one 1st level cleric spell a day, or two with wisdom 14 or more. Great Insight lets the character cast any one spell, up to 6th level, as a 12th level cleric, but does not give a high-level cleric's full range of spells. Each spell must be studied separately; a character who can cast command still knows nothing of cure light wounds. Novices can also learn to turn undead. Learning a spell and casting it once is free; casting it again costs 1 AP.

Gods dislike being trifled with, and novices' trivial requests may annoy them. Each time a zero-level character casts a spell, roll 1d20. If the roll is above the character's wisdom, the spell fails and a small boil appears on the caster's forehead, lowering charisma by 1 for the rest of the day. The check fails automatically if the character has broken a clerical code in the last 24 hours; the most widespread code forbids edged weapons, and some gods have more. Characters with wisdom 12 or less must also check for spell failure as usual (see the PHB). Characters with wisdom below 9 cannot learn cleric spells.

A character who gives up religious study usually keeps the clerical skills and at worst gets a passionate lecture from a senior priest, though this depends on the religion. A character who switches to an opposing religion or alignment tendency is seen as a traitor who took the church's blessings and betrayed it, and is struck by a random disease from the DMG. Some religions have special punishments or enemies for such heretics.

Druidic Skills

The woodland cult of druids demands a great deal of its followers. Its rites are never described openly and are performed only at nature's will. Druids are very reluctant to teach anyone who has not already shown deep communion with the powers of nature, and teaching novices is not a druid's main goal. The DM should set quests and ordeals for would-be druids, but the best way to win a druid's favor is to perform some great druidic feat by luck.

Druid powers work like other clerical talents: one 1st level druid spell a day, with a wisdom check to cast it correctly. The check fails automatically if the character wore metal armor or used forbidden weapons in the last 24 hours. Great Insight may allow high-level druid abilities such as shapechanging or knowledge of plants and animals. Learning a spell and casting it more than once costs 1 AP.

Students of druidism need not tend toward true neutral, but all must have close ties to nature and the nature deities. Rangers and bards learn druid spells whatever their alignment, and zero-level characters may be allowed the same latitude. Using druid powers does not change a character's alignment tendency. Druids never punish former students for their choice of alignment; what they hate is crimes against nature. A zero-level character who desecrates an unspoiled place catches a disease as fallen clerics do and loses all druidic magic. Worse, once the deed is known, every druid in the world will seek revenge.

Fighting Skills

Fighting skills are the easiest to master. A budding warrior need only study weapon proficiencies and specializations, perhaps with physical training for the extra constitution bonus or exceptional strength. Exceptional strength requires strength 18 first. If the character successfully learns how to build muscle, Great Insight gives 18/00; any other success means rolling percentile dice for exceptional strength as usual.

Zero-level characters may try any ranger or paladin ability, including the techniques for extra damage against giant-type humanoids and the arts of dodging (dexterity bonus), endurance (hit point bonus) and avoiding harm (saving throw bonuses). Only a few solitary rangers and holy warriors know these skills. Characters must brave the wilderness to find them and then prove themselves worthy; few woodsmen like to share their secrets, and all paladins scorn the impure. Wilderness study also limits other learning, since the student must stay with the teacher far from civilization.

Each time a zero-level character uses a paladin ability, add 1 point to both law and good, and the DM records it. The gods themselves grant a paladin's benefits, so a character who accepts this help and later abandons lawful good loses all paladin powers and is cursed the next time he or she enters battle (the reverse of the 1st level cleric spell bless). Some gods have special punishments for such traitors. A paladin will train any zero-level character acceptable to his or her god, and most gods care nothing for mortal social rank. Few teachers demand such strict obedience, though: most paladins take only pupils who want to become paladins and would be outraged to catch them exploring less honorable arts.

Magical Skills

Magic is hard to master and leaves those who go deep into it little time for anything else. A novice mage must learn each spell separately, and knowing a spell is not enough to cast it: the novice must memorize it from a spellbook each day like any mage. A zero-level character can memorize no more than one 1st level spell or four cantrips a day. Insight lets the character cast one spell, of up to 6th level, as a 12th level caster, but does not give a 12th level mage's full selection of spells. Each spell learned and used more than once costs 1 AP.

Few beginners own spellbooks, so apprentices borrow their teacher's each day. They must justify each spell they want to the teacher, but they have many spells to choose from. The DM decides which spells a wizard owns and which students may use. Normal intelligence limits on learning spells apply (see the PHB); nobody with intelligence below 9 can learn magic.

Novices never fully understand any spell but cantrips. When a zero-level character casts higher magic, roll 1d20; if the roll is higher than the character's intelligence, the spell backfires or fails. Harmful spells may hurt the caster; others produce nothing but clouds of blue smoke. The DM may improvise funny or horrifying failures. A failed spell is not lost: the caster can try again next round, and keeps the spell memorized until it is finally used. The Learning Table decides whether a spell has been properly memorized in the first place.

Armor and weapons disturb a magician's mental powers. No one can cast spells in armor. Using a weapon forbidden to mages within 24 hours before casting adds 3 to the intelligence check roll. Most teachers forbid weapons and armor entirely and may refuse lessons or punish students caught using them, with warnings about famous magical disasters.

Some spells are essential for a zero-level mage to move beyond borrowing scraps of magic from a patron. Read magic is needed for all magic-user work, and identify, detect magic and erase make the trade much easier; most teachers require students to learn these and record them in their first spellbooks.

Spellbooks cannot simply be bought, even with money in hand. They must be made by bookbinders skilled in the art and filled with spells by a magician. In a world without printing presses, few scribes know bookbinding, and they gather near universities or the courts of learned kings. Even with a book, most teachers will not give their formulas permanently to anyone but a fellow mage, so a zero-level character will probably have to adventure to get copies of spells and then find a friendly mage to help write them in.

Thieving Skills

Almost every zero-level character learns a few thieving skills: stealth often saves a life where force cannot, and thief skills help in any class. Bulky armor hampers or prevents them. Those who rely on thievery will want lessons, but although every community has many thieves, few admit it and fewer teach. Apprentice thieves usually train in cities, where victims are many and criminals are often bold enough to run fairly organized burglary schools; these courses give one extra learning point per month.

Monk Skills

Few zero-level characters want a monk's lonely life. Martial arts teachers are found at any monastery, but monastic isolation rules out all other study, and few can bear the rigid discipline. A student who finds the life too hard may leave freely, but no master will ever teach him or her again.

A character who breaks monastic codes cannot keep the monk's open hand attack, running ability or thief skills. Hoarding excess treasure or using forbidden weapons bars a zero-level character from studying monk skills. Armor prevents monk martial arts, just as it hampers thieves. Mental powers learned through insight vanish once the character defies the monks' laws. Only characters with a lawful tendency can learn monk skills, and each use of a monk power adds 1 point to law/chaos.

Proficiencies

Many skills belong to no particular class. A zero-level character may study any proficiency for which a teacher can be found, and teachers are much easier to find in cities. Where a guild controls a craft, the character must follow its rules. Guilds usually limit how many new artisans are trained, to avoid a surplus, and they regulate quality and charge dues. Each proficiency costs 1 AP and takes two weeks of instruction.

Zero-level characters will need weapon proficiencies; using a weapon without proficiency is -3 to hit. Weapon specialization is a fighter class skill and can be learned only from a specialist. No character may ever specialize in more than two weapons.

Languages

Every character starts knowing one language, the local common tongue. When intelligence rises high enough to allow more languages, they can be studied as one-slot proficiencies. Study time is halved if the student is surrounded by speakers of the language and doubled if no native speakers are present. A character cannot use luck with a language until having heard it spoken for at least an hour. Learning Table results for languages mean:

  • Partial Success: can hold a general conversation and ask for basic needs.
  • Learning: fluent, but with a strong accent that marks the speaker as foreign.
  • Insight: can pass as a native with a successful intelligence check on 1d20.
  • Great Insight: speaks the language completely naturally.

Characters may travel to learn languages or look for teachers from distant lands: usually sailors, pilgrims, scholars, merchants or foreign exiles sheltering at a noble's court. Teachers of non-human tongues are especially hard to find. Elves may teach their language, but dwarves keep theirs secret, and most humanoids are too barbaric to trade knowledge formally. Orc or goblin can be learned only by living with those creatures or by finding a veteran of wars against them who knows the tongue. The DM may decide that a teacher's knowledge is incomplete, leading to funny or deadly misunderstandings.

pages.name: Into Play and Into a Class

text.content:
Source: GA p.124-126 (Appendix 1: Zero-Level Characters). Rewritten in plain words; figures as printed.

Combat and Wounds

Most of the combat rules for zero-level characters come from their abilities, class skills and proficiencies. They always attack and save as zero-level fighters. The only exception is a flash of Insight with a weapon proficiency, which lets the character attack as a 12th level fighter. Luckily, most enemies underestimate zero-level characters, which gives them extra chances to be heroes.

Zero-level characters often survive terrible wounds through sheer energy. When reduced to 0 hit points or fewer, a character may spend 1 AP to stop losing hit points, and then heals 1 hit point per hour, at a cost of 1 AP for each point healed. This can bring the character back to no more than 1 hit point; after that, normal healing applies. A character is maimed below -6 hit points and dies past -10. While at negative hit points the character is in a coma and is treated as if under a feign death spell. Most enemies assume they struck a fatal blow and leave the victim, but especially determined foes may check for signs of life, or imprison or dismember the victim to be sure.

Equipment and Money

Zero-level characters are often poor, but not always. They often have more money than a 1st level character, since they have not yet spent it on teachers and gear. As a rule, they start with ordinary clothing and 2d10 × 10 gp (20-200 gp).

The DM may replace this money with other, more fitting wealth. Children of nomad herders might own weapons, food and horses but no cash. A character might inherit the gear and loot of a recently dead adventurer. A DM might start a whole campaign by giving a character an enchanted item, or a cursed one. Even weak magic can give a character the confidence to adventure and a reason to live up to the item's history.

Using Magic Items

Zero-level characters may use any magic item. Using items limited to one class is a class skill, so the character must study or make luck rolls to learn each item's secrets, one item at a time, at a cost of 1 AP per item learned. Zero-level characters can even use spell scrolls, though with high chances of failure, as shown in the DMG.

Joining a Character Class

Joining a class is the turning point of a zero-level life; every apprentice dreams of graduating as a real 1st level adventurer. To do so, a character must meet the class's minimum requirements and then prove worthy of the new title. Characters may try whenever they wish, and nothing forces them to choose a class, but once their AP are gone the only alternative is to stagnate, unable to improve or rise in level. Wise characters choose a class early and prepare while they still have AP to spend on the skills they need. The more powers a class offers, the more study it takes to qualify.

To actually reach 1st level, the character must learn the last secrets of the class from a patron, who always tests the novice with an initiation. Rangers go through nature rites, clerics are ordained, knights are dubbed, and other classes have similar ceremonies. Some are less formal: apprentice thieves may be used and humiliated for months to see whether they grow bold enough to rob their own masters, and fighters are likely to face their final test on the battlefield.

After the final lesson, the character becomes 1st level:

  • The alignment tendency becomes a fixed alignment.
  • Hit points are rolled in the normal way.
  • Ability scores are fixed at their current values.
  • Proficiencies and languages stay as they are; a character with fewer than allowed may learn more normally.
  • Any remaining AP become experience points, at 10 XP per AP.
  • The character earns experience points normally from now on.
  • The character gains all the abilities of a 1st level member of the class. Professional spellcasters no longer check for spell failure.

On rising in level, a character loses every skill not used by his or her main class unless making a special effort to keep it, as follows.

Keeping Skills from Other Classes

Zero-level characters try many trades and naturally hope to keep their old skills after joining a class. They can, but the classes have little in common, and the more time spent on one field, the less there is for others. A character must practice these extra skills and pay experience points for them, at the prices below.

Character's classType of skill
ClFMUTMk
Cleric5%*10%25%25%10%
Fighter25%5%*50%10%25%
Magic-User25%50%5%*10%25%
Thief25%10%25%5%*25%
Monk25%50%50%50%5%*

* Subclasses count under their main class (a ranger is found under fighter), and paladins can be treated as fighters. Using a skill of a different subclass of one's own general type costs only 5%, instead of the larger out-of-class prices. The book's table is titled "Experience Price for Auxiliary Abilities"; it does not say in so many words how the percentage is applied.

A character must also use each extra skill at least once per level, in a crucial moment on an actual adventure, or lose it on reaching the next level. The DM keeps a list of when characters use skills from other classes. If a player rises in level without practicing a skill, the DM does not remind them: if the player cannot remember the skill, neither can the character, and when the character finally tries it, it is gone for good.

Each level gained wipes out all neglected extra skills, including 12th level skills gained through Great Insight. Forgotten skills no longer cost experience. Some combinations carry further limits:

  • Cleric and druid skills: anyone using divine powers must obey the gods; the DM should deny clerical magic to characters who break their alignment or fail to behave piously. Clerics and druids may never use forbidden weapons or items, even through a proficiency kept from another class. Members of other classes cannot use clerical abilities on a day they wield edged weapons or, for druid spells, wear metal armor. Non-clerics may never cast more than one cleric spell a day (two with high wisdom), and must always make the wisdom check against spell failure.
  • Fighter skills: little interferes with fighting, so only rangers and paladins must avoid other classes' skills; no ranger or paladin would ever use thief abilities. This does not work in reverse: any class may use ranger and paladin abilities. A paladin's magical powers count as cleric spells for both experience price and limits, and no one may use them without keeping the paladin's restrictions.
  • Magic-user skills: no one can cast spells in armor or without a spellbook. Everyone but mages must make intelligence checks or fail their spells, as described under Magical Skills, and even true mages must check if they have used a forbidden weapon in the last 24 hours. So low-level mages often use forbidden weapons, but powerful ones keep to daggers, since a failure with their great magic can ruin kingdoms. Other classes can never cast more than one mage spell a day.
  • Thief skills: the only limit is that they cannot be used in most armor. At the DM's option, leather or padded armor may be worn, with penalties. Lawful and good characters must take care not to break their principles with thief skills.
  • Monk skills: cannot be used in armor. Any character may keep the monk's running, monk thief abilities, weapon damage bonuses or open hand attack, but only a real monk can keep the mental or magical skills. Monks never use other classes' skills; those belong to the worldly life they have given up.

NPCs

These rules show how beginning player characters become adventurers; they are not meant to change the zero-level NPCs who fill every fantasy world. Ordinary peasants and townsfolk usually use up their AP young, competing with their peers, surviving childhood dangers and learning to work, and many people are not adventurous and never had a full 90 AP. The DM may still give NPCs AP. A party will treat ordinary people with much more respect after attacking a helpless beggar who makes a luck roll and strikes back like a 12th level fighter. Many zero-level NPCs use AP to excel at their trades: a blacksmith might study until he has enough points to qualify for Great Insight in casting enchant an item. This is one way dwarves, who are not mages, might enchant hammers +3 and dwarven throwers.

Oriental Characters

Characters from the Far East face more social pressure than Western ones, but underneath they are much the same, and they also develop through AP. A zero-level character who starts with ability bonuses earned by the honor of the player's previous character gets those points as extra AP. Starting money can be converted from gold pieces to an equal value in tael.

The DM can set the requirements for entering an Oriental class by listing the skills its members can use at 1st level. Oriental classes have so many special abilities, such as ki powers, that Eastern characters must spend their AP with great care; this reflects a layered society in which the young are expected to study without pause.

Most Oriental class skills can be handled like their Western counterparts: noble warriors learn similar skills everywhere, whether called rangers or samurai. Study times, effects on alignment tendency, chances with spells and so on are the same. Use this table for which category applies:

Oriental classWestern category
BarbarianFighter
BushiFighter (or thief for pickpocket skills)
KensaiFighter (kensai teachers demand total dedication, like monk masters)
MonkMonk
NinjaThief
SamuraiFighter or paladin
ShukenjaCleric
SoheiPaladin (fighter) or cleric
Wu jenMage
YakuzaThief

Eastern education rests on respect for elders and devotion to study. Learned masters teach every art, and any character may win a teacher over. Sohei, shukenja and some monk orders recruit eagerly; ninja and yakuza train only a few trusted associates. Those seeking wu jen skills must spend long periods alone in the wilderness, since Oriental wizards dislike civilization. All Oriental teachers use inventive tests and ordeals, which may become adventures.

Roll for family and birthrights normally. The DM should play the character's relatives carefully, since they always strongly influence a zero-level life: they may drag the character into their political schemes, or be poor and need help. Characters are expected to study their father's profession, and each failed attempt at another class's skill costs 1 honor point (zero-level characters only).

A zero-level character starts with honor equal to the family's but at once begins building a personal reputation. All the usual honor awards and penalties apply, plus these:

ActionPoints
Unquestioning obedience to master+3
Disobedience to any superior-2
Studying a skill from father's character class+1
Extreme devotion to parents+3
Dishonoring a superior-2
Gaining a peaceful proficiency+1
Pleasing someone of higher rank+1
Quarrel with other apprentices-1

Characters cannot combine Oriental skills with Western ones (the book says "gajin") without actually studying in both the West and the East.

Running Games for Zero-Level Characters

The DM has much more control when characters start at zero level. They depend entirely on their teachers, who can become the DM's voice, handing out quests or hints. By limiting which teachers are available, the DM controls which classes characters can become: a DM running a wilderness campaign need not forbid a courtly assassin outright, but simply provides no one to teach assassination.

Adventures must fit the characters too. Zero-level characters cannot win fierce battles and need training more than gold. Simple things like learning to hunt, fight or sail a ship can be exciting adventures. Their main goal is to develop as characters, so the story can be simple as long as it brings out personality, perhaps through moral dilemmas or problems that can be solved with the skills of one class or another. The characters will be eager to discover the world, and this period is a chance to introduce important NPCs and give the characters opinions about the great issues of the day. Those discoveries can keep them adventuring for many years.

Source: GA p.104. Rewritten in plain words.

GA closes with a set of short adventures. Some show off magic items, NPCs, monsters and places described elsewhere in the book; others are built to test players at particular levels. Some offer several ways to draw the player characters in, others just one. Some tell a story with a beginning, middle and end; others are a series of encounters, and making a story of them is up to the DM and the players.

Source: GA p.104-105. Rewritten in plain words; statistics as printed.

This adventure is for zero-level characters (see Running the Game: Zero-Level Characters). A sage named Erollson has agreed to take the player characters as apprentices. On their first day at his country house he asks them to stack hay for his prized horses while he goes to town. The barn catches fire, and the characters must escape and save as many horses as they can, putting whatever skills they have to new uses.

Strong, brutish types may try to drag horses out by force; others may pray for druid spells or clerical healing. How the characters save the horses, and themselves, decides what Erollson chooses to teach them. No outside help can come until the fire is out, since Erollson lives more than five miles from town.

Erollson

Erollson is a short man with a red beard fading to white. If his horses are saved he will not punish anyone for the fire, though he may tease them about it once a new barn is up and the matter is less painful.

AC10
MV12"
HD8

AbilitiesStr 10, Int 18, Wis 17, Dex 9, Con 11, Cha 14
THAC020
ALNG
SAtwo first-level druid spells per day; minor fields in Fauna and Supernatural & Unusual, major field in Humankind, special categories in Weapons & Strategy, Theology & Myth, Crime & Criminals, and Languages.

His special categories are printed as "Weapons & Strategy"; the zero-level rules (GA p.119) call the new category "Weapons & Warfare."

The Barn

Early in the morning Erollson takes the characters to the barn and tells them to stack hay in the loft. The hay lies in a pile with pitchforks beside it. He has locked the main doors, but there is a man-sized hole cut in one panel for going in and out. A few silver harness pieces hang on display; nothing else of interest is in sight.

Unknown to the characters, Erollson keeps a decanter of endless water for watering his animals, hidden under a secret panel in the horses' trough. Its command words are "clear" (a clear stream), "blue" (a fountain, range 5'), "white" (a foaming geyser, range 20') and "black" (stop). A hint on the stopper reads, "What color is the water?"

Seven horses live here: six magnificent warhorses named Wind, Steel, Blaze, Arrow, Lightning and River, and Whitey, a wise but stubborn mare. The barn is 100' long and 40' wide, and the stalls begin 20' from the door.

The Fire

The night before, when Erollson blew out the barn's lanterns, one kept smoldering and has now flared up again. During the characters' first two turns in the barn it sets the pitch-soaked beams alight. It is hidden in a feed stall, so the only warning comes from Whitey, who stamps and whinnies constantly. Then fire sweeps across the ceiling and runs along every beam while the horses kick and scream in their stalls.

Each round, every character and horse has a 10% cumulative chance of being struck by burning debris; characters are hit automatically after ten rounds. A hit does 1-8 points of damage from smoke and flaming cinders.

A character who uses a luck roll to cast precipitation (silver buckles from the horses' harness could serve as the material component) damps the fire enough to halve the chance of being hit while the spell lasts. Cloudburst would prevent all damage for its duration, but can be cast only with Insight. The fire can easily kill the horses. A character reduced to 0 hit points may survive by spending AP and will be found in the ashes later, unconscious but alive.

Saving the Horses

The panicking horses refuse to be led. Opening a stall takes a round, and then the horse must be got out:

  • Forcing a horse out takes a strength check with a +4 penalty (+2 for Whitey).
  • A character with horsemanship proficiency, perhaps gained by a luck roll, can try to coax a horse out with a wisdom check at a +3 bonus.
  • Whenever a character fails to command a horse, the frightened animal attacks with both hooves, using normal combat. One round later the character may try again.
  • Two successful checks are needed to bring a horse to the barn door.
  • Blindfolding a horse takes a round and the same strength or proficiency check as leading it, but afterward it follows its leader nervously.

At the door it takes one more round to lead a horse through the narrow human-sized opening, and only one can pass at a time. A horse that is not blindfolded is afraid to go through, needing two more strength or proficiency checks. The characters could instead open the main doors: a bend bars roll breaks the hinges, or a luck roll gives a thief's lock picking skill; plenty of loose wire lies on the floor for picks. With the main doors open, horses that are out of their stalls can easily be herded outside.

Most horses stamp and breathe hard once they reach safety. Whitey, like some fire-crazed animals, stubbornly tries to go back in. If the characters let her, she leads them to the trough and nuzzles the panel hiding the decanter. Used against the fire, it halves the chance of falling debris; or it can douse one character or horse and save that one from serious harm.

Aftermath

Erollson returns that evening. When he learns of the fire he tears at his beard and runs to his beloved horses. If they all died, he orders the characters out of his sight forever and refuses to teach them. If the horses were saved, he calms down and sees that the characters were not to blame. Recovering his decanter, he reflects that they have had a more realistic test of their talents than any teacher could devise.

His horses saw everything, so the sage talks with them by speak with animals. Erollson, the horses and the party discuss what omens the event holds and what training it suggests for each character. The DM plays Erollson and the horses and helps each player decide what to study. Raise each character's good/evil tendency by 1 point toward good for every hit point lost while rescuing horses.

Erollson will train the characters for the next several months, possibly longer. The DM may change his personality and fields of knowledge to suit the campaign.

Source: GA p.105-107. Rewritten in plain words; statistics as printed.

In this zero-level adventure the player characters are apprentices to Tharkun, a bright young wizard eager to put them through the same ordeals he suffered as a novice. The first test involves a wooden beam weighing 100 pounds. The students must find a way to hold it up off the ground using only their own powers and wits, and without using their hands. Any material spell components must be obtained in the city market, without using money.

To prepare them, Tharkun will teach any of these spells or cantrips: floating disc, message, detect magic, sleep, change, color, palm and distract.

A floating disc would lift the beam easily, but the spell needs mercury, which the characters must steal or earn. Clever characters may think of other ways to raise the beam; Tharkun accepts them, though with groans of surprise.

Tharkun

AbilitiesStr 10, Int 17, Wis 15, Dex 15, Con 12, Cha 11
AC9
MV12
HD6
hp14
#AT1
THAC019
SASpells
ALCG
Dmg1-4 (Dagger)

Spellbook: burning hands, charm person, detect magic, identify, magic missile, read magic, write, knock, levitate, strength, web, wizard lock, fireball, hold person, lightning bolt, slow, suggestion.

Tharkun is a harsh master but firmly believes in paying for a good day's work. If the characters raise the beam on their first try, they need not repay him for teaching them the spells. If they fail, they must work twice as long to earn their instruction points. To persuade them not to cheat him, Tharkun blasts down a large tree with a lightning bolt and tells them the last person who crossed him was turned into a tree like the one he just fried.

The Market

The characters come here if they need supplies or spell components. People of every sort buy and sell here: peasants with pigs and chickens under their arms stand beside merchants crying their racks of pottery. The characters at once notice a sign in pictures reading "Linneus, Barber, Apothecary and Doctor of Physic." The other stalls nearby are held by ten peasants selling animal furs, each with a purse of 50 sp, and two pottery merchants, each with a locked coin box holding 100 gp.

Robbing anyone costs the thief 2 points from both law/chaos and good/evil. A character caught stealing sets off an uproar, and 1d8 passersby chase the thief and hold him until the Town Constable arrives. Captured thieves are jailed for 1d4 days.

People at the market:

AC10
MV12
HD1/2
hp2
#AT1
Dmgunarmed combat rules
THAC020
ALN.

Town Constable (long sword and chain mail):

AbilitiesStr 16, Int 14, Wis 11, Dex 15, Con 12, Cha 14
AC4
MV9
HD5/F
hp38
#AT1
Dmg1d8 +1
THAC016
ALLG

Linneus the Barber

The characters should realize that only the barber, of everyone in the market, would have quicksilver. Linneus specializes in surgery but keeps an assortment of chemicals and sells mercury at 25 sp an ounce. He is fat and serious, and balances his medical knowledge with sound advice and a little sorcery. Asked for mercury for free, he refuses: his business is mending bodies, not charity. A magic mouth shouts "Stop, thief!" if anyone but Linneus takes something from his shelf, and the shouting always draws a crowd.

Tricking Linneus into handing over mercury costs 2 points from both law/chaos and good/evil. If the characters offer work in exchange, he gladly accepts and has plenty of jobs for them.

AbilitiesStr 9, Int 16, Wis 11, Dex 15, Con 12, Cha 15
AC10
MV12
HD3/MU
hp6

THAC020

ALLN
Spellbookcharm person, comprehend languages, friends, light, mending, read magic, write, forget, knock, magic mouth, shatter, strength.

Ghen the Barbarian

If the characters use magic in the market, there is a 35% chance that Ghen, a barbarian fighter, notices. He also turns up in any crowd the characters draw.

Ghen (spear and leather armor):

AbilitiesStr 17, Int 8, Wis 8, Dex 17, Con 14, Cha 9
AC5
MV12
HD3/F
hp21
#AT1
Dmg1-6 +1
THAC018
ALCN

Ghen has come from the lands of the Tiger Nomads to trade furs for iron weapons. All through his journey he has grown more and more shocked at how sorcery, which his tribe hates, fills the whole civilized world. If he sees the characters casting spells, he confronts them: "No, no, you fools. Sorcery is evil! You do not know the danger of your actions!"

He is 7 feet tall, muscular and fierce-looking. The only way to avoid a fight is for every character to agree with everything he says and then move away; the rest of the crowd backs off, wanting nothing to do with such a warrior. If the characters will not humor him, he wades in with fists swinging. When the constable comes to stop the fight, Ghen knocks him out with one blow. If the characters run, Ghen does not follow; otherwise the fight goes on until Ghen or the characters are out cold.

Source: GA p.107-109. Rewritten in plain words; statistics as printed.

This adventure is for three or four player characters of 4th-5th level. For a much stronger or weaker party, adjust the number and statistics of the opposition.

The Hook

On an ocean voyage, the characters stop at a small island for supplies. Its people are tribal fishermen, simple in their ways and friendly to strangers. In passing conversation the characters hear that a rich merchant ship went down in a storm several years ago at a nearby uninhabited atoll. Oddly, the fishermen have no interest in finding the wreck or salvaging anything from it.

Soon after, a young woman asks for the characters' help. Her father captained the lost ship, she says, and she and her three brothers want to recover some family heirlooms from the wreck, valuable for sentiment rather than money. The fishermen will not help them. Will the characters?

The woman calls herself Bella and does the talking; she introduces her companions as her brothers Stront, Tethus and Torok. When they heard of their father's death, she explains, they came to the islands hoping to find where his ship sank. The locals told them readily enough where the wreck lies but refused to help, believing that what the sea takes, the sea should keep.

If the characters agree, Bella and her "brothers" come aboard, each with a light pack of belongings. Once under way, Bella gives the captain a course to a group of tiny coral atolls ringed by vicious reefs. She says, and any experienced sailor agrees, that it is suicide to approach her father's resting place in anything larger than a ship's 12' longboat.

The Truth

There is only a grain of truth in Bella's story. The four are related only by trade and purpose: they are thieves who have heard rumors of a rich treasure ship wrecked on a coral atoll, and its captain was no relation to any of them. Unwilling to walk into danger alone, they decided to find a trusting crew to take them there and, if possible, clear the wreck of anything dangerous.

If the characters die in the attempt, no great loss: the thieves will take what they can and escape in the longboat, slipping through the reefs where a bigger ship cannot follow. If the characters survive and bring up anything of value, the thieves mean to kill them at the first good chance and steal the longboat, or the characters' ship if they are sure they can get away with it.

Bella:

AbilitiesStr 12, Int 13, Wis 10, Con 15, Dex 17, Cha 15
AC10
MV12"
T7
hp33
#AT1
Dmgby weapon type
SAbackstab
ALCE. Thief abilities: PP 60%, OL 52%, FT 50%, MS 55%, HS 43%, HN 25%, CW 94%, RL 35%.

Stront:

AbilitiesStr 18, Int 10, Wis 8, Con 15, Dex 13, Cha 9
AC10
MV12"
T5
hp25
#AT1
Dmgby weapon type
SAbackstab
ALCN. Thief abilities: PP 50%, OL 42%, FT 40%, MS 40%, HS 31%, HN 20%, CW 90%, RL 25%.

Tethus:

AbilitiesStr 9, Int 11, Wis 10, Con 10, Dex 13, Cha 13
AC10
MV12"
T5
hp20
#AT1
Dmgby weapon type
SAbackstab
ALCN. Thief abilities: PP 50%, OL 42%, FT 40%, MS 40%, HS 31%, HN 20%, CW 90%, RL 25%.

Torok:

AbilitiesStr 10, Int 9, Wis 8, Con 10, Dex 12, Cha 10
AC10
Move12"
T4
hp18
#AT1
Dmgby weapon type
SAbackstab
ALCN. Thief abilities: PP 45%, OL 37%, FT 35%, MS 33%, HS 25%, HN 15%, CW 88%, RL 20%.

None of the four carries weapons openly; their gear is hidden in their packs. Bella's pack holds a short sword, a hand axe, 6 darts, and a potion of water breathing she bought before the voyage. She tells no one about the potion, not even her partners; it is her secret reserve if she must do any salvage herself. Torok's pack holds a light crossbow, two daggers and six darts. Each of the others has a short sword, two daggers and a dozen darts. All carry lockpicks and other tools of the trade hidden in their packs and on their persons.

The four play their parts well. Bella is plainly the spokesperson, but the others can answer questions about their background and their "father" convincingly. Around the characters they try to seem harmless and even a little incompetent, moving almost clumsily to hide the fluid grace they show on the job, and Stront does nothing to reveal his unusual strength.

The Atoll

The island is made entirely of coral, just 50 yards across with a shallow central lagoon, and no more than 10 feet above high tide at its highest point. Around it runs a coral reef whose jagged top lies only inches below the breaking waves. The only ways through are a few channels no more than 10 feet wide, and even there the waves threaten to hurl a small boat onto the razor-sharp coral. Inside the reef, which acts as a breakwater, the water is calm and clear, full of brightly colored fish.

Part of the wreck can be seen from outside the reef: the front quarter of a fairly large galleon shows above water, smashed against the coral of the atoll itself, and farther out the tip of a broken mast breaks the surface. What happened is obvious: a storm drove the ship right over the reef, tearing its bottom out, and it sank quickly in the inner waters. Bella adds that, from what she has heard, the ship broke in two; the front section is partly aground on the atoll and the rest lies in deeper water, still inside the reef.

Bella points out that only a small ship's boat can reach the wreck, and it can carry no more than eight people across the reef. She and her "brothers" insist on going, since it is their father's ship, which leaves room for four characters. (One person with light gear weighs about as much as 2,000 gp, so if the thieves kill the four characters with them, they can expect to carry off 8,000 gp weight of treasure.)

Crossing the reef takes two rounds, with a 10% chance each round of running aground on the coral; the DM should make it seem far more dangerous. If a character with the secondary skill of fisher or sailor is at the helm, the chance drops to 5% a round, though it should still seem very dangerous.

The coral is hideously sharp. Walking on it barefoot or in footwear with soles weaker than leather does 1-3 points of damage. Anyone who falls on it, in a fight for example, has a 50% chance of taking 1-4 points from punctures and scrapes. Coral wounds are very painful and have a 50% chance of becoming infected unless treated promptly.

The Bow

The bow is partly aground and can be entered from shore without swimming. The state of the hull shows how violent the storm was, and that the wreck has lain here for several years. The ship is bow-high and lying partly on its port side, so the decks tilt at strange angles. The air inside is heavy and reeks of decay. The forward compartments, or what is left of them, are a chaos of wreckage. Several human skeletons lie there, most with broken bones showing that the storm and the wreck killed them, not drowning. Charts and papers have long since rotted, but a plaque broken loose from a bulkhead names the ship "The Outward Bound, Free Trader."

The rearmost part of the bow section is under water, but the water is clear enough to see that the bulkhead between the forward compartments and the hold has been smashed in. The load in the hold seems to have shifted forward and broken through; since the ship broke apart right at the hold, a shifting cargo may have been what finally broke its back.

In about 3 feet of water, in a rear corner, something shines dully: a platinum ingot weighing 200 gp and worth 1,000 gp, stamped with the mark of the treasury of the Prelacy of Almor. When it sank, "The Outward Bound" was carrying the loot from a daring raid on Almor's treasure rooms. Bella and her partners know this, which is why they want the ship, but they deny any knowledge of it if asked.

Jaws among the Coral

The rear two-thirds of the ship lies under 40 feet of water, about 50 feet offshore. Nine more platinum ingots like the first (200 gp weight, 1,000 gp value) are scattered on the coral slopes between the bow and the rest of the ship. Someone must dive for them. The thieves volunteer at once, but so eagerly that the characters will probably grow suspicious and do it themselves, which is just what the thieves want.

  • A character of average constitution can hold his or her breath for two rounds while working under water; with constitution 15 or more, three rounds.
  • Swimming down to the ingots takes about three segments, assuming the character can swim, and the same to come back up without a load.
  • A character with strength 12 or more can swim up carrying one ingot, and only one, taking six segments. With strength 11 or less, a character cannot swim up with an ingot.
  • Without magical help, characters working under water can wear no metal armor and can carry only the lightest weapons.

Two giant moray eels live in cracks in the coral. Each time a character dives to look at or retrieve ingots, there is a 25% chance an eel attacks. They usually bite once and hold on, trying to keep their prey under water until it drowns. A character who stays down longer than he can hold his breath drowns in 1d6+2 rounds. A trapped character can tear the eel loose from its grip on the rock by rolling under his strength on 5d6, which takes a whole round in which he can do nothing else. An eel pulled loose usually lets go and goes back to its lair to wait for easier prey. A dead eel pulls easily from the coral, but even in death its jaws stay locked in the victim's flesh and must be pried open.

Eels (2):

AC6
MV//9"
HD5
hp20
#AT1
Dmg3d6
THAC015
SAhold victim under water until it drowns
ALN.

Sea Sprites

The rest of the wreck is home to a family of eight sea sprites. As is their way, they believe that what the sea has taken should stay with the sea, and they try to stop any salvage. They will not willingly leave the wreck, preferring to wait inside and ambush anyone who enters. Before they appear, two barracudas under their orders attack anyone approaching the sunken stern.

Barracuda (2):

AC6
MV//30"
HD3
hp15
#AT1
Dmg2d4
THAC016
ALN.

Sea sprites (8):

AC6
MV6"//24"
HD1
hp5
#AT1
Dmg1-4
THAC017
SAweapons tipped with sleep potion, can cast slow spell three times per day at 5th level of ability
ALCN.

If the characters try to talk, the sprites explain that they are only "protecting the sea's property." If the intruders leave things as they are, the sprites have no quarrel with them and let them go unharmed.

The broken cargo hold holds 20 more platinum ingots. A chest in the captain's cabin at the stern contains a broadsword +1 and a mace +2, both so badly rusted that their nature is hidden; a weaponsmith can make them usable. The chest also holds the ship's log, wrapped in oiled leather and partly protected from the sea. It confirms that "The Outward Bound" was at times a pirate ship and that its cargo was stolen from the Prelacy of Almor.

Conclusion: The Danger Above

The thieves pick the best moment to kill the characters, perhaps as they surface exhausted from the dangers below, and make off with as much treasure as they can. They are sly and will not show their hand too soon; if a character comes back to the boat badly hurt, they might "help him along" and make his death look like the result of his wounds. If they get away with the boat, they escape through small gaps in the reefs. If the characters are foolish enough to follow in their larger ship, there is a 50% chance per turn of pursuit that it runs aground on the coral.

The treasure in the wreck may seem excessive, but it is under water, and the characters are unlikely to carry off more than a fraction of it. If they come back later, better equipped, they may find that another storm has wiped out every trace of the wreck.

pages.name: The Entrance to the Valley of the Mage

text.content:
Source: GA p.109-111. Rewritten in plain words; statistics as printed.

This adventure is for three or four characters of 5th-6th level. If the characters are to meet the Mage of the Valley himself, they will probably need to be more numerous or more powerful.

Those who seek the Valley of the Mage climb down into a bleak, barren valley. A permanent fog hangs over it, and the wind sounds like the voices of the restless dead. Scrubby grass and moss are the only signs of life.

Why the characters are here is up to the DM: they might be out to kill the Black One, the Mage of the Valley; on a thieving mission for valuable magic items known to be here; or they might stumble into the valley by accident. Once inside, the following happens.

The Gallows

Five turns after entering the valley, the characters see a gallows with six skeletons hanging from it, hands tied, dangling limp. When a character comes close, the skeletons seem to come alive, and magic mouth spells say: "Go back! There is nothing for you here! We displeased the Mage of the Valley, and you can see the result! Go back, and keep your necks!" The skeletons are not undead and, apart from the magic mouths, carry no enchantment.

If the characters try to cut the skeletons down, an invisible juju zombie guarding the gallows attacks, with surprise unless it was detected earlier. It was once an adventurer who angered the Mage and was slain by an energy drain spell; its punishment after death is to guard the gallows, and it will not willingly leave. If the characters retreat, it chases them until they are 100 feet from the gallows.

Invisible juju zombie:

AC6
MV9"
HD3+12
hp35
#AT1
Dmg3-12
SANil
SDhit only by +1 or better weapons, piercing or blunt weapon attacks do ½ damage, it is unaffected by mind-affecting magic or poison, electricity, magic missiles, death or cold-based spells, it takes ½ damage from fire, is turned as spectre
THAC013
ALNE.

Deeper in the valley the characters find broken bones and skulls underfoot, with broken, rusted weapons, rotted backpacks and other signs of a battle. The Mage had these scattered to make sure no one without good reason would come into the valley.

The Frog

Three turns past the gallows, an ordinary frog hops out from behind a rock and says: "Stop! Go back! I was once a noble paladin, until the Mage of the Valley became angered with me, and changed my form to this! Go back, and consider yourselves lucky that you can still leave!"

The frog radiates magic if checked, but it cannot be turned back into a paladin: the Mage simply put a magic mouth on an ordinary frog to fool people. In every other way it is just a frog, with no real attacks.

The Gnome Illusionists

While the characters deal with the frog, several gnome spellcasters learn they are here. These illusionists are the valley's outer guards. They have worked together for years and combine their spells expertly into truly frightening illusions with sight and sound.

Carl Sneakystuff:

AC8 (dexterity bonus)
MV12"
I7
HD7
hp22
#AT1
Dmgby weapon type (staff sling, dart, dagger)
AbilitiesStr 11, Int 17, Wis 10, Dex 16, Con 8, Cha 11
THAC019
ALCN
SASpells: 4-1st, 3-2nd, 2-3rd, 1-4th.

Piotr Prestochango:

AC7 (dexterity bonus)
MV12"
I5
HD5
hp16
#AT1
Dmgby weapon type (staff, dagger, dart)
AbilitiesStr 10, Int 18, Wis 9, Dex 17, Con 12, Cha 8
THAC020
ALN
SASpells: 4-1st, 2-2nd, 1-3rd.

Piotr's class and level is read from the page image as "I 5"; the scan's text reads "15".

Tatanya Stickyfingers:

AC7 (leather and dexterity bonus)
MV12"
I4/T 7
HD4/7
hp28
#AT1
Dmgby weapon type (short bow, short sword, dagger)
AbilitiesStr 12, Int 16, Wis 12, Dex 17, Con 13, Cha 14
THAC019
ALN
SASpells: 3-1st, 2-2nd, triple damage from back stab
SDspells.

Working together they cast very convincing illusions: one casts phantasmal force while another adds an audible glamer. The DM should have the characters save vs. spells twice, once to disbelieve each part of the illusion. A favorite trick is to conjure the image of a robed, hooded man and use ventriloquism to make it speak. It plays the Mage of the Valley, asking intruders what they want, scaring them with dire threats, and making it clear they are not welcome.

If the illusory "Mage" or other illusions are attacked, Tatanya slips behind the characters to pick a pocket or two. She loves magic items and tries to steal any that are not in use. If she feels she must, she backstabs at every chance. She is almost impossible to spot, wearing an elven cloak and boots and with improved invisibility cast on her.

The Valley Elves

Once past the gnomes, the characters meet the next guards 1d8 turns later, as arrows rain down from hidden positions. An elf or ranger may spot a hidden guard: the chance is 5% per level of the one looking.

Valley elf fighters (7):

AC5
MV9"
HD5
hp49, 45, 41, 38, 37, 34, 33
#AT1
Dmgby weapon type (long bow, long sword, dagger)
THAC016
ALCN
SA+1 to hit with bow and sword
SD90% resistance to sleep and charm.

These elves belong to the Valley Militia, ordered to let in only those the Mage has authorized. They wear elven chain mail and elven cloaks, making them very hard to see in the constant fog. If the characters kill four or more, the rest scatter back to their base in the valley. Their leader, Lemin Kainin, wears a golden circlet; if pursued, he calls up a skeleton in rusty plate mail and sets it on the characters, hoping they will think it a skeletal warrior.

Skeleton:

AC4 (rusty plate mail)
MV7"
HD1
hp8
#AT1
Dmg1-6
THAC019
ALN
SAnil
SDsharp weapons do 1/2 damage, amulet of proof against turning (turns as a Spectre)

Captured elves will not willingly talk. Forced by magic or otherwise, they turn out to know little about the Mage: only that he is a man of magic with the power to keep their valley safe. Despite their alignment they are fanatically loyal to him and do whatever he orders.

Anyone who gets past these first encounters is funneled by the shape of the valley to the Office of the First Protector.

The Office of the First Protector

From outside, the building looks like a small temple with a large statue of a man in front. Characters who look at the statue and fail a save vs. spells think it is a stone golem. It is really harmless and non-magical; a hidden gnome spellcaster is making it seem a golem. Attacking it only wastes spells and breaks weapons: any weapon that strikes it must save vs. crushing blow or break.

Room 1. An airy, clean room. Behind a counter, three pretty valley elf women smile and ask, "What can we do for you, please?" They are not what they seem. Sharlene and Elspeth are 8th level thieves; Marinian is a 6th level magic-user/6th level thief. They will not attack without cause but defend themselves if attacked. If they can tell the characters are not authorized to be in the valley, Marinian casts suggestion to have them wait there, and hold person on anyone who saves against the suggestion. Characters who fail either save are handed over to the Mage at once to explain their presence in his valley.

Sharlene and Elspeth:

AC5 (elven chain)
MV12"
T8
HD8
hp41, 40
#AT1
Dmgby weapon type (short bow, long sword, dagger)
AbilitiesStr 15, Int 13, Wis 11, Dex 14, Con 16, Cha 17
THAC019
ALLE, NE
SAtriple damage from back stab, +1 to hit with bow and sword
SD90% immunity to charm and sleep, normal thief abilities

The two are sisters and look much alike. They cheerfully flirt with male characters if it helps distract them. Neither carries treasure.

Marinian:

AC5 (elven chain)
MV12"
MU6/T 6
HD6/ 6
hp44
#AT1
Dmgby weapon type (long sword, long bow, dagger)
AbilitiesStr 16, Int 16, Wis 10, Dex 15, Con 12, Cha 13
THAC019
ALLE
SAtriple damage from back stab, +1 with sword or bow, Spells: 4-1st, 2-2nd, 2-3rd
SD90% resistance to sleep and charm, normal thief abilities.

Marinian outranks the others here and gives them any orders needed. She is ruthless and will do anything she can to keep intruders out of the valley. She owns a flame tongue long sword and a necklace of magic missiles.

Room 2. The room is full of papers. In the middle sits a skeleton, and what looks like a beholder floats just above it. The papers include detailed descriptions of the valley, all false, showing paths that lead to death traps of one kind or another. The "beholder" is a gas spore. The regular occupants know what it is and take care not to touch it; it is there so that snoops and thieves, two of the Mage's pet hates, will be scared off or killed. Most of the papers are files on enemies of the Mage or of the valley folk, and at the DM's option they may include very complete files on the characters.

Gas spore:

AC9
MVnil
HD1
hp1
#AT1
Dmgspecial
THAC019
ALN
SAtouch-infestation
SDexplosion for 6- 36 points damage when hit.

Room 3. Where Sharlene, Elspeth and Marinian sleep. Clothes and cosmetics lie about, and pictures of handsome, scantily clad elven and human men are pinned to the walls. A search turns up 3,800 gp in all, a dagger of venom, a manual in Elvish on assassination, and Marinian's spellbook, containing feather fall, charm person, magic missile, read magic, forget, invisibility, suggestion and hold person, with enough material components to cast each spell ten times.

Room 4. Exercise equipment, with several books in Elvish, Gnomish and Common on building strength or dexterity, and dummies of various races with their weak points marked in red. One dummy is animated to give the three women real combat practice; when a character or anyone else who does not normally use the room approaches, it rises and attacks. Its hits feel real, but when it has taken its full 24 points of damage it stops moving and the wounds stop hurting. Any thieves' or assassins' guild, or any teacher of fighting, would pay 15,000 gp for it.

Training dummy:

AC5
MV12"
HD3
hp24
#AT1
Dmgspecial
THAC016
ALN
SAnil
SDnil.

Room 5. Tysiln San's room. She is not in, but her things are scattered about: many sheer dresses, worth 500 gp each to any elven or human woman, and jewelry worth 8,089 gp in all. If anything is taken from here while she lives, a magic mouth appears on the wall and shouts "Thieves! Thieves! Thieves!" until she arrives, help comes, or the items are put back.

Courtyard. The courtyard looks out over the Valley of the Mage. Farms and fields can be seen in the distance, and for the first time since entering the valley the air is clear of fog.

Tysiln San waits here (see Hall of Heroes: Tysiln San). If the noise of fighting has warned her, she is ready for the characters; otherwise she is dozing in the sun in her glassteel mirrored sunglasses. She wears jewelry worth 2,000 gp. If the characters catch her by surprise she is smiling and friendly, and not necessarily as an act: she feels rather alone in the valley, where apart from the Mage and his rare visitors she is not much welcomed.

Beside her stands a stone golem with invisibility cast on it. Unless the characters save vs. spells or attack her, they will not know it is there. Its orders are to protect her, and any attack on her sets it in motion.

Stone golem:

AC5
MV9"
hp60
#AT1
Dmg3-24
THAC09
ALN
SAslow spell
SDhit only by +2 magic weapons, immunity to most spells.

Source: GA p.111-113. Rewritten in plain words; statistics as printed.

This adventure is for three to six characters of 3rd-6th level. A small party should be near the top of that range; a larger one may survive with less power.

The Summons

The party is in the Free City of Greyhawk looking for work. One day a messenger comes to their inn, asks for the group's leader, presses a paper into his or her hands, and asks for a tip. The paper reads: "Bold ones! Your reputation for bravery and skill has preceded you! Come to the headquarters of the Traders' Union, if you wish to learn something of advantage." It is unsigned, but the seal of the Traders' Union at the bottom vouches for it. If the messenger boy is still waiting for his tip, he will guide the group there.

The Traders' Union

The building stands in a respectable part of the city, guarded by five 6th level fighters. They are courteous but let no one in without proper authorization. If the boy is with the party, the guards take his word; if not, the sealed letter gets the characters in.

Inside, the Union is busy and crowded, with members of every race in Greyhawk haggling over bales of goods. The guards escorting the characters are always polite but tolerate no idle sightseeing and no theft. Magic mouth spells in every room catch anyone who tries to steal, and the thief is made to pay compensation.

The characters are led through the building to an upper floor, where a respectable-looking dwarf, an incredibly old elf and several prosperous-looking humans wait. The oldest human rises, welcomes them, and asks them to sit. When all are settled he begins:

"My good sirs (and/or ladies), welcome to the humble headquarters of the Traders' Union of the City of Greyhawk. My name is Strimtin Cannasay, and these good merchants with me help to keep the Union free, respected, and honest. We called you in for your, well, let us say, expertise in certain matters with which we are not able to deal.

"The Master of the Traders' Union, Ren o' the Star, has disappeared. We have determined that he was captured by certain unsavory people with whom he was wont to play at games of chance. We believe that his kidnappers wish to extort money from him. We know where he is being held, and we want you to get him back to us."

Asked how they know where Ren is held, Strimtin only grins and says, "Professional secret." The traders provide a guide to the area and to the exact house.

What the Traders Are Not Saying

The traders know far more than they tell. The Union itself approved Ren's kidnapping, as a way to frighten him into giving up or cutting back his gambling (see Hall of Heroes: Ren o' the Star). They dislike the way his losses force him to treat his customers, and know his behavior reflects badly on all of them. None of them will admit any part in it. The whole affair was arranged through go-betweens, so the kidnappers do not even know who really hired them.

Ren was snatched neatly off the street, but things soon went wrong. Drunk on the power of holding a rich and powerful merchant at their mercy, the kidnappers began making absurd demands. Instead of simply playing out the charade they were paid for, to scare Ren away from the gaming tables, they asked a ransom of 100,000 gp and safe passage out of Greyhawk.

The traders, understandably upset, just want their colleague back, and if the kidnappers are silenced for good, so much the better. The Union will pay the characters' expenses plus a reasonable reward, and they may keep whatever they take from the kidnappers.

At last a gang of ragged youths blocks the way. "Ten coppers apiece to pass, strangers. Nobody goes through Owlbear's turf without paying Owlbear's toll!" sneers the leader, while the rest swing knives, daggers and clubs.

This setting can be used in any campaign, with any number of characters of any level; the DM decides how dangerous each situation is. To play the optional encounters, four to six players with characters of 3rd-7th level are best.

Always seeking fame and fortune, the characters have come to the city of Elredd on the Wild Coast for its reputation for adventure and fast money. The House of Cards is a gambling den with a bar, but no rooms to rent. It is known for its tough customers and the large sums gamblers claim to have won there; anyone with a brave heart and a little luck can hope to win a small fortune in a night. Rumor says the House has dealings with the local Thieves' Guild, but outsiders do not know what they are. The Guild is powerful in Elredd, and nobody asks too many questions.

The Salesman

Before the characters go in, a shifty-looking salesman, really a thief, stops them in the street. He offers them the Luck Ring of the Wild Coast, which he claims is enchanted to sway dice rolled in the hand that wears it. He asks 5,000 gp but can be talked down within reason, to 3,000 gp at the lowest. As he leaves there is an 80% chance he tries to pick the pocket of a random character. His chance is 40%, minus 5% for each level of the character above 3rd.

The thieves act as secret guards, mingling unnoticed with the customers and striking only when there is trouble. They never bother or rob customers without Garon's permission, which he seldom gives.

The fighter henchman is a half-orc who works as the bouncer. He is doubly proficient in boxing and wears chain mail gauntlets, but carries a long sword for serious fighting. Any customer who starts trouble is likely to be thrown out. The half-orc is rather dull and wholly loyal to Garon, and will fight to the death for him.

The Building

Main floor. Most of it is the spacious common room. Along one side is the bar, selling ale (1 sp a pint) and rum (2 sp a shot). Behind the bar a door leads to a storeroom and a stair to the second floor. Beside the bar is an iron-barred window where the clerk sits to pay winners, with a loaded crossbow and spare bolts always at hand. The middle of the room holds four gambling tables and six customer tables. The 0 level staff are the clerk, the bartender, three serving maids, and a dealer (dice or cards) at each gambling table.

The House opens in early evening. By nightfall the common room holds 3d10+30 gamblers, drinkers, rogues and mercenaries. At first light, when most customers have gone home or passed out, the half-orc clears out the rest and locks the doors.

Second floor. Quarters for Garon's henchman and followers. Each door is double-locked and trapped, usually with an arrow trap. A hidden compartment in each room holds 50-500 gp and 0-3 pieces of jewelry. The twelfth and last room is also trapped and holds the stair to the third floor.

Third floor. A small maze of winding corridors. Somewhere in it is a secret door into Garon's room, protected by two arrow traps and two gas traps, one causing nausea (as stinking cloud) and one sleep (as sleep). Only Garon can switch all four traps on and off at will. A secret compartment in the room holds 3,500 gp and four pieces of jewelry. Garon is here 20% of the time in the morning or daytime and 50% in the evening and night; otherwise he is in town (75%) or in disguise in the common room (25%).

Gambling at the Tables

Each dealer's table offers a different game. Where it matters, a dealer has three levels of gambling proficiency (each level of gambling proficiency costs one proficiency slot). The minimum bet in every game is 10 gp and the maximum 50 gp, and all bets are placed before dice are rolled or cards dealt. Winners get signed notes to take to the clerk. No character is paid more than 2,000 gp in one night, so a lucky gambler may have to come back the next evening to collect the rest.

  • Table 1, Dragon Cards: a card game pitting an army of knights (the player's hand) against a red dragon (the dealer's hand). Both sides roll 1d20, and the higher score wins. A character with gambling proficiency adds +1 per level. The player chooses which dragon to challenge: a young dragon adds +6 in total to the dealer's roll and pays 2:1; an adult dragon adds +10 and pays 5:1; an ancient dragon adds +14 and pays 10:1.
  • Table 2, In Between: the bettor rolls percentile dice twice for two numbers, then tries to roll a third number that falls between them.
  • Table 3, Two and Three: the dealer rolls 1d20 and the player rolls 5d4; the higher total wins, ties going to the dealer. Pays 2:1.
  • Table 4, Dice Racing: each player rolls one six-sided die at a time, trying to reach 25 before the others. The highest roll each round gets +1. The dealer gets +1 on every roll, plus the +1 bonus when he has the highest roll of the round.
  • Tables 5-10, Card Games: of these other tables, one has card players for every ten customers in the room, with 2-5 customers playing at each, usually a kind of poker. A character may join an existing game of NPCs with a positive reaction check, or start a new game with other characters. Each random NPC poker player has wisdom 3d4+6 and 0-3 levels of gambling proficiency. To settle a hand, each player rolls 1d6 and adds wisdom and +1 per level of gambling proficiency. Bets are made and raised until a final amount is reached; then the scores are revealed and the highest wins.

The book says "Of the five other tables" for Tables 5-10, which would be six tables.

Optional Encounter 1: Raiders of the Law

A murder in a nearby street sets off a raid by 23 city watchmen: 2nd level mercenaries led by a lieutenant (4th level fighter), all in chain mail with short swords used at +1 to hit. At first the watchmen strike to subdue, but if one of them is killed they do full damage to everyone who does not surrender.

If the watch is beaten, reinforcements arrive in one turn: a lieutenant (5th level fighter), two sergeants (3rd level fighters) and 20 watchmen (1st level fighters). Every customer found in the House is arrested, and the lieutenant tells the staff that Garon must appear in court in four days. Anyone who resists is dealt with severely.

Anyone who tries to damage or rob the House in the confusion is attacked by Garon's henchman and followers. Prisoners taken by the watch are jailed for 2-5 days, with an 8% chance per day of catching a disease and a 10% chance per day of parasitic infestation.

Source: GA p.20 (Monsters of Greyhawk). Rewritten in plain words.

The monsters in the Greyhawk Monsters and Avatars compendium are found near the city of Greyhawk, and sometimes in it. The area has so many strange creatures because of a craze that gripped the city several hundred years ago, when everyone seemed to want mated pairs of unusual animals. There was a huge market in expensive pairs of rare and often dangerous creatures, and the trade was big business.

Too often the new owners did not know how to care for them. Many were set free and others escaped into the wilds around the city, where they thrived and bred. That is why creatures normally found only in the Crystalmist Mountains or the Plains of the Paynims turn up near Greyhawk.

There is now, of course, a law against bringing mated pairs of any creature into the Greyhawk area, and strangers are always astonished to see their male and female donkeys killed before their eyes right outside the city gates. Such measures are rather like locking the barn door after the horse has gone: countless unusual creatures flourish around Greyhawk.

New Headings

Three headings in the monster entries may be unfamiliar to players of the first edition game. Each is explained more fully in the second edition rules.

  • Reaction Modifier guides the DM in deciding a creature's first reaction. Roll 2d10 and add (or sometimes subtract) the modifier. The higher the total, the less aggressive the creature; a low total means it acts more aggressively.
  • Size is how big or small the creature is. First edition players can treat Tiny creatures as Small, and Huge and Gargantuan creatures as Large.
  • Morale measures how likely a creature is to stand its ground against danger, hardship or overwhelming odds. Roll 2d10: if the total is less than or equal to the number in parentheses, the creature stands firm. If higher, it might surrender, flee or do whatever else the DM thinks fitting.

The compendium holds the thirteen monsters of GA p.20-34 and the avatars of the eleven deities in Deities.

Source: GA p.51 (Magical Spells). Rewritten in plain words.

It is common knowledge across all the planes that the spellcasters of Oerth are the most powerful in all the multiverse, and every one of the greatest has at some time lived in the city of Greyhawk. GA presents a selection of their little-known but very useful spells, taking care to give the most useful ones without giving away the whole store. There are no 8th or 9th level spells, because those were too well guarded for even this powerful scribe to obtain, and spells such as Instant Stripping and Gelatinous Cube Transformation to Edible Gel were left out as too obscure even for the most curious spell crafter.

Because their makers lived in Greyhawk, a highly magical town, all these spells may be seen in use in and out of the city. Scrolls of them turn up in all the best treasure hoards, and strange wands and rings often hold them ready for instant use.

The Greyhawk Spells compendium holds the 106 wizards' spells, given generic names and grouped by theme, and the 12 cleric spells of the deities (see Deities). GA Appendix 2 (p.127-128) lists the wizards' spells by level.

Source: GA p.73 (Magical Items of Greyhawk). Rewritten in plain words.

Every magic item from the Flanaess in GA is named for the region it came from, because these items were not made for general use by mercenaries and adventurers (that is, player characters). Some were designed by magic-users who sold them for profit, but most were made for a particular purpose, and only by chance, diplomacy or combat does such an item pass from its maker to an unintended, and sometimes unwanted, owner. Only fairly recent and well-guarded items are still in their makers' hands.

Player characters usually find an item in its place of origin, though well-traveled items are not uncommon and can bring surprises of their own. No item is limited to the area whose name it bears, but often an item will not work elsewhere, or is of little use there; examples are the Cloak of the Hellfurnaces and the Medegian Bracelet of Lost Ships.

Each entry gives the experience points awarded to a character who keeps the item and its sale value in gold pieces. Class limits are abbreviated C (clerics), F (fighters), M (magic-users) and T (thieves); any subclass may use items limited to its main class.

The 97 items are in the Greyhawk Magic Items compendium.
